01-intake.collateral-information.s: When to involve parents, partners, family or other providers at intake, how to get valid consent, what to ask, and how to weigh reports that disagree, for children and adults.
01-intake.collateral-information.when: The client is a child or adolescent, insight or recall is limited, adult ADHD is in question, risk is a concern, or other providers hold relevant information.
01-intake.collateral-information.b: Collateral information from parents, partners, teachers or other clinicians fills gaps the client cannot fill, such as childhood behavior, how a problem looks from outside, or recent risk. Decide what question the informant can answer, get the client's informed permission (or the legally required permission for a minor), and treat disagreement between informants as information about context, not as a contest over who is right.
src: Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 Assessment to obtain a diagnosis and initial case formulation
DIVA-Site § About DIVA-5; Instructions for DIVA-5
HHS-45CFR164 § 164.502(g) Personal representatives; 164.508(c) Authorization core elements; 164.510(b) Involvement in care

01-intake.first-session-structure.s: The aims and running order of the first CBT contact, from consent and confidentiality through risk screen, assessment and goals to an agreed next step and feedback.
01-intake.first-session-structure.when: You are about to meet a new client for the first time, or planning how to run an evaluation or first therapy session.
01-intake.first-session-structure.b: The first contact has four jobs: obtain informed consent (including the limits of confidentiality), understand the problem well enough to screen risk and judge whether cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) fits, give the client a first taste of structured, collaborative CBT, and end with hope and a clear next step. Many services split this into an evaluation session followed by a first therapy session [Beck-2021]. Whatever the format, consent and the risk screen come before depth.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 5 The Evaluation Session; Ch. 6 The First Therapy Session; Ch. 11 Problems in Structuring Sessions
Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 Elements of the case formulation approach (pretreatment phase)

01-intake.goals-and-expectations.s: How to turn hopes into shared, concrete therapy goals, check what the client expects from therapy, honor preferences, and gauge motivation and readiness at intake.
01-intake.goals-and-expectations.when: You have a picture of the problem and need agreed goals and a realistic shared expectation of therapy before planning treatment.
01-intake.goals-and-expectations.b: Goals the client and therapist agree on, a hopeful but realistic expectation of what therapy will do, and a treatment that respects the client's preferences all predict better outcomes. At intake, ask what the client hopes will change, translate it into concrete goals in their words, ask what they expect therapy to involve, and check how ready they feel to act.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Problems in Structuring Sessions (Engaging the client)

01-intake.history-taking.s: What to ask about psychiatric, medical, medication, substance, family, developmental, social, cultural and trauma history and strengths, with screening questions and how to prioritize when time is short.
01-intake.history-taking.when: You have the presenting problem and need the background that shapes diagnosis, risk, formulation and treatment choice.
01-intake.history-taking.b: History tells you whether something other than the presenting problem must be treated or ruled out first (a medical cause, a substance, a past manic episode, current danger), and it supplies the predisposing and protective factors for the formulation. Cover every domain briefly at intake, go deeper only where the answer changes a decision, and always ask about strengths.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Principle 1 Levels of conceptualization; Principle 3 Strengths

01-intake.intake-record-checklist.s: The complete, grouped checklist of what a CBT intake record should contain, with why each item matters, for clinicians auditing notes and for designers of intake forms and tools.
01-intake.intake-record-checklist.when: You are writing or auditing an intake record, building an intake form or template, or designing a tool that captures intake information.
01-intake.intake-record-checklist.b: A complete intake record lets another clinician pick up the case safely: who the client is, what was consented to, what the problem is, what the risks are, what else is going on, what the client wants, and what was agreed. Record "not assessed" rather than leaving gaps, label informant reports as such, and keep the risk entry specific.
src: Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 Elements of the case formulation approach
NICE-NG225 § 1.6 Risk assessment tools and scales
ACA-Ethics-2014 § A.10.c Establishing Fees; A.10.d Nonpayment of Fees

01-intake.pitfall-general-not-specific.s: The client describes the problem only in sweeping terms, the therapist summarizes with labels, and intake ends with no concrete episode, thoughts or behaviors to formulate.
01-intake.pitfall-general-not-specific.when: Your intake notes contain phrases like "anxious all the time" or "low self-esteem" but no dated example with thoughts, emotions, body sensations and behavior.
01-intake.pitfall-general-not-specific.b: General descriptions ("I'm always anxious", "I have no confidence") tell you a theme but not what happens. Without at least one recent, specific episode slowed down into situation, thoughts, emotions, body and behavior, the first formulation is guesswork and the client cannot see the cognitive model in their own life.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Principle 1 Levels of conceptualization; research on reliability
Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 Developing an initial case formulation

01-intake.pitfall-interrogation-intake.s: The first session becomes a question-by-question form, no specific example or shared understanding emerges, and the client leaves without hope, a plan or reason to return.
01-intake.pitfall-interrogation-intake.when: Your intakes run out of time, clients do not return after the first session, or feedback suggests the session felt like paperwork.
01-intake.pitfall-interrogation-intake.b: An intake that only collects data can lose the client before therapy starts. Use forms for facts, the interview for understanding, and protect time for a first shared picture of the problem, a dose of realistic hope, and an agreed next step.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Problems in Structuring Sessions

01-intake.pitfall-missed-medical-and-sub.s: CBT starts for anxiety, depression or insomnia while an untreated medical condition, medication effect, substance use or past manic episode keeps driving the symptoms.
01-intake.pitfall-missed-medical-and-sub.when: Symptoms are atypical, started with a new medicine or illness, do not respond to good CBT, or the intake did not cover medical history, substances and past mood elevation.
01-intake.pitfall-missed-medical-and-sub.b: Psychological symptoms can be caused or maintained by physical illness, prescribed or over-the-counter medicines, alcohol or drugs, or an unrecognized bipolar disorder. Ask about all four at every intake, use brief validated screens, and refer for medical review when the picture suggests it, before concluding that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) alone is the answer.

01-intake.pitfall-risk-screen-skipped.s: Suicide and harm questions are left to a form or asked vaguely or late, and a positive answer is noted but not followed by assessment, planning or escalation.
01-intake.pitfall-risk-screen-skipped.when: Intake records state no risk without the questions asked, risk was first raised in the last minutes, or a positive screen had no documented follow-up.
01-intake.pitfall-risk-screen-skipped.b: The commonest intake risk failures are not asking directly, asking too late to act, and asking without following up. Ask every client plainly and early, treat any positive answer as the start of an assessment, and record what you asked, what you heard, your judgment and what you did.
src: NICE-NG225 § 1.6 Risk assessment tools and scales

01-intake.presenting-problem.s: How to turn the client's account into a problem list with onset, triggers, frequency, severity and impact, plus one recent specific example broken into situation, thoughts, emotions, body and behavior.
01-intake.presenting-problem.when: You need a clear, specific picture of what brings the client to therapy before formulating or planning treatment.
01-intake.presenting-problem.b: First get a short list of every problem the client wants help with, then, for the main ones, establish onset, course, triggers, frequency, severity and impact on daily life. Then walk through one recent, specific episode moment by moment: situation, thoughts and images, emotions with ratings, body sensations, and what the client did. That one concrete example is the raw material for the first formulation.
src: Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 Assessment to obtain a diagnosis and initial case formulation
Padesky-Mooney-1990 § Whole article (five areas of the cognitive model)

01-intake.risk-screen-at-intake.s: A brief, universal intake screen for suicide, self-harm, harm to others, safeguarding and urgent medical risk, with what to ask, when to escalate, crisis contacts and what to document.
01-intake.risk-screen-at-intake.when: Any new client at first contact, before deeper assessment, or whenever intake information suggests danger to the client or others.
01-intake.risk-screen-at-intake.b: Ask every new client, directly and early, about suicidal thoughts, self-harm and thoughts of harming others, and check for anyone in their care who may be at risk. Asking has not been found to plant the idea. A negative screen is documented and revisited; a positive screen moves you into full risk assessment in the same session; imminent danger means emergency services now.
src: NICE-NG225 § 1.6 Risk assessment tools and scales

01-intake.socializing-to-cbt.s: How to explain the cognitive model with the client's own example, give the rationale for structure and homework, and set up collaboration so the client knows their role.
01-intake.socializing-to-cbt.when: A client is new to CBT, is unsure what therapy will involve, or is struggling with structure, feedback or homework early in treatment.
01-intake.socializing-to-cbt.b: Clients new to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) do not know they will be asked to report on their week, set an agenda, give feedback, summarize, and practice between sessions [Beck-2021]. Teach the cognitive model through the client's own recent example rather than a lecture, explain why sessions are structured and why practice matters, and invite the client into an active, collaborative role. Then check understanding and adjust.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Problems in Structuring Sessions (Socializing the client; Addressing dysfunctional cognitions)

01-intake.structured-interviews.s: What the SCID-5-CV, MINI, ADIS-5 and DIVA-5 cover, how long they take, what they cost and need in training, and when each is worth using at intake.
01-intake.structured-interviews.when: You need a reliable diagnosis, suspect missed comorbidity, are working in a research or protocol setting, or are assessing adult ADHD.
01-intake.structured-interviews.b: Structured and semi-structured interviews make diagnosis more reliable and catch comorbidity that routine interviews miss. Use the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI) for a fast broad screen, the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5, Clinician Version (SCID-5-CV) for a thorough general diagnosis, the Anxiety and Related Disorders Interview Schedule for DSM-5 (ADIS-5) when anxiety and mood differential diagnosis matters, and the Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults (DIVA-5) for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). None replaces clinical judgment, and diagnosis is restricted by license in many places.

02-risk.asking-about-suicide.s: How to ask directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts and behavior, respond to a disclosure, and avoid wording that invites a false "no", with example phrasings.
02-risk.asking-about-suicide.when: A clinician or tool designer needs the words for raising suicide with a client, or for responding when a client discloses suicidal thoughts.
02-risk.asking-about-suicide.b: Ask about suicide directly, using the word, in a calm and matter-of-fact tone, and move from passive wishes to active thoughts, plans, intent and behavior. Asking does not plant the idea: studies of asking about suicide found no significant increase in suicidal ideation [Dazzi-etal-2014]. How you respond to a "yes" (steady, thankful, curious) strongly shapes whether the client keeps telling you the truth (expert consensus).
src: C-SSRS-Site § About the scale; Screener with triage points for primary care
VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024 § Routine Care A. Acute Warning Signs; Sidebar 3a Acute risk

02-risk.c-ssrs.s: The C-SSRS versions, what each subscale rates, which screener answers trigger referral versus same-day safety action, and how to use it without treating it as a predictor.
02-risk.c-ssrs.when: A service needs a structured suicide screen or severity rating, or a clinician must decide what a C-SSRS answer means for action.
02-risk.c-ssrs.b: The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) rates the severity and intensity of suicidal ideation and the types of suicidal behavior, in versions from a two-to-six question screener to a full clinician scale. On the primary care screener, intent, a plan with intent, or suicidal behavior in the past three months triggers behavioral health consultation and safety precautions; other yes answers trigger referral [C-SSRS-Site]. It structures and documents risk; it does not predict who will die by suicide.
src: C-SSRS-Site § About the scale; Communities and healthcare versions; Screener with triage points for primary care (2026)

02-risk.crisis-response.s: Step-by-step actions when a client in session is at imminent risk of suicide or violence, with US and UK crisis contacts, escalation routes and follow-up after the crisis.
02-risk.crisis-response.when: A client in session reports intent, a plan with intent, recent preparatory behavior, or cannot agree to stay safe, or a third party reports an imminent threat.
02-risk.crisis-response.b: When a client has intent to die and cannot keep themselves safe without outside help, the job shifts from therapy to securing safety: stay with them, reduce access to means, get emergency evaluation, and hand over directly. Such high acute risk typically requires psychiatric hospitalization, voluntary or involuntary, to maintain safety [MIRECC-TRM-2024]. Afterward, the days and weeks following discharge are a period of elevated risk, so follow up actively [VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024].

02-risk.harm-to-others.s: How to assess violent ideation and threats in therapy, structure violence risk by severity and timing, respond clinically, and when duty-to-warn or protect laws apply.
02-risk.harm-to-others.when: A client voices anger with intent, threatens a person, describes violent thoughts or plans, or has a history of violence that bears on current safety.
02-risk.harm-to-others.b: Ask about violent thoughts as directly as you ask about suicide: who, how often, intent, plan, preparation, access to weapons or other means, history and triggers. Structured tools predict violence only low to moderately well (median positive predictive value 41% for violent offending), so use them to organize judgment, not to decide outcomes [Fazel-etal-2012]. If a client makes a serious threat against an identifiable person, most US states impose or permit a duty to warn or protect, so consult and act the same day [NCSL-Duty-to-Warn-2022]. If harm is imminent, call 911 (US) or 999 (UK).
src: Wortzel-etal-2020 § Abstract (Stratifying Risk and Characterizing Violence)

02-risk.ongoing-risk-monitoring.s: How to check risk every session, follow up any positive PHQ-9 item 9 answer, recognize events that call for full reassessment, and keep the safety plan current.
02-risk.ongoing-risk-monitoring.when: A client in ongoing therapy has had suicidal thoughts or self-harm at any point, or routine measures such as the PHQ-9 are used in sessions.
02-risk.ongoing-risk-monitoring.b: Risk changes, so check it briefly every session for anyone with past suicidal thoughts or self-harm, and act on any positive answer the same day. On the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), item 9 answered "nearly every day" carried about ten times the one-year risk of a suicide attempt compared with "not at all" [Simon-etal-2013], yet most later suicides in a large Veterans Health Administration (VHA) cohort followed a "not at all" answer [Louzon-etal-2016]. So a positive item 9 always needs a conversation, and a negative one never ends the inquiry.
src: VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024 § Recommendation 2 and its discussion; Key topics 2 Selection of screening tool; Routine Care A, C
C-SSRS-Site § Since Last Visit and Since Last Contact versions

02-risk.pitfall-avoiding-the-question.s: The clinician skips asking about suicide, asks vaguely or in a way that invites "no", or changes the subject quickly when the client hints at not wanting to live.
02-risk.pitfall-avoiding-the-question.when: A clinician hesitates to ask about suicide for fear of upsetting the client, planting the idea, or having to act on the answer.
02-risk.pitfall-avoiding-the-question.b: Not asking, or asking in a way that signals the wanted answer, is a common way risk is missed (expert consensus). Asking directly does not increase suicidal ideation [Dazzi-etal-2014], and the questions need no special training to ask [C-SSRS-Site]. Ask plainly, use the word "suicide", and follow hints rather than steering away from them.
src: VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024 § Routine Care A. Acute Warning Signs

02-risk.pitfall-no-suicide-contracts.s: The clinician asks a suicidal client to promise, verbally or in writing, not to harm themselves, and treats the promise as a safety measure or as legal protection.
02-risk.pitfall-no-suicide-contracts.when: A clinician is tempted to end a risk conversation with "Can you promise me you will stay safe?" or a signed agreement.
02-risk.pitfall-no-suicide-contracts.b: No-suicide contracts have no evidence that they prevent suicide and no evidence that they protect clinicians from liability [Rudd-etal-2006a] [Lewis-2007]. In a randomized trial, a crisis response plan reduced suicide attempts compared with a contract for safety [Bryan-etal-2017]. Replace the promise with a collaborative safety plan and a commitment to treatment.

02-risk.pitfall-risk-label-as-prediction.s: A client rated "low risk" by a checklist or score is discharged, not followed up, or not offered treatment, and the label replaces a formulation and a plan.
02-risk.pitfall-risk-label-as-prediction.when: A service or clinician uses risk categories or tool scores to decide who gets care, discharge or follow-up.
02-risk.pitfall-risk-label-as-prediction.b: Risk categories and scores do not predict which individual will attempt or die by suicide; most people labeled high risk do not, and many who do were labeled lower risk [Large-etal-2016] [Carter-etal-2017]. Use levels only to choose actions and resources, and never to withhold assessment, treatment or follow-up [NICE-NG225].

Mughal-etal-2023 § Psychosocial assessment not risk assessment
VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024 § Recommendation 4; Routine Care A.c Predictive Analytics
MIRECC-TRM-2024 § Acute and chronic risk table

02-risk.pitfall-unaddressed-positive-scr.s: A client marks PHQ-9 item 9 or a suicide screener item positive, and the score is filed, averaged into a total, or noticed only after the client has left.
02-risk.pitfall-unaddressed-positive-scr.when: A service collects questionnaires with suicide items, on paper, in an app or in the electronic record, before or between sessions.
02-risk.pitfall-unaddressed-positive-scr.b: A screen only helps if someone acts on it. Any positive answer on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) item 9 or on a suicide screener needs a same-day clinical conversation, because excess risk after a positive answer emerges over several days [Simon-etal-2013]. Build the workflow so positive items are seen before the client leaves and so a "no" is never treated as clearance [Louzon-etal-2016].
src: C-SSRS-Site § Screener with triage points for primary care (2026)

02-risk.risk-documentation.s: What to write after any risk assessment or risk event, so the record shows the information gathered, the formulation, the decision, the rationale and the plan.
02-risk.risk-documentation.when: A clinician has assessed suicide, self-harm, violence or safeguarding risk, made a risk decision, or responded to a crisis and must write the note.
02-risk.risk-documentation.b: A good risk note lets a later reader see what you knew, how you thought about it, what you decided and why, and what happens next. The Joint Commission, a US accreditor, requires the suicide risk assessment to cover ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behavior, risk factors and protective factors, and requires documented risk stratification and a mitigation plan [VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024]. The reasoning matters more than the label: the note should hold up to the review that often follows a suicide or attempt [Wortzel-etal-2013].

02-risk.safeguarding.s: What to do when therapy reveals child abuse, elder or dependent adult abuse, or domestic violence, covering US mandatory reporting and UK safeguarding referral routes.
02-risk.safeguarding.when: A client discloses, or the clinician suspects, abuse or neglect of a child, an older or dependent adult, or intimate partner violence.
02-risk.safeguarding.b: In the US, about 38 states name counselors, therapists and other mental health professionals as mandated reporters of child abuse and neglect, and four more require every person to report without listing professions (laws as of May 2023), so assume you must report; the usual threshold is suspicion or reason to believe, not proof [CWIG-Mandatory-Reporting-2023]. Duties for elder and dependent adult abuse vary by state [NAPSA-Site]. In England, anyone with concerns about a child should consider a referral to local authority children's social care, and make it immediately if the child is suffering or likely to suffer significant harm [DfE-Working-Together-2026]. Explain these limits to confidentiality at intake, and act the same day.

02-risk.safety-planning.s: How to build a Stanley-Brown safety plan with a client, hold a lethal means conversation without method detail, and follow up, plus the evidence and its limits.
02-risk.safety-planning.when: A client has had suicidal thoughts, a suicidal crisis or an attempt, or has been assessed as needing a plan for future crises.
02-risk.safety-planning.b: A safety plan is a short, prioritized, written list of what the client will do, in order, when a suicidal crisis starts, made with the client in their own words. The Stanley-Brown version has seven steps, from recognizing warning signs to making the environment safer and naming reasons for living [Stanley-Brown-SPI-Site]. With follow-up calls it was associated with about half the odds of suicidal behavior in a large cohort study [Stanley-etal-2018], though guideline bodies still rate the trial evidence as limited [VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024].

02-risk.self-harm.s: What non-suicidal self-injury is, why people do it, how to assess and respond without alarm or punishment, and which CBT and DBT-informed approaches have evidence.
02-risk.self-harm.when: A client discloses or shows signs of self-injury, or a clinician must decide how to assess, respond to and treat repeated self-harm.
02-risk.self-harm.b: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is deliberate damage to one's own body without intent to die, most often used to change an unbearable internal state or to affect other people [Nock-2010]. It is common in adolescents and young adults [Swannell-etal-2014] and raises the risk of later suicidal behavior [Ribeiro-etal-2016], so ask about suicidal intent for every episode. Respond with calm curiosity, assess function, and treat with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)-informed or dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) skills, not contracts or punishment.

02-risk.suicide-focused-cbt.s: Brief CBT protocols that target suicidal thoughts and behavior directly, what they contain, and the trial and guideline evidence for them and for DBT.
02-risk.suicide-focused-cbt.when: A client has made a recent suicide attempt or has ongoing suicidal ideation, and the clinician must decide how treatment should target suicidality itself.
02-risk.suicide-focused-cbt.b: Treat suicidality as a target in its own right, not only as a symptom that will fade when depression lifts. Brief cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) protocols focused on suicide cut repeat attempts by about half or more in two randomized trials [Brown-etal-2005] [Rudd-etal-2015], and the 2024 US guideline suggests CBT-based therapy focused on suicide prevention after recent suicidal behavior (weak recommendation) [VA-DoD-Suicide-CPG-2024].

02-risk.suicide-risk-assessment.s: How to assess suicide risk as a structured conversation that yields a formulation and an action plan, and why risk factors and tools cannot predict suicide.
02-risk.suicide-risk-assessment.when: A client screens positive, discloses suicidal thoughts, shows warning signs, or is at intake or a care transition and suicide risk must be assessed.
02-risk.suicide-risk-assessment.b: Suicide risk assessment is a structured clinical conversation about ideation, plan, intent, past behavior, access to lethal means, risk factors, warning signs and protective factors, ending in a formulation and a plan. No risk factor, tool or risk category predicts who will die by suicide much better than chance [Franklin-etal-2017]. So the output is a shared understanding of what is driving risk now and what will reduce it, never a label that decides whether someone gets care [NICE-NG225].

03-formulation.choosing-a-model.s: Decision steps for picking an anchoring problem and the matching CBT model, with a map from common presentations to model papers and the condition pages in this wiki.
03-formulation.choosing-a-model.when: Assessment is done and the clinician must decide which evidence-based model will anchor the formulation, especially with comorbidity or no clear diagnosis.
03-formulation.choosing-a-model.b: Anchor the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) formulation in the evidence-based model for the problem that explains the most difficulties or matters most to the client's goals, then individualize it with the client's own thoughts, behaviors and history. Use a transdiagnostic or generic model when no specific model fits. Where a guideline names a manualized model, keep to that model's manual; the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) does this for generalized anxiety and social anxiety. For US guideline choices see `04-treatment-planning.guideline-map`.

03-formulation.cognitive-conceptualizati.s: Step-by-step method for completing the Beck cognitive conceptualization diagram, from three typical situations up to core beliefs and life history, plus the strength-based version.
03-formulation.cognitive-conceptualizati.when: The clinician has several sessions of data and wants to link a client's recurring automatic thoughts and behaviors to beliefs, coping strategies and history.
03-formulation.cognitive-conceptualizati.b: The cognitive conceptualization diagram (CCD) links three or more typical problem situations (automatic thought, its meaning, emotion, behavior) to the client's core beliefs, intermediate beliefs, coping strategies and relevant history. Fill it in between sessions from the bottom up, mark every inference with a question mark until the client confirms it, and show clients a simplified version rather than the full form.

03-formulation.cognitive-model-levels.s: Explains automatic thoughts, intermediate beliefs (attitudes, rules, assumptions), core beliefs and coping (compensatory) strategies, how they connect, and which level to target when.
03-formulation.cognitive-model-levels.when: The clinician needs to place a client's thought, rule or belief at the right level of the cognitive model before choosing how to work with it.
03-formulation.cognitive-model-levels.b: Beck's cognitive model has layers. Situation-specific automatic thoughts sit on the surface; beneath them are intermediate beliefs (attitudes, rules and conditional assumptions), and beneath those are global core beliefs about the self, others, the world and the future. People develop coping strategies to live with their core beliefs, and these strategies often keep the beliefs intact. Work from the surface down, and treat deeper layers as hypotheses until the client confirms them.

03-formulation.five-part-model.s: How to build the Padesky and Mooney five-part model of one recent episode with a client, how its parts interact, and what treatment targets it suggests.
03-formulation.five-part-model.when: Early in therapy, or for any presentation, the clinician wants a simple shared map linking situation, thoughts, emotions, body and behavior in a specific episode.
03-formulation.five-part-model.b: The five-part model maps one specific, recent episode as an environment or situation plus four interacting parts: thoughts, moods, physical reactions and behaviors. It is the usual first, descriptive formulation in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) because clients grasp it quickly and it shows that changing one part can change the others. Build it together, in the client's own words, from a concrete example.

Williams-Garland-2002 § Bringing things together, the Five Areas model

03-formulation.five-ps-formulation.s: How to organize a case into presenting, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors, what questions fill each, and how to turn the grid into a treatment focus.
03-formulation.five-ps-formulation.when: The clinician needs a whole-person summary of why a problem arose and persists, for team communication, a complex history, or a referral letter.
03-formulation.five-ps-formulation.b: The Five Ps sort what you know into presenting problems, predisposing factors (vulnerabilities), precipitating factors (triggers of onset), perpetuating factors (what keeps it going) and protective factors (strengths and supports). It answers "why this person, why this problem, why now?" [Macneil-etal-2012]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) acts mainly on the perpetuating column, so make that column specific, and never leave the protective column empty.

03-formulation.formulation-evidence.s: Summarizes research on formulation reliability, quality, training, competence measurement, client experience and treatment outcome, and what it means for practice and tool design.
03-formulation.formulation-evidence.when: A clinician, supervisor or tool designer needs to know how far formulation is evidence-based and which practices the evidence supports.
03-formulation.formulation-evidence.b: Formulation is treated as a core cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) skill, but direct evidence that it improves outcomes is weak. Therapists agree on descriptive content and disagree on inferred beliefs and mechanisms; training and experience improve quality; formulation-guided CBT does about as well as protocol CBT; and the best-supported element is routine progress monitoring. Practice should favor simple, collaborative, testable formulations.

Padesky-etal-2011 § CCC-RS score sheet, ratings summary
Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Evidence base supporting the method

03-formulation.formulation-to-treatment.s: How to turn a formulation into treatment targets, goals, intervention choices and sequence, predict what should change, monitor it, and revise when progress stalls.
03-formulation.formulation-to-treatment.when: A working formulation exists and the clinician must decide what to target first, which intervention to use, and how to tell whether the formulation is right.
03-formulation.formulation-to-treatment.b: Each maintaining mechanism in the formulation becomes a treatment target, each target gets an intervention chosen from the evidence-based model, and each intervention carries a prediction you can check with session-by-session measures. Target the problems that drive other problems first. If progress stalls, re-examine the formulation before changing technique at random.
src: Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Treatment planning and practice, Identify targets, Set good treatment goals, Solve problems, Evidence base
BeckInstitute-Worksheet-Packet-2020 § Case Write-Up Part Five Treatment Plan

03-formulation.functional-analysis.s: How to run a functional analysis of a target behavior (antecedents, behavior, short- and long-term consequences), judge which links are causal and changeable, and use it to choose interventions.
03-formulation.functional-analysis.when: The problem is a specific behavior (avoidance, bingeing, drinking, self-injury, outbursts, checking) and the clinician needs to know what triggers and reinforces it.
03-formulation.functional-analysis.b: A functional analysis (often taught as ABC: antecedents, behavior, consequences) identifies the important, changeable, causal relationships that control a specific problem behavior for this person: what reliably comes before it, and what follows it in the short and long term. It is the formulation strategy with the most empirical support, partly because it is the most studied, and it tells you which trigger or reinforcer to change [Persons-Hong-2016]. Keep it specific to one behavior, check both antecedents and consequences, and test it with monitoring.
src: Virues-Ortega-Haynes-2005 § Abstract, Functional analytic clinical case models, Limitations
Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Evidence base supporting the method

03-formulation.maintenance-cycles.s: How to identify the vicious cycles that keep a problem going, draw them with the client (including Moorey's vicious flower for depression), and turn each cycle into a treatment target.
03-formulation.maintenance-cycles.when: The clinician needs to show a client how their own coping keeps the problem going and choose which loop to break first.
03-formulation.maintenance-cycles.b: A maintenance cycle is a loop in which the person's response to a problem (avoiding, checking, withdrawing, ruminating) brings short-term relief but keeps the problem going. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works mostly by breaking these loops. Draw them from the client's own examples, name what each response costs in the long run, and pick one loop to target first.
src: Padesky-2020 § Abstract, Box arrow in arrow out model
Williams-Garland-2002 § How the five areas interact
Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Conceptual framework (parsimony), Identify targets for treatment

03-formulation.pitfall-formulation-drift.s: Sessions become open-ended talk about history and beliefs "because the formulation is complex," while exposure, activation and other behavior change quietly stop.
03-formulation.pitfall-formulation-drift.when: The clinician is moving away from the evidence-based protocol on the grounds that this client's formulation is individual or complex.
03-formulation.pitfall-formulation-drift.b: In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), individualizing treatment means adapting the evidence-based model to this client, not replacing its active ingredients. When a formulation is used to justify dropping exposure, activation or other behavior change, outcomes suffer. Deviate from the protocol only on data, and decide it with the client.

03-formulation.pitfall-imposed-formulati.s: The therapist hands over a completed, jargon-heavy diagram as fact; the client nods, feels blamed or lectured, does not use it, and sometimes leaves therapy distressed.
03-formulation.pitfall-imposed-formulati.when: A formulation was written by the therapist or a tool and is being explained to the client rather than built with them.
03-formulation.pitfall-imposed-formulati.b: A formulation the client did not help build is often not understood, not believed and not used, and it can be experienced as a judgment. Build it together in the client's words, offer every link as a guess, include strengths, and ask how it lands.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Evidence on client experience, Principle 2 Collaborative empiricism

03-formulation.pitfall-static-formulatio.s: The formulation drawn in session two sits unchanged in the file; therapy continues on the same plan while scores flatline, and new information never changes the targets.
03-formulation.pitfall-static-formulatio.when: Therapy is several sessions in and nobody has looked at the formulation since it was drawn, or progress has stalled without a review.
03-formulation.pitfall-static-formulatio.b: A formulation is a hypothesis, so it has to be tested and changed. Review it with the client at set points and whenever progress data surprise you. Poor progress is a signal to re-examine the formulation, not only to try another technique.
src: Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Conceptual framework, Build a strong therapeutic relationship, Solve problems, Evidence base
Macneil-etal-2012 § How formulation guides intervention, Cautions regarding formulation

03-formulation.pitfall-too-deep-too-soon.s: In the first sessions the therapist announces core beliefs and childhood causes the client has not described, and the client looks confused, upset or quietly disagrees.
03-formulation.pitfall-too-deep-too-soon.when: A clinician, trainee or formulation tool is producing belief-level or developmental explanations before a descriptive map of current episodes exists.
03-formulation.pitfall-too-deep-too-soon.b: Jumping to core beliefs and childhood origins in the first sessions produces the least reliable part of a formulation at the moment the client trusts you least. Start with a descriptive map of recent episodes, add triggers and maintaining factors next, and add longitudinal explanation only if treatment needs it and the client's own data support it.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Principle 1 Levels of conceptualization, What is the evidence base

03-formulation.sharing-the-formulation.s: How to build the formulation with the client in their own language, pace and present it so it helps rather than distresses, check their reaction, and revise it over therapy.
03-formulation.sharing-the-formulation.when: The clinician is about to draw, explain or revise a formulation with a client, or the client reacts to one with doubt, distress or disagreement.
03-formulation.sharing-the-formulation.b: Build the formulation with the client, not for them: they supply the content, the words and the corrections, and you supply structure and theory. Keep it as simple as the stage of therapy allows, include strengths, present it as a best guess, and check how it lands. Most clients find a shared formulation helpful, but some find it distressing, so watch for that and respond.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Principle 2 Collaborative empiricism, Evidence on client experience
Persons-Tompkins-2022 § Build a strong therapeutic relationship

03-formulation.strengths-in-formulation.s: How to search for client strengths, record them in the formulation and strength-based diagram, build a personal model of resilience, and use strengths in the treatment plan.
03-formulation.strengths-in-formulation.when: The formulation lists only problems and vulnerabilities, the client feels defined by their difficulties, or therapy is moving toward relapse prevention and resilience.
03-formulation.strengths-in-formulation.b: A formulation should explain what helps as well as what hurts. Look for strengths from the first session, record them in the formulation, and link at least one strength to each part of the plan. In later therapy, strengths can become a client-built personal model of resilience used for relapse prevention.
src: Kuyken-etal-2008 § Principle 3 Include client strengths and conceptualize resilience
BeckInstitute-Worksheet-Packet-2020 § Strength-Based Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram instructions, Case Write-Up best lifetime functioning

03-formulation.what-is-case-formulation.s: Defines case formulation, contrasts it with diagnosis, explains descriptive to explanatory levels, and summarizes the collaborative (Kuyken, Padesky, Dudley) and hypothesis-testing (Persons) approaches.
03-formulation.what-is-case-formulation.when: A clinician or tool designer needs to know what a CBT case formulation contains, how it differs from a diagnosis, and which approach to follow.
03-formulation.what-is-case-formulation.b: A case formulation is a working hypothesis, built with the client, that first describes and then explains why this person has these problems now and what keeps them going, so that treatment can be chosen and tested. It works alongside a diagnosis rather than replacing it. Start descriptive, add explanation only as evidence builds, include strengths, and revise it whenever progress data disagree with it.

04-treatment-planning.combining-with-med.s: When to offer CBT plus medication, how to sequence them, how collaborative care works, and how a non-prescribing therapist coordinates with prescribers safely.
04-treatment-planning.combining-with-med.when: A client is taking or considering psychiatric medication, or the guideline suggests combined treatment, and you need to plan how CBT fits.
04-treatment-planning.combining-with-med.b: For depression (mostly moderate to severe in the trials), psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) plus an antidepressant outperforms either alone at the end of treatment, and psychotherapy alone equals medication alone [Cuijpers-etal-2020a]. Combined treatment is also favored for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and adding CBT helps people who respond poorly to medication [NICE-CG31; Wiles-etal-2013]. Non-prescribing therapists do not advise on starting, changing or stopping medication; they share measures with the prescriber.
src: APA-Depression-Guideline-2019 § Table 3 initial treatment and partial or nonresponders

04-treatment-planning.guideline-map-othe.s: Where CBT sits in NICE and US guidance for eating disorders, psychosis, bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, self-harm, insomnia, adult ADHD and co-occurring substance use.
04-treatment-planning.guideline-map-othe.when: You need to know whether CBT is first-line, an add-on or a second choice for a client whose main problem is outside depression and anxiety.
04-treatment-planning.guideline-map-othe.b: For these presentations cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the first psychological step for some (bulimia and binge eating, via CBT-based guided self-help; insomnia; adult self-harm), one of several equal options for others (adult anorexia), offered to everyone alongside medication in psychosis, and not the main treatment for borderline personality disorder or adolescent anorexia. Most protocols here are longer than for anxiety and need specialist training. Use the table to place CBT, then read the condition page.

04-treatment-planning.guideline-map.s: One table of what NICE and the American Psychological Association recommend for depression, anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD, with doses, plus how Division 12 ratings fit.
04-treatment-planning.guideline-map.when: You need the guideline-recommended first-line treatment and usual dose for an adult with depression, an anxiety disorder, OCD or PTSD.
04-treatment-planning.guideline-map.b: For adult depression and anxiety disorders, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a guideline-recommended first-line option almost everywhere, but guidelines differ on dose, format and whether medication or another therapy is an equal choice. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) gives the most detailed doses. In the US, the American Psychological Association (APA) updated its posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) guideline in 2025, its 2019 depression guideline is past its planned expiry, and the American College of Physicians (ACP) covers acute adult depression. Check the row, then confirm details in the source.

04-treatment-planning.managing-non-respo.s: How to detect early that a client is not improving, work through the likely causes in order, reformulate, and choose between adjusting, intensifying, switching, adding medication or referring.
04-treatment-planning.managing-non-respo.when: Session measures are flat or worsening, the client is not reaching agreed goals, or a formal review point arrives without reliable improvement.
04-treatment-planning.managing-non-respo.b: Measure every session, because clinicians rarely predict who will fail without data, while simple tracking flagged most deteriorating clients by session 3 [Hannan-etal-2005]. If there is no response after 4 to 6 weeks, check fixable causes first (attendance, homework, life stressors, other conditions), then review the diagnosis and formulation, then change the plan, for example by switching therapy or adding medication [NICE-NG222], intensifying, or referring. Take not-on-track cases to supervision; feedback with supervision review improved their outcomes in a randomized trial [Delgadillo-etal-2018].
src: Persons-2008 § Ch. 9 Monitoring Progress; Ch. 11 Handling Nonadherence and Treatment Failure; Ch. 12 Decision Making over the Course of Therapy

04-treatment-planning.pitfall-continuing.s: Sessions roll on past the planned number with flat or worsening scores, no review date, and a therapist who believes the client is improving.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-continuing.when: A client has had many sessions without a formal review, or you notice measures have not moved for several weeks.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-continuing.b: Therapists are poor judges of who is failing to improve, so treatment continues by default long after it should have been reviewed. Clinicians rarely predict deterioration, while simple session-by-session measures flagged 85% of deteriorating clients by the third session [Hannan-etal-2005]. Fix it by setting review dates at planning, graphing scores every session, and acting on a not-on-track signal within the next session.

04-treatment-planning.pitfall-mismatched.s: A client with severe or complex problems is cycled through brief self-help, or a client with mild symptoms gets long open-ended therapy, and nobody revisits the fit.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-mismatched.when: You are choosing a first level of care, or a client has stayed at one level of intensity despite poor fit or poor progress.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-mismatched.b: Intensity mismatch happens in both directions: complex or severe problems routed to brief low-intensity help and left there, or mild problems given long, open-ended therapy. Guidelines already name presentations that need high intensity from the start, and matching complex cases directly to high intensity improved depression outcomes in a randomized trial [Delgadillo-etal-2022]. Decide the level from severity, impairment, risk, complexity and preference, and revisit it at every review.
src: Bower-Gilbody-2005 § Principles and assumptions of stepped care
NICE-NG222 § 1.4.2; 1.5.2 to 1.5.3; Table 2 guided self-help row

04-treatment-planning.pitfall-vague-or-i.s: Goals read like "feel better" or "reduce anxiety," were chosen by the therapist, have no measure or date, and the client is polite but not practicing.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-vague-or-i.when: A treatment plan has goals nobody can tick off, or the client seems to be working toward someone else's agenda.
04-treatment-planning.pitfall-vague-or-i.b: Goals that cannot be observed, are not timed, or belong to the therapist make progress invisible and weaken collaboration. Agreement on goals and active collaboration each have a medium-sized link with outcome across dozens of studies [Tryon-etal-2018]. The fix is to co-write a few specific, measurable, timed goals in the client's own terms and check them at every review.
src: Tryon-etal-2018 § Abstract, goal consensus and collaboration results
Persons-2008 § Ch. 6 Setting Treatment Goals; Ch. 7 Treatment Plan and Consent

04-treatment-planning.problem-list-and-g.s: How to build a full problem list, turn the client's priorities into SMART goals with measures, and decide which problem to work on first.
04-treatment-planning.problem-list-and-g.when: Assessment is complete and you and the client need to agree what therapy will target, in what order, and how progress will be judged.
04-treatment-planning.problem-list-and-g.b: A problem list names every difficulty you and the client can see, in plain words, across symptoms and life areas. Goals turn the problems the client most wants to change into specific, measurable targets with a time frame and a measure attached. Order the work by safety first, then by what drives the other problems, then by what matters most to the client. Client and therapist agreement on goals is associated with better outcome [Tryon-etal-2018].

04-treatment-planning.session-planning.s: How to set a provisional number of sessions from guideline doses, choose session frequency and length, map the phases of a CBT course, and schedule reviews and tapering.
04-treatment-planning.session-planning.when: You are agreeing with a client how many sessions to plan, how often to meet, and when progress will be reviewed.
04-treatment-planning.session-planning.b: Set a provisional number of sessions from the guideline dose for the condition and severity, tell the client, and review it against measures rather than running on by default. Meet at least weekly; in a randomized trial, twice-weekly sessions of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or interpersonal psychotherapy for depression beat weekly sessions [Bruijniks-etal-2020]. Plan three phases (engage and formulate, active change, consolidate and prevent relapse) and space the last sessions out.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 9 Treatment Planning; Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

04-treatment-planning.stepped-care.s: What stepped care is, how low-intensity and high-intensity CBT differ in NHS Talking Therapies, when to step up, and when to start at a higher step.
04-treatment-planning.stepped-care.when: You are deciding how intensive a first treatment should be, or whether a client in low-intensity care needs to step up.
04-treatment-planning.stepped-care.b: Stepped care starts with the least intensive treatment likely to help, monitors outcome, and steps up when the person is not improving [Bower-Gilbody-2005]. In NHS Talking Therapies, the National Health Service (NHS) program in England (formerly IAPT, Improving Access to Psychological Therapies), low-intensity work is about 5 to 8 brief sessions of guided self-help and high-intensity therapy runs up to 12 to 20 sessions [Thew-etal-2025]. Stepped care has a moderate advantage over usual care but is not proven to be the best model, so start some clients at high intensity, and step up promptly when measures stall [VanStraten-etal-2015; Delgadillo-etal-2022].

04-treatment-planning.treatment-plan-doc.s: What a written CBT treatment plan contains, how to write measurable goals and objectives, record client agreement and update it, and what US payers and UK care plans expect.
04-treatment-planning.treatment-plan-doc.when: You need to write, update or audit the formal written treatment plan for a client's record, a payer review, or a UK care plan.
04-treatment-planning.treatment-plan-doc.b: The written cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) treatment plan records what you and the client agreed: problems, measurable goals and objectives, interventions, dose, measures and review dates. Draft it together after the case formulation, record agreement, and update it at every review. In the United States (US), Medicare local coverage determinations (LCDs) expect type, amount, frequency and duration of services, diagnoses, goals and periodic updates [CMS-LCD-L34353]. In the United Kingdom (UK), the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) expects jointly developed care plans with a written copy [NICE-CG136].

04-treatment-planning.when-cbt-is-not-in.s: A decision sequence for when to defer CBT, adapt it, add other care, or refer to another therapy such as DBT, ACT, IPT, EMDR or family therapy.
04-treatment-planning.when-cbt-is-not-in.when: You doubt standard outpatient CBT is the right treatment now, because of risk, medical or substance issues, the diagnosis, the client's preference, or your competence.
04-treatment-planning.when-cbt-is-not-in.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has few absolute contraindications, but it is the wrong next step when something else must come first (acute risk, medical illness, mania, intoxication), when another treatment is the guideline first choice (family therapy for adolescent anorexia, structured programs for borderline personality disorder, environmental changes and medication for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or ADHD), or when you lack the competence. Comorbid personality disorder, substance use or a risk score alone are not reasons to refuse treatment. Decide among four options: proceed, adapt, defer while other care comes first, or refer.

05-session-structure.agenda-setting.s: How to set and prioritize a shared session agenda in about five minutes, handle clients who ramble, freeze or feel hopeless, and decide when to change course.
05-session-structure.agenda-setting.when: Early in a treatment session when client and therapist must agree which one or two problems or goals to work on today and in what order.
05-session-structure.agenda-setting.b: The agenda is a short, shared list of what this session will work on, set at the start, named rather than discussed, and limited to one or two target problems [Young-Beck-1980; Beck-2021]. Prioritize by risk, distress, stage of therapy and the chance of progress. Follow it by default, and change it openly and together when something more important appears.

05-session-structure.homework-design.s: How to design specific, collaborative between-session tasks with a clear rationale, if-then plans and anticipated obstacles, and the evidence that homework improves CBT outcomes.
05-session-structure.homework-design.when: The therapist is turning what was learned in session into a between-session task and wants the client to understand it, agree to it and actually do it.
05-session-structure.homework-design.b: Homework (between-session practice, called an "action plan" in Beck's current text [Beck-2021]) is how learning in session transfers to daily life, and it adds measurably to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) outcomes [Ryum-Kazantzis-2024]. Tasks get done when they are designed with the client, flow from the session, carry a clear reason, are specific about when and where, and have obstacles planned for in advance [Ryum-Kazantzis-2024; Young-Beck-1980].

05-session-structure.homework-review-and.s: How to review between-session tasks every session, draw out what was learned, assess quality as well as quantity, and respond to partial or non-completion without blame.
05-session-structure.homework-review-and.when: Early in a session when the therapist reviews last week's action plan, or when a client repeatedly does not complete agreed tasks.
05-session-structure.homework-review-and.b: Review the action plan near the start of every session, focus on what the client learned rather than whether the form is filled in, and summarize the conclusion [Young-Beck-1980]. If the client did not do it, treat that as information: look for practical obstacles, task difficulty, unhelpful beliefs, distress or a strain in the relationship, and adjust the task rather than blame the client [Ryum-Kazantzis-2024].

05-session-structure.mood-check-and-brid.s: How to open a CBT session with a brief mood rating, a discussed measures review, a risk screen and a bridge from the last session, in a few minutes.
05-session-structure.mood-check-and-brid.when: The first minutes of a treatment session, when the therapist needs to know how the client has been, how scores have moved and what carries over from last time.
05-session-structure.mood-check-and-brid.b: Start each session by getting a number and a word for how the client has been, comparing it with last time, and discussing what the change means. Then bridge: a two or three sentence update on the week and on last session's work, which feeds the agenda [Beck-2021; Young-Beck-1980]. Keep it brief, talk about the scores rather than just collect them, and treat any risk signal as the first priority.

05-session-structure.pitfall-homework-as.s: Tasks are set vaguely in the last minute, never asked about next session, and completion steadily falls until the client stops doing anything between sessions.
05-session-structure.pitfall-homework-as.when: Homework completion is low or falling, or the therapist realizes they often forget to ask about last week's task.
05-session-structure.pitfall-homework-as.b: Clients learn quickly whether homework matters by whether the therapist asks about it. If tasks are vague and never reviewed, clients may conclude there is no need to do them, and one of cognitive behavioral therapy's (CBT) main routes to change is lost [Young-Beck-1980]. Make action plan review a standing agenda item, reread your notes before each session, and design tasks during the session rather than in the last minute [Beck-2021; Ryum-Kazantzis-2024].
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 11 Homework, reviewing previous homework
Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Difficulties in Reviewing the Action Plan

05-session-structure.pitfall-rigid-struc.s: The therapist enforces agenda, forms and timing mechanically, interrupts too much, overrides the client's distress, and the client becomes irritated, silent or drops out.
05-session-structure.pitfall-rigid-struc.when: A client reacts to structure with irritation, compliance without engagement, or complaints about forms or interruptions, or the therapist follows the agenda despite obvious distress.
05-session-structure.pitfall-rigid-struc.b: Structure in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) serves the client; imposed in a controlling or demanding way, it strains the relationship and puts the client's engagement at risk [Beck-2021]. Watch for affect shifts when you structure, ask about them, apologize when you overstep, and negotiate a compromise. Deviate from the agenda when risk, distress or the relationship requires it, and move back toward standard structure over time [Beck-2021].
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Interrupting the Client; Addressing Dysfunctional Cognitions; Negative Reactions to Forms; Deviating from the Agenda
Young-Beck-1980 § Item 1 Agenda, flexibility and switching problems

05-session-structure.pitfall-uninformati.s: Progress notes read "discussed stressors, provided CBT", carry no scores, plan or risk status, are copied from last week, or mix private process reflections into the shared record.
05-session-structure.pitfall-uninformati.when: A clinician or supervisor reviewing a record cannot tell from the notes what was worked on, how the client is progressing, or what the plan is.
05-session-structure.pitfall-uninformati.b: A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) note that names no problem, technique, score, response, risk status or plan fails every reader: the next clinician, an auditor, the client, and you at the next session. Build the note from the session structure, record scores and the action plan every time, keep private process reflections out of the main record, and write in language the client could read without feeling judged [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-501; Monaci-etal-2025].
src: Monaci-etal-2025 § Discussion, implications for clinical practice
Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 Difficulties in Reviewing the Action Plan

05-session-structure.pitfall-unstructure.s: Sessions are spent recounting the week, jump between topics, end without an intervention or action plan, and the client feels heard but nothing changes.
05-session-structure.pitfall-unstructure.when: A therapist notices that sessions feel pleasant but unproductive, run over time, or that scores have plateaued while sessions consist mostly of updates.
05-session-structure.pitfall-unstructure.b: A common structural failure in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is drift: the update expands to fill the hour and no problem is worked on to the point of change. The fix is gentle interruption, a short agenda of one or two items, frequent summaries, and a check before the end that the session produced a response, a partial solution or an action plan [Beck-2021; Young-Beck-1980].
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 11 General Difficulties in Structuring; Unfocused Discussion; Failing to Make a Therapeutic Intervention
Young-Beck-1980 § Item 1 Agenda; Item 6 Pacing and Efficient Use of Time

05-session-structure.session-notes.s: What to document after each CBT session, how SOAP and DAP formats organize it, and how progress notes differ from HIPAA psychotherapy notes.
05-session-structure.session-notes.when: The clinician is writing or templating the note for a treatment session and needs to know what to include, in what format, and what belongs where.
05-session-structure.session-notes.b: Each cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) progress note should let another clinician, or you next week, see what was worked on, measure scores, what was done, how the client responded, the risk picture and what happens next. SOAP (subjective, objective, assessment, plan) and DAP (data, assessment, plan) are two common layouts for the same content. In the United States (US), process notes kept separately can qualify as "psychotherapy notes" under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), but the core session facts always belong in the main record [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-501].

05-session-structure.session-structure.s: The default sequence of a cognitive behavioral therapy treatment session, from mood check to feedback, with timing rules, when to deviate, and what to record.
05-session-structure.session-structure.when: A clinician is planning or running any CBT treatment session after the evaluation and needs the default sequence, timing and rules for deviating from it.
05-session-structure.session-structure.b: A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) session follows a predictable arc: mood check, agenda, brief update and action plan review, work on one or two agenda items with new action plans set along the way, then a summary and feedback [Beck-2021]. The structure protects time for change work; it is not an end in itself. Deviate on purpose when risk, acute distress or a strained relationship makes the agreed agenda the wrong priority [Beck-2021].

05-session-structure.session-summaries-a.s: How to use brief capsule summaries during the session, have the client summarize at the end, and elicit honest feedback, including how to respond to criticism.
05-session-structure.session-summaries-a.when: The therapist needs to check shared understanding during a session, close it with a summary, or ask the client how the session went.
05-session-structure.session-summaries-a.b: Summarize often and briefly during the session so both of you hold the same picture, and ask the client to say the main points in their own words, ideally writing them down to review during the week [Young-Beck-1980]. End by asking the client to summarize, confirming the action plan and asking for feedback. Thank the client for any criticism, apologize where it fits, and act on it [Beck-2021].
