05-session-structure.telehealth-adaptati.s: How to adapt CBT session structure, safety planning, privacy, materials and engagement for video and telephone delivery, and what the evidence says about remote CBT.
05-session-structure.telehealth-adaptati.when: The therapist is starting or running CBT sessions by video or telephone, including switching an in-person client to remote sessions.
05-session-structure.telehealth-adaptati.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) by live video appears about as effective as in person, and telephone CBT shows promise for depression and anxiety [Fernandez-etal-2021; Coughtrey-Pistrang-2018]. Keep the usual session structure, and add three routines: a safety and location check at the start of every session, a privacy check, and a backup plan for dropped connections [Chiauzzi-etal-2020]. Expect to work harder to read emotion and convey warmth, because therapists tend to show lower skill levels in teletherapy [Lin-etal-2025].
src: Chiauzzi-etal-2020 § Clinical considerations; emergency planning; telephone versus video

05-session-structure.therapist-competenc.s: What CBT competence means, how the CTRS and CTS-R rate it and set pass thresholds, how competence relates to outcome, and how supervision and deliberate practice build it.
05-session-structure.therapist-competenc.when: A therapist, supervisor or trainer wants to rate CBT session quality, prepare for a competence assessment, or plan how to improve skills.
05-session-structure.therapist-competenc.b: Competence is how skillfully a therapist delivers cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), as distinct from adherence (whether the prescribed techniques were used at all). It is usually rated from session recordings on the Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale (CTRS, usual pass mark 40 of 66) or the Revised Cognitive Therapy Scale (CTS-R, usual pass mark 36 of 72) [Creed-etal-2021; James-etal-2001]. Competence can be trained, but its link to client outcome is weaker and less consistent than many expect, so rate it alongside client outcome data, not instead of it [Webb-etal-2010].
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Rating directions and items 1 to 11
Creed-etal-2021 § Method, Measures, CTRS benchmark of 40

alliance-and-stance.collaborative-empiri.s: Explains collaborative empiricism, the CBT stance of working as a team to treat beliefs as testable hypotheses, with concrete behaviors, phrasings and the evidence on collaboration.
alliance-and-stance.collaborative-empiri.when: The therapist is setting goals, proposing a hypothesis about a thought, designing homework or an experiment, or the client either defers completely or resists testing a belief.
alliance-and-stance.collaborative-empiri.b: Collaborative empiricism means therapist and client work as a team, treating the client's beliefs as hypotheses to be tested against evidence from the client's own life rather than errors to be argued away. Its core is "sharing the work" [Tee-Kazantzis-2011]. Collaboration (r = .29) and goal consensus (r = .24) both predict outcome [Tryon-etal-2018], so make goals, agendas, homework and experiments joint decisions, and treat your own ideas as hypotheses too.
src: Norcross-Karpiak-2025 § Table 21.1; Goal Consensus and Collaboration

alliance-and-stance.empathy.s: Explains what accurate empathy is, the three forms it takes, how to show and check it while doing CBT techniques, and the evidence linking it to outcome.
alliance-and-stance.empathy.when: The therapist needs to convey understanding of the client's experience, especially before or during structured CBT techniques, or wants to know whether the client feels understood.
alliance-and-stance.empathy.b: Empathy is understanding what the client is experiencing or trying to express, and showing that understanding in a way the client recognizes. Therapist empathy predicts outcome (r = .28 across 82 samples and 6,138 clients), and the link did not differ by theoretical orientation [Elliott-etal-2018]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), show you understand why something is hard before and while you ask the client to do it, and check your understanding instead of assuming it.
src: Elliott-etal-2018 § Definitions and Measures; Moderators and Mediators; Therapeutic Practices

alliance-and-stance.facilitative-interpe.s: Explains therapist effects and what distinguishes more effective therapists, namely facilitative interpersonal skills under pressure, professional self-doubt, and deliberate practice, and how to develop them.
alliance-and-stance.facilitative-interpe.when: A clinician, supervisor or tool designer asks why some therapists get better outcomes than others, or how to improve relational skill beyond experience and protocol adherence.
alliance-and-stance.facilitative-interpe.b: Therapists differ in effectiveness: on average about 5% of the variation in client outcome lies between therapists, with a range of 0.2% to 29% across studies [Johns-etal-2019]. Experience, profession and adherence to a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) protocol explain little of this. What distinguishes more effective therapists is skill under interpersonal pressure (facilitative interpersonal skills), professional self-doubt held alongside self-acceptance, and time spent deliberately practicing difficult moments [Anderson-etal-2009; Nissen-Lie-etal-2017; Chow-etal-2015].

alliance-and-stance.hope-and-expectancy.s: Shows how to build realistic hope by giving a credible, personalized CBT rationale, setting honest expectations, and making early progress visible, with the evidence on expectancy and credibility.
alliance-and-stance.hope-and-expectancy.when: The therapist is explaining the CBT model or plan, the client doubts therapy will help, asks how long it will take, or expresses hopelessness about change.
alliance-and-stance.hope-and-expectancy.b: Clients who expect therapy to help tend to do better (r = .18 across 81 samples and 12,722 patients), and so, more weakly, do clients who find the treatment credible early on (r = .12) [Constantino-etal-2018a; Constantino-etal-2018b]. Build hope honestly: give an explanation of the problem that the client accepts as fitting their experience, set realistic expectations, and make early progress visible. Hopelessness about the future is also a risk signal and must be assessed, not just reassured.

alliance-and-stance.outcome-and-alliance.s: Step-by-step routine outcome monitoring and session-by-session alliance feedback, including the Outcome and Session Rating Scales, how to discuss scores, and what to do when progress stalls.
alliance-and-stance.outcome-and-alliance.when: The therapist is setting up session-by-session measurement, deciding how to use outcome and alliance scores in the session, or a client is not improving as expected.
alliance-and-stance.outcome-and-alliance.b: Measure outcome every session and the alliance at the end of every session, look at the scores with the client, and change course when progress stalls or the alliance dips. Feedback improves outcomes modestly (d = 0.15 across 58 studies) and slightly reduces dropout [DeJong-etal-2021]; its main value is catching clients who are not on track, whom therapists rarely spot by judgment alone [Hannan-etal-2005; Lambert-etal-2018].
src: Norcross-Karpiak-2025 § Table 21.1; Collection of Client Feedback; What Does Not Work

alliance-and-stance.pitfall-assuming-the.s: The therapist judges the relationship good without asking, the client seems polite and compliant, and stalled progress, deterioration or dropout arrive as a surprise.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-assuming-the.when: A therapist relies on their own impression of how therapy is going, has no client-rated alliance or progress data, or is surprised by a no-show or unplanned ending.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-assuming-the.b: Therapists are poor judges of their own alliances and outcomes. Clinicians overestimate improvement and underestimate deterioration [Walfish-etal-2012], rarely predict who will deteriorate [Hannan-etal-2005], and their alliance ratings predict outcome less well than clients' ratings [Cameron-etal-2018]. Ask the client, every session, in a form that makes criticism easy.
src: Safran-etal-2011 § Definitions and Measures; Therapeutic Practices

alliance-and-stance.pitfall-collecting-f.s: Outcome and alliance forms are completed every session but scores are never discussed, perfect or flat ratings go unexamined, and the plan does not change when progress stalls.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-collecting-f.when: A service or therapist collects session measures routinely, but the numbers rarely come up in the session or lead to changes in treatment.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-collecting-f.b: Measurement helps only when it changes the conversation and, when needed, the plan. Feedback offers clinicians a chance to strengthen the alliance, shift focus, revisit goals or alter interventions [Ostergard-etal-2020]; forms that are filed and forgotten add burden without benefit. Look at the score with the client in the first minutes, ask about any dip, and act when progress stalls.

alliance-and-stance.pitfall-pushing-tech.s: The client pushes back or goes quiet during a technique, the therapist argues the rationale harder, and the strain grows until homework stops or the client drops out.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-pushing-tech.when: A client resists, withdraws from, or argues with a CBT technique and the therapist feels pressure to keep going or to win the point.
alliance-and-stance.pitfall-pushing-tech.b: When a client resists or withdraws during a technique, doing more of the technique usually makes the rupture worse. In cognitive therapy for depression, therapists who responded to alliance strains by increasing their focus on distorted cognitions appeared to deepen the strains, and that focus correlated with worse outcome [Castonguay-etal-1996]. Pause the technique, attend to the relationship, then return to the work in a form the client can accept.

alliance-and-stance.positive-regard-and-.s: Describes positive regard (warm, nonjudgmental valuing of the client) and genuineness (congruence), how each looks in CBT sessions, and the outcome evidence for both.
alliance-and-stance.positive-regard-and-.when: The therapist needs to convey warmth and acceptance without collusion, respond to lapses or shameful disclosures, or decide how openly to share their own reactions.
alliance-and-stance.positive-regard-and-.b: Positive regard means valuing and caring about the client as a person, and genuineness (congruence) means being authentic, so that what you say matches what you think and do. Both predict outcome: positive regard g = .28 across 64 studies, and congruence r = .23 across 21 studies [Farber-etal-2018; Kolden-etal-2018]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) they look like steady warmth that does not depend on the client's compliance, plus honest, respectful feedback.
src: Norcross-Karpiak-2025 § Table 21.1; Affirmation and Validation; Congruence/Genuineness; What Does Not Work

alliance-and-stance.rupture-and-repair.s: How to spot withdrawal and confrontation ruptures, pause the technique, invite and own your part, and repair by changing the task or exploring, with phrasings and records.
alliance-and-stance.rupture-and-repair.when: The client goes quiet, gives minimal answers, over-agrees, changes the subject, criticizes the therapy, pushes back, or alliance ratings drop.
alliance-and-stance.rupture-and-repair.b: A rupture is a tension or breakdown in collaboration, ranging from a barely noticed strain to an open impasse [Safran-etal-2011]. Watch for withdrawal (moving away) and confrontation (moving against), pause the technique, invite the client's view, own your part without defensiveness, then repair by adjusting the task or goal or by exploring what happened. Repair episodes are associated with better outcome (r = .29 across 11 studies and 1,314 patients) [Eubanks-etal-2018]; "addressing ruptures works; ignoring them does not" [Norcross-Karpiak-2025].
src: Safran-etal-2011 § Definitions and Measures; Clinical Examples; Therapeutic Practices
Bordin-1979 § Working alliance goals, tasks and bond
Norcross-Karpiak-2025 § Table 21.1; Repair of Alliance Ruptures

alliance-and-stance.self-disclosure-and-.s: When therapist self-disclosure and immediacy help or harm in CBT, how to answer personal questions, and how to tell helpful boundary crossings from harmful boundary violations.
alliance-and-stance.self-disclosure-and-.when: The therapist is considering sharing personal information or reactions, a client asks a personal question, or a boundary question arises such as gifts, contact outside sessions, or out-of-office exposure work.
alliance-and-stance.self-disclosure-and-.b: Brief, relevant self-disclosure that serves the client, followed by a quick return of focus to the client, is usually followed by a stronger relationship and client gains, while inappropriate disclosure, such as disclosure driven by the therapist's own needs, weakens the alliance [Hill-etal-2018; Goldfried-etal-2003; Ackerman-Hilsenroth-2001]. Boundaries are flexible standards judged in context: a crossing (such as accompanying a client on an exposure task) can help, while a violation exploits the client [Gutheil-Gabbard-1993]. Sexual intimacy with a current client is always prohibited [APA-Ethics-2017].

alliance-and-stance.therapeutic-alliance.s: Defines the therapeutic alliance as agreement on goals and tasks plus a working bond, and summarizes the evidence linking it to outcome and dropout in CBT.
alliance-and-stance.therapeutic-alliance.when: A clinician or tool designer needs to know what the alliance is, why it predicts CBT outcome, and how to build and check it from the first session.
alliance-and-stance.therapeutic-alliance.b: The therapeutic alliance is the collaborative part of the therapy relationship: agreement on the goals of therapy, agreement on the tasks used to reach them, and a bond of trust that holds the work together [Bordin-1979]. Across 295 studies and more than 30,000 patients, a stronger alliance predicts better outcome (r = .28), and the same link appears in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [Fluckiger-etal-2018; Cameron-etal-2018]. Build it deliberately and check it every session; do not assume it.
src: Bordin-1979 § Working alliance goals, tasks and bond
Norcross-Karpiak-2025 § Table 21.1; What Works; Cautions and Caveats

alliance-and-stance.what-harms-the-relat.s: Lists therapist attitudes and behaviors linked to weaker alliances, worse outcomes and dropout, such as criticism, rigidity, confrontation and ignoring feedback, with what to do instead.
alliance-and-stance.what-harms-the-relat.when: A clinician, supervisor or tool designer wants to know which therapist behaviors damage the relationship or predict dropout, or is reviewing a stalled or ruptured case.
alliance-and-stance.what-harms-the-relat.b: The behaviors that damage the relationship are predictable: hostile or critical comments, rigid over-structuring, confrontation, pushing cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) techniques through a strain, assuming you know how the client sees therapy, and imposing your own cultural views [Norcross-Karpiak-2025; Ackerman-Hilsenroth-2001; Castonguay-etal-1996]. About 1 in 5 adult clients drop out of therapy, and weaker alliances predict dropout [Swift-Greenberg-2012; Sharf-etal-2010]. Most of these behaviors are subtle, so watch for them in yourself and in recordings.

responding-in-session.core-response-skil.s: How to choose each therapist turn from open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries, with ratios, decision rules and example wording.
responding-in-session.core-response-skil.when: You are deciding what kind of response to give next, or designing how a therapist or tool should reply to a client turn.
responding-in-session.core-response-skil.b: Almost every therapist turn can be built from four moves, known as OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries, plus information given with permission. Reflect more than you ask: the motivational interviewing (MI) coding standard treats one reflection per question as fair and two per question as good [Moyers-etal-2015]. Pick the move by what the client's last turn needs, not by habit.
src: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 4 Engaging; Ch. 8 Deeper Listening; Ch. 11 Offering Information and Advice
Moyers-etal-2015 § E.4 Behavior Codes; H Summary Scores; I Competence Thresholds
Padesky-1993 § Definition of Socratic questioning; Stage 3 Summarizing

responding-in-session.language-and-tone.s: Word choice and delivery rules for therapists and tools, covering plain language, tentative hypotheses, the client's own words, tone of voice and nonverbal behavior.
responding-in-session.language-and-tone.when: You are choosing words for a reflection, hypothesis or explanation, or reviewing why a technically correct response landed badly.
responding-in-session.language-and-tone.b: Use the client's words, plain language and short sentences, and offer ideas as hypotheses the client can correct. Tone and body language decide how words land: the same reflection said with disapproval counts as a confrontation [Moyers-etal-2015]. Aim for warmth, genuineness and relaxed confidence, never condescension [Young-Beck-1980].
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 3 Understanding; Item 4 Interpersonal Effectiveness; Item 8 Clairvoyance and underlying assumptions; Item 10 Application

responding-in-session.pacing-silence-and.s: How much to talk, when to stay silent, how to interrupt respectfully, and how to pace a session so the client can absorb new ideas.
responding-in-session.pacing-silence-and.when: Sessions feel rushed, stuck or one-sided, the client talks at length without focus, or you are unsure whether to fill a pause.
responding-in-session.pacing-silence-and.b: Pace the session to the client's capacity to absorb new information: not so slow that points are belabored, not so fast that topics change before the client integrates them [Young-Beck-1980]. Keep your turns short and mostly reflective, use silence on purpose rather than by default, and interrupt politely when discussion drifts or stops being productive.
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 1 Agenda; Item 5 Collaboration, Balancing structure against patient autonomy; Item 6 Pacing and Efficient Use of Time

responding-in-session.phrasing-library.s: Example therapist phrasings for common in-session situations, each with a helpful version, an Avoid version and the reason, for clinicians and tool designers.
responding-in-session.phrasing-library.when: You need concrete wording for a common moment in session, or are writing response templates for a clinical tool.
responding-in-session.phrasing-library.b: Good phrasing is short, tentative, uses the client's words and leaves room for correction; poor phrasing argues, labels, lectures or rushes past feeling. Use these lines as starting points, then adapt them to the client's language and culture. Any mention of suicide or self-harm moves you to the risk pages, whatever the agenda.

responding-in-session.pitfall-interrogat.s: The therapist asks question after question, often several at once or leading toward a set answer, and the client gives short, guarded or compliant replies.
responding-in-session.pitfall-interrogat.when: A session transcript shows long runs of questions with few reflections or summaries, or the client seems defensive during Socratic questioning.
responding-in-session.pitfall-interrogat.b: Too many questions, stacked questions and leading questions turn Socratic questioning into cross-examination. The fix is to reflect at least as often as you ask, ask one open question at a time, summarize every few minutes, and give up the "right answer" you were steering toward [Moyers-etal-2015; Padesky-1993].

responding-in-session.pitfall-missing-ri.s: A client says things will never get better, and the therapist moves straight to disputing the thought or reassuring, without asking about suicidal thoughts.
responding-in-session.pitfall-missing-ri.when: A client expresses hopelessness, being a burden, or "what's the point", and you are about to restructure the thought or continue the agenda.
responding-in-session.pitfall-missing-ri.b: Hopelessness is a thought to work with and also a well-established marker of suicide risk [Beck-etal-1985], though a weak predictor on its own [Ribeiro-etal-2018]. Before you restructure it, ask directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts, act on the answer, and record it. Asking does not have to derail the session; skipping it can be the costliest error in this domain.
src: NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help for mental health

responding-in-session.pitfall-premature-.s: The therapist reassures, cheerleads or jumps to a technique while the client is upset, and the client feels unheard, argues back, withdraws or says "you don't get it".
responding-in-session.pitfall-premature-.when: A client reacts to your reassurance or technique with frustration, flatness or "I know, but", especially just after disclosing something painful.
responding-in-session.pitfall-premature-.b: Reassurance ("I'm sure it'll be fine"), vague praise and quick techniques feel kind but often tell the client their reaction is wrong or too much. Validate first, check it landed, and only then move to change [Linehan-1997]. Save affirmation for specific, genuine strengths.
src: Moyers-etal-2015 § E.4.f.2 Affirm; D Empathy global
Young-Beck-1980 § Item 3 Understanding; Item 10 Example of a Desirable Application

responding-in-session.pitfall-righting-r.s: The therapist argues for change, warns, lectures or rushes to fix, and the client answers with more reasons not to change, "yes, but" or quiet disengagement.
responding-in-session.pitfall-righting-r.when: You find yourself explaining why the client should change, the client keeps saying "yes, but", or homework and exposure plans stall after you pushed them.
responding-in-session.pitfall-righting-r.b: The righting reflex is the helper's urge to set things right by persuading, warning or fixing. When a client is ambivalent, it pushes them to defend the other side, so they talk themselves out of change [Miller-Rollnick-2023]. Notice the urge, reflect instead, and ask for the client's own reasons.
src: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 1 The Mind and Heart When Helping; Ch. 14 Responding to Sustain Talk and Discord

responding-in-session.psychoeducation-wi.s: How to explain treatment models, rationales and facts collaboratively using elicit-provide-elicit, small chunks, the client's own examples and teach-back.
responding-in-session.psychoeducation-wi.when: You need to explain how a problem works, why a technique is used, or what to expect from treatment, and want the client to understand and own it.
responding-in-session.psychoeducation-wi.b: Teach in short exchanges, not speeches: ask what the client already knows, give one small piece tailored to them, then ask what they make of it (elicit-provide-elicit) [Moyers-etal-2015]. Build models from the client's own recent example, check understanding with teach-back, and write the key point down. Information supports cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) but is not the treatment by itself.
