responding-in-session.reflective-listeni.s: How to form simple and complex reflections, including feeling, meaning, double-sided and amplified reflections, and how deep to go on each turn.
responding-in-session.reflective-listeni.when: You want to show understanding of what the client just said, deepen it, or steer gently without asking another question.
responding-in-session.reflective-listeni.b: A reflection is a statement, not a question, that returns what the client said, either as said (simple) or with added meaning (complex). Aim for at least 40 percent complex reflections, which the motivational interviewing (MI) coding standard treats as fair, and 50 percent as good [Moyers-etal-2015]. Go one step deeper than the client's words, not three, and let the client correct you.
src: Moyers-etal-2015 § E.4.e Reflections; D Empathy global; E.4.g.2 Confront
Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 8 Deeper Listening; Ch. 14 Responding to Sustain Talk and Discord

responding-in-session.responding-to-ambi.s: How to respond when a client is ambivalent about change, using motivational interviewing skills for change talk, sustain talk and discord, and resisting the righting reflex.
responding-in-session.responding-to-ambi.when: A client argues for staying the same, says "yes, but", skips homework, hesitates at exposure, or pushes back against you.
responding-in-session.responding-to-ambi.b: Ambivalence is normal: most clients hold reasons to change and reasons to stay the same at once. Arguing for change pushes the client to argue the other side, so reflect, ask for their own reasons, and respect their choice [Miller-Rollnick-2023]. Treat pushback against you (discord) as a relationship signal and repair it before returning to the task.
src: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Ch. 1 The Mind and Heart When Helping; Ch. 10 Evoking; Ch. 14 Responding to Sustain Talk and Discord
Moyers-etal-2015 § D Global scores Cultivating Change Talk, Softening Sustain Talk, Partnership; E.4.f.4 Emphasizing Autonomy

responding-in-session.responding-to-hope.s: How to respond turn by turn to hopelessness, shame and harsh self-talk, including when hopelessness requires a direct suicide risk check.
responding-in-session.responding-to-hope.when: A client says nothing will help, that they are worthless or a failure, or speaks about themselves with contempt or shame.
responding-in-session.responding-to-hope.b: Treat hopelessness as both a symptom to understand and a risk marker: whenever a client expresses it, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, then respond with validation and a small testable step rather than argument [Beck-etal-1985]. Treat harsh self-criticism as a pattern with a function, not a fact to debate; reflect it, get curious about it, and build a kinder inner voice [Gilbert-2009]. Reassurance alone rarely lands.
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 4 Interpersonal Effectiveness; Item 9 Testing automatic thoughts
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help for mental health

responding-in-session.responding-to-stro.s: What to say and do when a client cries, panics, becomes angry or dissociates in session, including grounding, pacing, de-escalation and when to check risk.
responding-in-session.responding-to-stro.when: A client becomes tearful, highly anxious, angry or detached during a session and the planned work cannot continue as is.
responding-in-session.responding-to-stro.b: Strong emotion in session is both useful information and a signal to change pace. If the client can still think, slow down, validate and ask what went through their mind just before the feeling surged [Young-Beck-1980]. If they cannot (flooded, enraged or detached), regulate first with short sentences, grounding or de-escalation, and return to the work only when they are back in the room.
src: Young-Beck-1980 § Item 8 Mood Shift During the Session; Item 3 Understanding
Richmond-etal-2012 § Ten domains of de-escalation; Clinicians should self-monitor
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help for mental health

responding-in-session.socratic-dialogue.s: How to run guided discovery with Padesky's four stages, which question types to use, and how to keep Socratic questioning from turning into interrogation or debate.
responding-in-session.socratic-dialogue.when: You want the client to examine a thought, belief or plan and reach their own conclusion rather than being told.
responding-in-session.socratic-dialogue.b: Socratic questioning in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) aims to guide discovery, not to change the client's mind toward an answer the therapist already holds. Run it in four stages: informational questions, listening, summarizing, and a synthesizing question that applies what was found to the original belief [Padesky-1993]. If it feels like cross-examination, slow down, reflect and summarize.
src: Padesky-1993 § Definition of Socratic questioning; Four stages of guided discovery
Young-Beck-1980 § Item 7 Guided Discovery; Item 8 Focusing on Key Cognitions; Item 9 Inductive questioning

responding-in-session.validation.s: Linehan's six levels of validation, how to validate the valid without endorsing distorted conclusions, and when to validate before moving to change techniques.
responding-in-session.validation.when: A client is distressed, feels misunderstood, or is about to be asked to change a thought or behavior they experience as understandable.
responding-in-session.validation.b: Validation tells the client that their emotion, thought or action makes sense in some way, without agreeing that the conclusion is true. Marsha Linehan describes six levels, from attentive listening to radical genuineness [Linehan-1997]. Validate first, briefly and specifically, then invite change; change requests that skip validation tend to be heard as "you are wrong to feel this".
src: Linehan-1997 § Validation and psychotherapy, levels of validation
Richmond-etal-2012 § Domain VII Agree or Agree to Disagree
Young-Beck-1980 § Item 3 Understanding; Item 10 Example of a Desirable Application

behavioral.activity-monitoring-and-sched.s: How to run an activity diary with mood, mastery and pleasure ratings, read it with the client, and turn it into a specific, graded weekly activity schedule.
behavioral.activity-monitoring-and-sched.when: A client needs a baseline of how they spend their time and how activity relates to mood, or a concrete weekly plan of activities.
behavioral.activity-monitoring-and-sched.b: An activity diary shows what the client actually does and how each activity links to mood, mastery and pleasure. Read it together to find patterns, then turn those patterns into a short, specific, graded schedule. Monitoring and scheduling appear in every behavioral activation (BA) protocol, and activity scheduling alone has a large effect on depression in randomized trials [Kanter-etal-2010] [Cuijpers-etal-2007].
src: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 4 Identifying the Ingredients of the Behavioral Antidepressant; Ch. 5 Activity Scheduling and Structuring
Lejuez-etal-2011 § Abstract, revised Daily Monitoring Form and low-literacy version

behavioral.behavioral-activation.s: How to deliver behavioral activation for depression, from rationale and functional analysis to values-based scheduling and work on avoidance and rumination, with session counts and evidence.
behavioral.behavioral-activation.when: A client with depression has withdrawn from rewarding activity, avoids tasks or people, or ruminates instead of acting.
behavioral.behavioral-activation.b: Behavioral activation (BA) treats depression by helping clients act according to a plan and their values rather than their mood. You and the client work out what depressed behavior does for them (often avoidance), then schedule specific, graded activities that restore contact with reward. BA is supported by randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analyses, performs about as well as full cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and is a guideline-recommended option for both less and more severe depression in the United Kingdom (UK) [Uphoff-etal-2020] [Richards-etal-2016] [NICE-NG222].
src: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 2 Core Principles; Ch. 6 Avoidance Modification; Ch. 7 How Thinking Can Be Problematic Behavior; Ch. 8 Troubleshooting
Kanter-etal-2010 § Abstract, core components of BA
Lejuez-etal-2011 § Abstract, life areas, values and activities
Uphoff-etal-2020 § Abstract, main results and authors' conclusions
Ekers-etal-2014 § Abstract; Discussion, number of sessions and non-specialist therapists
NICE-NG222 § Table 1 and Table 2, individual and group BA rows (reviewed by NICE January 2026, no change)

behavioral.behavioral-experiments.s: How to design, run and debrief behavioral experiments that test a specific belief or prediction, with experiment types, a planning template, phrasings and evidence.
behavioral.behavioral-experiments.when: A client holds a specific belief or prediction that verbal discussion has not shifted, or that can be tested more convincingly through direct experience.
behavioral.behavioral-experiments.b: A behavioral experiment is a planned activity that tests a specific belief or prediction through direct experience, done in or between sessions. It turns a belief into a testable prediction, gathers real-world data, and reviews what the result means. Experiments are a core cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) method, and limited evidence suggests they shift beliefs faster and more broadly than verbal methods or exposure alone [Bennett-Levy-etal-2004] [McMillan-Lee-2010] [McManus-etal-2012a].
src: Bennett-Levy-etal-2004 § Ch. 1 introduction; Ch. 2 Rouf and colleagues on devising effective experiments
Kaczkurkin-Foa-2015 § Cognitive therapy and behavioral experiments

behavioral.exposure-and-response-prevent.s: The core exposure and response prevention procedure for obsessive-compulsive problems, covering rationale, hierarchy, exposure trials, ritual and reassurance prevention, family involvement and expected outcomes.
behavioral.exposure-and-response-prevent.when: A client with obsessive-compulsive symptoms performs rituals, mental neutralizing or reassurance seeking that keep the obsessional fear going.
behavioral.exposure-and-response-prevent.b: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) asks the client to face obsessional triggers on purpose and then not perform the rituals, mental neutralizing or reassurance seeking that usually follow. It is the first-line psychological treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and is supported by many randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [Hezel-Simpson-2019] [Ost-etal-2015]. Its most common failures come from the therapist: stopping short of the core fear, allowing distraction, and giving reassurance [Gillihan-etal-2012].
src: Hezel-Simpson-2019 § ERP components; Outcomes and dropout; Inhibitory learning
NICE-CG31 § 1.5.1.1 to 1.5.1.4, stepped care for adults with OCD (update in progress)

behavioral.exposure-hierarchy.s: How to build a graded exposure hierarchy with distress and expectancy ratings, choose a starting point, and move through it flexibly instead of in rigid order.
behavioral.exposure-hierarchy.when: A client with anxiety, obsessive-compulsive or trauma-related avoidance has agreed to exposure and you need a shared, rated list of practice tasks.
behavioral.exposure-hierarchy.b: An exposure hierarchy is a list of concrete feared situations, each rated for expected distress on the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS, 0 to 100) and for the likelihood of the feared outcome. It lets client and therapist agree a starting point and a direction. Use it as a map, not a staircase: it must reach the most feared items, and varying the order and conditions helps learning last [Gillihan-etal-2012] [Craske-etal-2014].
src: Hezel-Simpson-2019 § ERP components, assessment and hierarchy
Lee-etal-2006 § Methods, rating and ranking of exercises

behavioral.exposure-principles.s: Why exposure works, comparing emotional processing and habituation with inhibitory learning, and how expectancy violation and related strategies change how you design and end each trial.
behavioral.exposure-principles.when: A clinician is planning or troubleshooting exposure and needs to decide what each trial should teach, what to measure, and when to end it.
behavioral.exposure-principles.b: Exposure, a core technique of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), is planned, repeated contact with what the client fears, without escape or safety behaviors. The older view held that fear must activate and then fall (habituation); the current inhibitory learning view holds that exposure builds a new "safe" memory that competes with the old fear memory, and that how much fear falls in session does not reliably predict outcome [Craske-etal-2008] [Craske-etal-2014]. In practice: aim each trial at testing a specific feared outcome, end it when that expectation has been tested rather than when the client feels calm, and vary the practice so the learning generalizes.
src: Foa-Kozak-1986 § Emotional processing theory, whole article
Kaczkurkin-Foa-2015 § Exposure techniques; Emotional processing theory
Craske-etal-2022 § Abstract, OptEx Nexus strategy groups

behavioral.exposure-types.s: How to choose and run in vivo, imaginal and interoceptive exposure, matched to the feared stimulus, with example exercises, formats, safety checks and evidence by condition.
behavioral.exposure-types.when: You have an exposure plan and need to decide which form fits the client's feared stimulus, whether situations, memories, images or body sensations.
behavioral.exposure-types.b: Match the type of exposure to what the client actually fears. In vivo exposure confronts real situations and objects, imaginal exposure confronts memories, images and feared consequences, and interoceptive exposure deliberately brings on feared body sensations [Kaczkurkin-Foa-2015]. Most plans combine types, and combining in vivo with imaginal exposure gives better results in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) [Kaczkurkin-Foa-2015].
src: Kaczkurkin-Foa-2015 § Exposure techniques; evidence by disorder
Lee-etal-2006 § Methods, interoceptive exercises and ratings; Results
VA-NCPTSD-PE § Prolonged Exposure overview, sessions and components
Hezel-Simpson-2019 § New directions, virtual reality and internet-delivered ERP

behavioral.pitfall-activity-without-func.s: The client's diary fills with scheduled activities but mood stays flat, tasks feel like chores, key avoidance continues, and rumination runs through everything they do.
behavioral.pitfall-activity-without-func.when: Behavioral activation is underway and the client is doing more but feeling no better, or activities are being completed without engagement.
behavioral.pitfall-activity-without-func.b: Behavioral activation (BA) is not a list of nice things to do. Its active ingredient is changing what depressed behavior does for the client, especially avoidance, and reconnecting with activities that matter to them [Martell-etal-2022] [Kanter-etal-2010]. If you schedule generic pleasant events without asking what function the client's current behavior serves, the diary fills up but mood does not move.
src: Martell-etal-2022 § Ch. 2 Core Principles; Ch. 6 Avoidance Modification; Ch. 7 How Thinking Can Be Problematic Behavior; Ch. 8 Troubleshooting
Lejuez-etal-2011 § Abstract, values and life areas

behavioral.pitfall-chasing-habituation.s: Exposure trials end only once anxiety drops, sessions with high fear are counted as failures, clients say they must feel calm first, and gains fade in new settings.
behavioral.pitfall-chasing-habituation.when: Exposure work is stalling, clients judge trials by how anxious they felt, or fear returns after apparently successful treatment.
behavioral.pitfall-chasing-habituation.b: Making "anxiety comes down" the test of a good exposure teaches clients that anxiety is dangerous and must be reduced before they are safe. In-session fear reduction does not reliably predict outcome [Craske-etal-2008]. Set each trial up to test a feared outcome and to build tolerance of distress, and judge success by what was learned [Craske-etal-2014] [Hezel-Simpson-2019].
src: Craske-etal-2014 § Abstract, expectancy violation and variability

behavioral.pitfall-overly-cautious-expos.s: Exposure stalls at low hierarchy items, the therapist allows escape, distraction or reassurance, top items are never attempted, and sessions drift into talk about anxiety.
behavioral.pitfall-overly-cautious-expos.when: An exposure-based treatment has run many sessions with little change, or you notice reluctance in yourself to push exposure forward.
behavioral.pitfall-overly-cautious-expos.b: Many therapists hold negative beliefs about exposure, such as that it is harsh or risky, and those beliefs predict more cautious delivery [Deacon-etal-2013]. Cautious delivery shows up as hierarchies that never reach the core fear, exposures that allow distraction or reassurance, and treatment that turns into talk. Expert supervisors list not encouraging clients to approach their most distressing situations as a common therapist pitfall that reduces the effectiveness of exposure [Gillihan-etal-2012].
src: Hezel-Simpson-2019 § Dropout and adherence; therapist fidelity

behavioral.pitfall-unnoticed-safety-beha.s: The client completes exposures or experiments yet beliefs barely shift, because hidden checking, reassurance, distraction, relaxation or mental rituals got the credit for safety.
behavioral.pitfall-unnoticed-safety-beha.when: Exposure or behavioral experiments are being done as planned but belief ratings and symptoms change little.
behavioral.pitfall-unnoticed-safety-beha.b: A safety behavior that the client credits with preventing disaster stops the disaster belief from being tested [Salkovskis-1991]. When obvious avoidance is gone but subtle or mental safety behaviors remain, exposures look complete but teach little. Ask about them directly before and after every trial.
src: Gillihan-etal-2012 § Abstract, distraction, reassurance and mental compulsions

behavioral.problem-solving-therapy.s: How to teach structured problem solving, from building a constructive problem orientation through defining, generating, choosing, doing and reviewing solutions, with formats, phrasings and evidence.
behavioral.problem-solving-therapy.when: A client's distress is tied to practical problems they feel stuck on, or they avoid, rush or ruminate over decisions instead of acting.
behavioral.problem-solving-therapy.b: Problem-solving therapy (PST) teaches clients a constructive attitude toward problems plus a repeatable sequence: define the problem, generate options, decide, act, and review. It is supported by many randomized trials for depression, with effects similar to other psychotherapies, and works best when it includes the problem-orientation training and all four core skills [Cuijpers-etal-2018] [Bell-DZurilla-2009]. It is brief and can be delivered by trained nurses and primary care clinicians [Mynors-Wallis-etal-2000].

behavioral.relaxation-and-arousal-reduct.s: How to teach applied relaxation and breathing skills, where they help, where they add little, and how to spot and handle relaxation used as a safety behavior.
behavioral.relaxation-and-arousal-reduct.when: A client needs a coping skill for physical tension or arousal, or you are deciding whether relaxation or breathing work belongs in an anxiety treatment plan.
behavioral.relaxation-and-arousal-reduct.b: Applied relaxation is an evidence-based treatment for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), with outcomes similar to cognitive therapy in randomized trials [Ost-Breitholtz-2000] [Arntz-2003] [Siev-Chambless-2007]. For panic disorder, relaxation adds little or may reduce effectiveness, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with interoceptive exposure does better [Siev-Chambless-2007] [Pompoli-etal-2018]. Any calming skill can turn into a safety behavior if the client uses it to prevent a feared catastrophe, so check its function before teaching it.
src: Ost-1987 § Description of applied relaxation; review of controlled studies
NICE-CG113 § 1.2.18 and 1.2.20, Step 3 high-intensity psychological interventions for GAD (last updated 2020; NICE has flagged an update)

behavioral.safety-behavior-reduction.s: How to find a client's safety behaviors, including subtle and mental ones, decide which to drop and when, and fade them through exposure and behavioral experiments.
behavioral.safety-behavior-reduction.when: A client's anxiety persists despite facing feared situations, or they rely on actions, objects or mental strategies to prevent a feared outcome.
behavioral.safety-behavior-reduction.b: Safety behaviors are actions a client takes to prevent a feared catastrophe, such as gripping a cart to avoid fainting or rehearsing sentences to avoid sounding stupid. Because the client credits them with preventing disaster, they block the discovery that the disaster was unlikely [Salkovskis-1991]. Dropping them during exposure produced larger belief change in an experiment [Salkovskis-etal-1999], but meta-analytic evidence is mixed and some researchers argue for temporary, judicious use [Meulders-etal-2016] [Rachman-etal-2008].
src: Salkovskis-1991 § Abstract, threat cognitions and safety-seeking behavior
Goetz-etal-2016 § Abstract, preventive versus restorative safety behaviors
Craske-etal-2014 § Abstract, removal of safety signals

behavioral.skills-training.s: How to teach assertiveness, social skills and organization and planning skills using instruction, modeling, rehearsal, feedback and real-world practice, with evidence by population.
behavioral.skills-training.when: A client's problems stem partly from missing or rusty skills, such as asserting needs, handling social situations, or organizing time and tasks.
behavioral.skills-training.b: Skills training teaches specific behaviors the client lacks or does not use, through a fixed loop: explain, model, rehearse, give feedback, and practice in real life. Within cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) it is used for assertiveness, social skills and organization and planning. Social skills training improves functioning in schizophrenia, and CBT-based organization and planning training improves symptoms in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in randomized trials [Kurtz-Mueser-2008] [Safren-etal-2010] [Solanto-etal-2010].
src: Kanter-etal-2010 § Abstract, skills training as a BA component
Speed-etal-2018 § Abstract and introduction, history and current status

cognitive.cognitive-restructuring.s: How to evaluate a hot thought through guided discovery, examining evidence, generating alternatives, decatastrophizing and checking usefulness, ending in a believable balanced response.
cognitive.cognitive-restructuring.when: You and the client have one specific hot thought with a belief rating and want to test whether it is accurate and helpful.
cognitive.cognitive-restructuring.b: Cognitive restructuring tests one hot thought against the client's own experience, using questions about evidence, alternative explanations, realistic outcomes and usefulness. The aim is a balanced response the client believes and can use, not a more positive thought or a win in an argument [Beck-2021; Padesky-1993]. If the thought turns out to be accurate, the work shifts to problem solving or acceptance.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts; Ch. 15 Responding to Automatic Thoughts
Padesky-1993 § Reevaluating distorted thinking and problem solving when accurate; definition of Socratic questioning; four stages of guided discovery

cognitive.core-belief-work.s: How to weaken old core beliefs and build new ones using the positive data log, continuum methods, the historical test, core belief worksheets and experiential work.
cognitive.core-belief-work.when: A client has solid automatic-thought skills but a global belief such as "I'm worthless" or "People will hurt me" keeps driving chronic problems or relapse.
cognitive.core-belief-work.b: Core beliefs are absolute, global beliefs about the self, others or the world ("I'm unlovable"). They are kept going because people notice and remember fitting evidence and discount the rest, so evidence alone rarely shifts them [Padesky-1994]. Effective work names a new belief in the client's words and then builds it slowly with a positive data log and continuum ratings over months, adding the historical test and experiential methods [Padesky-1994; Wenzel-2012].
src: Padesky-1994 § Identifying Alternative Schemas; Continuum Methods; Positive Data Log; Historical Test of Schema; Psychodrama; Core Belief Worksheets
Wenzel-2012 § 3 Modification of core beliefs; 4 Challenges and future directions
Beck-2021 § Ch. 18 Modifying Beliefs; Appendix D Restructuring the Meaning of Early Memories
Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 12 New Core Beliefs, Gratitude, and Acts of Kindness

cognitive.downward-arrow.s: How to move from a hot automatic thought to the assumptions and core beliefs beneath it by repeatedly asking what the thought would mean if it were true.
cognitive.downward-arrow.when: A hot thought recurs across situations, or the emotion seems out of proportion to the thought, and you suspect a deeper rule or belief is driving it.
cognitive.downward-arrow.b: The downward arrow takes one hot thought, provisionally assumes it is true, and asks what that would mean, again and again, until you reach a global statement about the self, other people or the world. It was first mentioned by Beck and colleagues in 1979 and elaborated by Burns as the vertical arrow technique [Wenzel-2012; Burns-1980]. Use it to find beliefs for the case formulation, not to change them in the same moment.
src: Padesky-1994 § Identifying Maladaptive Schemas (following affect, sentence completions, belief questionnaires); Identifying Alternative Schemas
Wild-etal-2008 § Method, semistructured interview and encapsulated belief

cognitive.identifying-automatic-thoughts.s: How to elicit automatic thoughts and images, catch the hot thought behind a mood shift in session, and rate belief and emotion before any evaluation.
cognitive.identifying-automatic-thoughts.when: A client reports a distressing reaction, or their emotion visibly shifts in session, and you need the specific thought or image driving it.
cognitive.identifying-automatic-thoughts.b: Automatic thoughts are the quick words or images that pass through a client's mind in a situation and shape how they feel and act. Find them by following emotion: when mood shifts, ask what just went through the client's mind, then pick the hot thought, the one carrying most of the feeling [Beck-2021; Greenberger-Padesky-2016]. Rate belief and emotion before you evaluate anything.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 12 Identifying Automatic Thoughts; Ch. 13 Emotions
Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 4 Identifying and Rating Moods; Ch. 6 Situations, Moods, and Thoughts; Ch. 7 Automatic Thoughts

cognitive.identifying-cognitive-distorti.s: How to teach clients to label common thinking traps as a prompt for testing thoughts, and why labels alone do not establish that a thought is false.
cognitive.identifying-cognitive-distorti.when: A client can already catch automatic thoughts and you want a quick way to spot recurring patterns in how they reason.
cognitive.identifying-cognitive-distorti.b: Cognitive distortions (thinking traps) are recurring biased patterns such as all-or-nothing thinking, mind reading and catastrophizing. Naming the pattern helps a client step back from a thought and choose a testing question [Burns-1980; Beck-2021]. A label is a hypothesis, not a verdict: categories overlap, independent annotators often disagree on them, and a thought can fit a trap and still be partly true [Shreevastava-Foltz-2021].
src: Shreevastava-Foltz-2021 § 1 Introduction; 2.1 Annotation of dataset; 4.2 Detecting the type of cognitive distortion
Padesky-1993 § Reevaluating distorted thinking and problem solving when accurate

cognitive.imagery-and-imagery-rescriptin.s: How to assess intrusive images and the memories behind them, and how to run imagery rescripting so the image's meaning changes, with safety limits and evidence.
cognitive.imagery-and-imagery-rescriptin.when: A client's distress is carried by recurring images, nightmares or early memories, or they say "I know it isn't true, but it feels true.
cognitive.imagery-and-imagery-rescriptin.b: Many distressing cognitions are images, and imagery evokes stronger emotion than verbal thought, so ask about images directly [Holmes-Mathews-2010]. Imagery rescripting (ImRs) has the client re-enter a distressing image or memory and change what happens in it so that its meaning changes. A meta-analysis of 19 trials found large effects, mostly from pre-post comparisons [Morina-etal-2017]. It needs specific training, supervision, careful preparation and attention to safety.
src: Wild-etal-2008 § Method (imagery interview; memory rescripting intervention; therapists)

cognitive.modifying-intermediate-beliefs.s: How to identify rules, attitudes and conditional assumptions, weigh their advantages and disadvantages, test them with behavioral experiments, and write flexible replacement rules.
cognitive.modifying-intermediate-beliefs.when: The same automatic thoughts keep returning because the client lives by a rigid rule or if-then assumption, such as "If I'm not perfect, I'll be rejected.
cognitive.modifying-intermediate-beliefs.b: Intermediate beliefs are the rules ("I must never let people down"), attitudes ("Making mistakes is terrible") and conditional assumptions ("If I ask for help, people will see I'm weak") that link core beliefs to everyday thoughts [Beck-2021; Wenzel-2012]. Find them, write them as if-then predictions, weigh their costs, and test them in action. Conditional beliefs are often best tested by behavioral experiments [Padesky-1994].
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 17 Introduction to Beliefs; Ch. 18 Modifying Beliefs
Wenzel-2012 § 1 Introduction; 3.3 Advantages-disadvantages analysis; 3.4 Behavioral experiments; 3.8 Restructuring early memories
Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 11 Underlying Assumptions and Behavioral Experiments

cognitive.pitfall-challenging-accurate-t.s: The therapist asks for evidence against a thought that reflects real loss, hardship or discrimination, and the client feels dismissed, argues back or becomes more hopeless.
cognitive.pitfall-challenging-accurate-t.when: The client's thought describes a real problem, such as a job loss, illness, poverty or unfair treatment, and restructuring is producing resistance or hurt rather than relief.
cognitive.pitfall-challenging-accurate-t.b: Not every negative thought is distorted. Cognitive therapy teaches clients to reevaluate thinking when it is distorted and to solve problems when it is accurate [Padesky-1993]. Challenging a true thought invalidates the client and damages the alliance. Validate what is true, then look for the distorted conclusion that may sit on top of it, or move to problem solving and acceptance.
src: Padesky-1993 § Reevaluating distorted thinking and problem solving when accurate

cognitive.pitfall-debating-the-client.s: The therapist builds a case against the client's thought, the client concedes "I suppose so," and the belief and mood are back by the next session.
cognitive.pitfall-debating-the-client.when: Restructuring feels like an argument, the client agrees in words but nothing shifts, or you notice you already know the answer you want them to reach.
cognitive.pitfall-debating-the-client.b: Questioning that aims to change the client's mind looks Socratic but works like a debate: a quick series of leading questions, then "So how can you still think that?" Clients often concede without believing, and change does not last [Padesky-1993]. Guided discovery uses genuine curiosity so the client reaches and owns the conclusion [Kazantzis-etal-2014].
src: Padesky-1993 § Example 1 Changing Stuart's Mind; Example 2 Guiding Discovery; four stages
Kazantzis-etal-2014 § Reinecke on not being disputatious; concluding comments (open style untested)

cognitive.pitfall-restructuring-as-reass.s: The client challenges the same worry many times a day seeking certainty, anxiety drops briefly then rebounds, and the method has become another compulsion or worry loop.
cognitive.pitfall-restructuring-as-reass.when: A client with obsessive, health or generalized worry does many thought records or asks you to go over the same fear again, and relief never lasts.
cognitive.pitfall-restructuring-as-reass.b: In obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), health anxiety and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), testing the content of a worry can turn into a way of neutralizing it. Each "balanced answer" brings brief relief, then a new doubt appears, and the client needs another answer. When the problem is the process of worrying or doubting, target the process and the reassurance-seeking, not each new content [Normann-Morina-2018].
src: Normann-Morina-2018 § Introduction (cognitive attentional syndrome; detached mindfulness; postponement)
Wells-2009 § Metacognitive model of generalized anxiety disorder

cognitive.pitfall-working-on-cold-though.s: Restructuring goes smoothly but mood barely moves, because the thought chosen is a vague, low-emotion description or question rather than the hot thought.
cognitive.pitfall-working-on-cold-though.when: A thought record or in-session restructuring looks complete, yet the client's emotion rating hardly changes and they say "It didn't really help.
cognitive.pitfall-working-on-cold-though.b: Restructuring only shifts emotion when it targets the thought that carries the emotion. Working on a description ("He didn't reply"), a question ("Why me?") or a mild side-thought produces tidy worksheets and no relief [Greenberger-Padesky-2016]. Find the hot thought first, often by following the strongest feeling or asking about images [Padesky-1994; Holmes-Mathews-2010].
src: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 7 Automatic Thoughts (identifying the hot thought)

cognitive.self-compassion-techniques.s: How to use compassion-focused methods within CBT for shame and harsh self-criticism, including compassionate imagery, a compassionate tone for alternative thoughts, and handling fears of compassion.
cognitive.self-compassion-techniques.when: A client produces good alternative thoughts but says "I know it logically, but I don't feel it," or meets every setback with harsh self-attack and shame.
cognitive.self-compassion-techniques.b: Some clients learn to generate balanced thoughts yet still feel no better, saying in effect "I understand the logic but it doesn't help" [Gilbert-2009]. Compassion-focused methods, drawn mainly from compassion-focused therapy (CFT), train a warm, supportive inner stance so that alternative thoughts are felt as kind and helpful, not just correct. Meta-analytic evidence is promising but based mostly on small trials [Kirby-etal-2017].
src: Gilbert-2009 § Clinical focus; Three types of affect regulation system; Compassionate attention; Compassionate imagery; Compassionate reasoning; Fear of compassion
Neff-Site § The Three Elements of Self-Compassion

cognitive.thought-records.s: How to teach and use thought records, building from three columns to the seven-column record, with column contents, rating rules and how to review them.
cognitive.thought-records.when: A client can name situations, moods and thoughts and is ready for a written, structured way to catch and test thoughts between sessions.
cognitive.thought-records.b: A thought record is a written worksheet that walks the client through one upsetting moment: situation, moods, thoughts, then evidence and a balanced alternative. Start with three columns to catch thoughts, then add columns as skills grow, ending with the seven-column record [Greenberger-Padesky-2016]. Its purpose is to teach the client to question their own thinking, so the record matters less than the skill it builds [Kazantzis-etal-2014].
src: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 6 to 9 (situations, moods, thoughts; evidence; alternative or balanced thinking)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts; Ch. 15 Responding to Automatic Thoughts
Kazantzis-etal-2014 § Padesky on the seven-column thought record as a way of teaching Socratic dialogue

cognitive.worry-and-rumination-technique.s: How to reduce repetitive negative thinking with worry postponement, metacognitive techniques such as detached mindfulness, and rumination-focused methods that shift from abstract to concrete thinking.
cognitive.worry-and-rumination-technique.when: The main problem is the process of thinking, such as long worry chains or brooding about why, rather than one hot thought, so testing content keeps feeding it.
cognitive.worry-and-rumination-technique.b: Worry (repetitive "what if" thinking about the future) and rumination (repetitive brooding about problems, causes and meanings) are processes, so arguing with each worry often adds fuel. Target the process instead: postpone worry to a set time, step back from trigger thoughts, test beliefs that worry is uncontrollable or useful, and shift rumination from abstract "why" questions to concrete "how" steps [Normann-Morina-2018; Watkins-2008].
src: Wells-2009 § Metacognitive model and treatment techniques

08-measurement.anxiety-measures.s: Format, cutoffs, severity bands, change rules and licensing for general and disorder-specific anxiety measures, including panic, social anxiety, health anxiety, worry and youth scales.
08-measurement.anxiety-measures.when: A clinician needs to pick, score or interpret a general or disorder-specific anxiety questionnaire for screening or session-by-session monitoring.
08-measurement.anxiety-measures.b: The free Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) is the default every-session anxiety measure: 10 or more suggests a probable anxiety disorder, and a drop of 4 or more points exceeds measurement error. Because it picks up several anxiety disorders, add a disorder-specific measure when the target is panic, social anxiety or health anxiety. Many specific scales are copyrighted, so check terms before electronic use.
src: Clark-etal-2018 § Methods, Measures of clinical outcome
Julian-2011 § Beck Anxiety Inventory; Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety

08-measurement.depression-measures.s: Format, scoring, severity bands, screening cutoffs, change thresholds and licensing for the PHQ-9, PHQ-2, BDI-II, QIDS-SR16 and EPDS, with rules for responding to the suicide item.
08-measurement.depression-measures.when: A clinician needs to choose, score or interpret a self-report depression measure for screening, severity rating or session-by-session monitoring.
08-measurement.depression-measures.b: Use the free Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) every session for most adults: 10 or more suggests probable major depression, and a drop of 6 or more points exceeds measurement error. The Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) is a licensed alternative, the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS-SR16) a brief one, and the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) suits pregnancy and the postpartum period. Any endorsement of the PHQ-9 self-harm item needs a same-session risk conversation.
src: Clark-etal-2018 § Methods, Measures of clinical outcome
Wang-Gorenstein-2013 § Cutoff scores; Description of the BDI-II

08-measurement.idiographic-measures.s: How to build and use personalized measures such as belief and emotion ratings, distress and expectancy ratings, frequency counts, goal attainment scaling and goal-based outcomes alongside standard scales.
08-measurement.idiographic-measures.when: A clinician wants to track a client's own target, belief or goal that a standard questionnaire does not capture, or needs ratings inside a thought record, exposure or experiment.
08-measurement.idiographic-measures.b: Idiographic measures are ratings built around one client's own problem, belief or goal [Haynes-etal-2009]. They make cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) targets concrete: how strongly a thought is believed, how distressing a situation is, how likely a feared outcome seems, how often a behavior happens, and how close a goal is. Use them alongside, not instead of, a standardized measure, and define each anchor in writing so ratings mean the same thing every week.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. Identifying and evaluating automatic thoughts; thought records
Craske-etal-2014 § Expectancy violation; ending exposure trials

08-measurement.instrument-licensing.s: How measures differ in copyright and license terms, which common CBT measures are free, conditionally free or sold, and what that means for paper, electronic and AI-assisted use.
08-measurement.instrument-licensing.when: A clinician, service or tool designer wants to copy, translate, display, score or build a questionnaire into software and needs to know whether that is allowed.
08-measurement.instrument-licensing.b: "Free to use" covers several different legal positions. Some measures are public domain, some are copyrighted but free with no permission needed, some are free only on paper or only for noncommercial use, and some are sold to qualified purchasers. Check the current terms from the rights holder before copying, translating or building a measure into software, and never reproduce the items of a proprietary instrument.
src: ITQ-Site § Home page; PTSD and CPTSD measures
Julian-2011 § Beck Anxiety Inventory; Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety

08-measurement.instrument-selection.s: A decision procedure and lookup table for picking a short battery of validated, licensable measures matched to the client's main problem, age, setting and planned repeat schedule.
08-measurement.instrument-selection.when: A clinician at assessment, or a team building a service or digital tool, must decide which questionnaires to give and how often.
08-measurement.instrument-selection.b: Pick one brief, validated primary symptom measure matched to the main problem and give it every session. Add a functioning measure, and a longer disorder-specific measure at baseline, midpoint and end if it tracks the target better. Check that each measure is validated for the client's age and setting and that your license covers how you will use it. Screeners suggest possible cases; they do not diagnose.
src: Clark-etal-2018 § Methods, Measures of clinical outcome

08-measurement.measurement-based-care.s: How to give a brief validated measure every session, review the score and trend with the client, and use it to adjust treatment, with the evidence on benefits and limits.
08-measurement.measurement-based-care.when: A clinician is setting up routine symptom tracking for a client or a service, or is unsure what to do with session-by-session scores.
08-measurement.measurement-based-care.b: Measurement-based care (MBC) means giving a brief validated measure before every or nearly every session, reviewing the score and its trend with the client, and changing the plan together when progress stalls [Lewis-etal-2019]. Progress feedback gives a small average benefit and fewer dropouts [DeJong-etal-2021], and for clients predicted to do poorly it reduced deterioration and nearly doubled reliable change [Lambert-etal-2018]. One-time screening, infrequent measurement, and feedback outside the clinical encounter do not help [Fortney-etal-2017].
src: Lewis-etal-2019 § Abstract; Core components and fidelity of MBC
Clark-etal-2018 § Summary; Methods, Measures of clinical outcome

08-measurement.other-measures.s: Format, cutoffs, change rules and licensing for adult ADHD, insomnia, eating disorder, alcohol and drug, functioning, general distress and emotion regulation measures used alongside CBT.
08-measurement.other-measures.when: A clinician needs a screening or monitoring measure for adult ADHD, insomnia, eating problems, alcohol or drug use, functional impairment, general distress or emotion regulation.
08-measurement.other-measures.b: These measures answer narrower questions: is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) likely, how severe is insomnia, how strong is eating disorder thinking, is drinking or drug use risky, and how impaired is daily life. Screeners such as the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) flag who needs fuller assessment. The Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Work and Social Adjustment Scale (WSAS) track change during cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).
src: CORE-Site § CORE-10 information; Copyright and licensing

08-measurement.pitfall-measuring-without.s: Questionnaires are collected every session but scores are filed unseen, never shown to the client, and flat or worsening trends run for weeks without any change to the plan.
08-measurement.pitfall-measuring-without.when: A service or clinician collects routine outcome measures but the scores are not reviewed in session or do not lead to decisions.
08-measurement.pitfall-measuring-without.b: Collecting scores is not measurement-based care. The benefit comes from reviewing the score with the client in the session and changing the plan when progress stalls. Scores filed unseen, fed back outside the encounter, or gathered only occasionally do not improve outcomes [Fortney-etal-2017].
src: Lewis-etal-2019 § Abstract; Core components of MBC

08-measurement.pitfall-overreading-score.s: A two- or three-point fall is celebrated as improvement, a similar rise triggers alarm, or success is declared from a percentage drop off a low baseline.
08-measurement.pitfall-overreading-score.when: A clinician, client or tool interprets session-to-session score movement or an end-of-treatment result without checking it against the measure's error.
08-measurement.pitfall-overreading-score.b: Every questionnaire score contains measurement error, so small changes are often noise. Judge single changes against the measure's reliable change amount, read trends across several sessions rather than one, and report end-of-treatment results as reliable and clinically significant change, not as raw differences or percentages alone.
src: PSYCTC-RCSC § Reliable change; Clinically significant change

08-measurement.pitfall-screening-score-a.s: A client is recorded as having depression, PTSD, ADHD or another disorder because a questionnaire passed its cutoff, with no clinical interview confirming it.
08-measurement.pitfall-screening-score-a.when: A questionnaire score above a cutoff is about to be entered as a diagnosis, shared with the client as one, or used by a tool to label a client.
08-measurement.pitfall-screening-score-a.b: A score above a screening cutoff means "probable" or "worth assessing", not a diagnosis. Cutoffs trade false positives against false negatives, and the balance shifts with the setting. Confirm with a clinical or structured interview, record the score as a screening result, and keep diagnosis within your scope of practice.

08-measurement.pitfall-unreviewed-risk-i.s: A client marks thoughts of death or self-harm on the PHQ-9 or another measure, and nobody notices or asks about it until after the session or not at all.
08-measurement.pitfall-unreviewed-risk-i.when: Questionnaires with a self-harm or suicide item are given in clinic, online or by app, especially when scoring happens after the session or automatically.
08-measurement.pitfall-unreviewed-risk-i.b: Any nonzero answer on a questionnaire's self-harm or suicide item needs a direct conversation in the same session, before other agenda items. Score forms before the session starts, set up same-day review for forms completed remotely, and tell clients in advance that forms are not monitored in real time. The item opens a risk assessment; it does not replace one.

08-measurement.process-measures.s: What the Outcome and Session Rating Scales, the Working Alliance Inventory short form and homework ratings measure, how to use them each session, and their licensing limits.
08-measurement.process-measures.when: A clinician wants to track the therapeutic alliance, session fit or homework completion alongside symptom scores, or a tool designer must choose a process measure.
08-measurement.process-measures.b: Process measures track how therapy is going, not only how the client is doing. The alliance predicts outcome modestly but robustly (r = 0.28 across 295 studies) [Fluckiger-etal-2018], so a brief end-of-session rating can catch ruptures early. Rate homework for both quantity and quality, because both relate to outcome in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [Kazantzis-etal-2016]. The Outcome Rating Scale (ORS) and Session Rating Scale (SRS) are free on paper for individual clinicians but may not be used electronically without a separate license [ORS-SRS-Site].
src: Kendrick-etal-2016 § Characteristics of included studies, ORS

08-measurement.reliable-and-clinically-s.s: How to apply the Jacobson and Truax reliable change index and clinical cutoffs to one client's scores, classify the outcome, and use the NHS Talking Therapies thresholds.
08-measurement.reliable-and-clinically-s.when: A clinician must decide whether a client's score change is real rather than measurement noise, or must classify an end-of-treatment outcome.
08-measurement.reliable-and-clinically-s.b: A change is reliable when it is larger than the measure's error, judged with the reliable change index (RCI) of Jacobson and Truax [Jacobson-Truax-1991]. A change is clinically significant when the client also moves from the clinical range into the healthy range. Report both together: reliably improved, recovered, no reliable change, or reliably deteriorated. For common measures, use the published thresholds: Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) change of 6 or more and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) change of 4 or more [Gyani-etal-2013].
src: PSYCTC-RCSC § Reliable change; Clinically significant change
Clark-etal-2018 § Methods, Measures of clinical outcome

08-measurement.trauma-and-ocd-measures.s: Format, cutoffs, change rules and licensing for the PCL-5, CAPS-5 and ITQ for trauma, and the Y-BOCS, OCI-R, DOCS and SI-R for obsessive-compulsive and hoarding problems.
08-measurement.trauma-and-ocd-measures.when: A clinician needs to screen, rate severity or monitor change in posttraumatic stress, complex PTSD, obsessive-compulsive or hoarding symptoms.
08-measurement.trauma-and-ocd-measures.b: For posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), give the free PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) weekly: 31 to 33 suggests probable PTSD and a 10-point drop suggests response. For obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the clinician-rated Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) is the reference severity measure, with a 35% reduction marking response; self-report scales such as the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) suit weekly tracking. DSM-5 here is the 2013 Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition.

09-ending.booster-sessions.s: When to offer booster sessions or a continuation phase after CBT, what the evidence shows for each, how to schedule them, and how to run a booster session.
09-ending.booster-sessions.when: A client is finishing CBT and you are deciding whether to schedule boosters or continuation sessions, or a client is returning for a booster.
09-ending.booster-sessions.b: Boosters are a few sessions scheduled after the end of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to review the relapse prevention plan and practice skills; a continuation phase is a longer series of spaced sessions for people at high relapse risk. Continuation CBT has the stronger evidence: it cut relapse in recurrent depression and panic disorder in randomized trials [Jarrett-etal-2001; White-etal-2013]. Offer a continuation phase to people at higher risk; pre-scheduled boosters for most others are expert consensus.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

09-ending.discharge-summary.s: What a CBT discharge summary contains, who receives it and with what consent, how to write it so the client can read it, and how long to keep records.
09-ending.discharge-summary.when: A course of CBT has ended, planned or unplanned, and you need to close the record and tell the client and other professionals what happened and what comes next.
09-ending.discharge-summary.b: Write a closing summary for every episode, planned or not. It states why the client came, what was done, what changed (with scores), the risk status and relapse plan at the end, why therapy ended, and how to get help again. Records should support continuity of care and document the nature, delivery, progress and results of services [APA-RecordKeeping-2007]. Write it so the client could read it, because they usually have a legal right to [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-524].
src: APA-RecordKeeping-2007 § Guideline 2 Content of Records; Guideline 7 Retention of Records; Guideline 13 Disposition of Records
CFR-42-482-61 § Paragraph (e) Discharge planning and discharge summary
ActionAlliance-2019 § Recommendations for inpatient providers (records and discharge summary)
HIPAA-45-CFR-164-524 § (a)(1) Right of access; (b)(2) Timely action

09-ending.dropout-and-unplanned-endings.s: How common dropout from CBT is, who is most at risk, what lowers it, and a step-by-step response when a client stops attending, including risk follow-up and closing the episode.
09-ending.dropout-and-unplanned-endings.when: A client has missed sessions without contact, says they want to stop abruptly, or shows early signs of dropping out, or you are designing a service's missed-appointment policy.
09-ending.dropout-and-unplanned-endings.b: About one in five adults drops out of psychotherapy (19.7%), and in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) about one in four starters (26.2%) stops during treatment [Swift-Greenberg-2012; Fernandez-etal-2015]. Lower it by agreeing expectations, accommodating preferences, watching the alliance and using progress feedback. When a client stops coming, reach out more than once, check risk first if risk is known, and close the episode in writing with a route back.
src: ActionAlliance-2019 § Recommendations for outpatient providers (follow up on missed appointments; caring contacts)
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

09-ending.ending-criteria.s: Decision rules for when to begin ending CBT, continue for relapse prevention, end and refer, or end early, based on goals, measures, residual symptoms, relapse risk and ethics.
09-ending.ending-criteria.when: A review point has arrived, the planned sessions are nearly used, or the client or a payer raises stopping, and you must decide whether to end, continue or refer.
09-ending.ending-criteria.b: Start ending when agreed goals are met and measures show reliable improvement to a non-clinical range that has held for a few weeks (expert consensus). Residual symptoms and other relapse risk factors are reasons to extend for relapse prevention, not to stop [Paykel-etal-1995; NICE-NG222]. If therapy is not helping after an adequate trial and a review, end and refer: ethics codes require it [APA-Ethics-2017].

09-ending.lapse-relapse-and-recurrence.s: Defines response, remission, recovery, relapse, recurrence, lapse and setback, explains why the distinctions matter at the end of CBT, and shows how to talk about them with clients.
09-ending.lapse-relapse-and-recurrence.when: You need shared language with a client or colleague about what counts as a setback versus a return of the disorder, or you are teaching the relapse prevention plan.
09-ending.lapse-relapse-and-recurrence.b: A lapse or setback is a brief return of old symptoms or behaviors; a relapse is the return of the full problem before recovery; a recurrence is a new episode after recovery [Rush-etal-2006; Larimer-etal-1999]. Teaching clients that setbacks are expected and recoverable is a core part of ending, because how a person interprets a lapse shapes whether it becomes a relapse [Larimer-etal-1999].
src: Rush-etal-2006 § Abstract (definitions of response, remission, recovery, relapse, recurrence)
Larimer-etal-1999 § Introduction; The Abstinence Violation Effect; Cognitive Restructuring
Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

09-ending.pitfall-abrupt-ending.s: The last weekly session arrives with no tapering, no written relapse plan and no route back; the client leaves anxious, credits the therapist, and returns in crisis months later.
09-ending.pitfall-abrupt-ending.when: You are within a few sessions of the planned end and have not yet discussed the ending, spaced sessions or written a relapse prevention plan with the client.
09-ending.pitfall-abrupt-ending.b: An ending that is not prepared wastes the consolidation phase that protects gains. The fix is simple and cheap: name the ending at the start, open the ending phase several sessions early, space sessions out, and hand over a written plan the client has already tested [Beck-2021; NICE-NG222].
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

09-ending.pitfall-ending-with-residual-s.s: Scores have dropped and the client feels better, so therapy ends while poor sleep, avoidance, rumination or low energy remain; months later the full problem returns.
09-ending.pitfall-ending-with-residual-s.when: A client has improved enough to talk about ending but still reports leftover symptoms, or scores have only just crossed below the clinical cutoff.
09-ending.pitfall-ending-with-residual-s.b: Response is not remission. Residual symptoms strongly predict relapse: in one depression cohort, 76% of people with residual symptoms relapsed, against 25% without [Paykel-etal-1995]. Before ending, list what is left, target it, and offer relapse prevention sessions to people at higher risk [NICE-NG222].

09-ending.pitfall-silent-dropout.s: A client stops attending, one voicemail is left, and the file is closed weeks later with no risk check, no closing letter, no summary and no route back.
09-ending.pitfall-silent-dropout.when: A client has missed one or more sessions without contact and you are deciding what to do, or your service closes files after non-attendance.
09-ending.pitfall-silent-dropout.b: Treating non-attendance as the client's decision and closing the file quietly misses risk, loses clients who could be re-engaged, and leaves no record of what happened. Make repeated contact, check risk first for anyone with known risk, offer a choice, and close in writing with a route back [ActionAlliance-2019; NICE-NG222].
src: ActionAlliance-2019 § Recommendations for outpatient providers (follow up on missed appointments; caring contacts)
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

09-ending.planning-the-ending.s: How to prepare for the end of CBT from the first session, space out the final sessions, run the ending phase, and close the episode of care ethically.
09-ending.planning-the-ending.when: You are starting a course of CBT and want the ending built in, or a client is nearing the planned number of sessions and you need to run the final phase.
09-ending.planning-the-ending.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is time-limited and aims to teach the client to be their own therapist, so say this in the first session and plan the ending from there [Beck-2021]. In the last phase, space sessions further apart (expert consensus), discuss how to keep the gains and write them into a relapse prevention plan [NICE-NG222], review progress, and say goodbye deliberately [Norcross-etal-2017]. End on the client's progress and the agreed criteria, not on the calendar alone.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

09-ending.referral-and-handover.s: When to refer a client on, how to prepare the client, what a referral letter contains, how to make a warm handover with consent, and when your responsibility ends.
09-ending.referral-and-handover.when: A client needs care you cannot provide, a higher step, a specialist, a prescriber or a new therapist because you or they are leaving, and you must transfer care safely.
09-ending.referral-and-handover.b: Refer on when the client needs something outside your competence, is not benefiting, needs a higher or specialist level of care, or when you or the client cannot continue [APA-Ethics-2017]. Prepare the client, get consent, send a focused referral, and keep clinical responsibility until the new provider has actually seen the client. For anyone with suicide risk, the handover must be fast and actively followed up [ActionAlliance-2019].
src: ActionAlliance-2019 § Recommendations for inpatient and outpatient providers (rapid referral; records; first appointment; missed appointments)
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

09-ending.relapse-prevention-blueprint.s: How to build a written therapy blueprint with the client covering what helped, keeping it going, high-risk situations, personal early warning signs, and a graded setback plan.
09-ending.relapse-prevention-blueprint.when: A client is in the last phase of CBT, or in relapse prevention sessions, and needs a written plan for staying well and handling setbacks after therapy ends.
09-ending.relapse-prevention-blueprint.b: The blueprint is a short written plan the client takes away: what kept the problem going, what helped, how to keep practicing, which situations and early warning signs to watch, and exactly what to do at each level of setback. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) lists these same components for relapse prevention work [NICE-NG222]. Write it in the client's words, rehearse it, and test it during spaced sessions before therapy ends.
src: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

10-diagnosis.communicating-a-diagnosis.s: How to tell a client their diagnosis collaboratively, link it to the formulation and treatment, handle relief, fear or disagreement, and explain who will see it in records and claims.
10-diagnosis.communicating-a-diagnosis.when: You have reached a working diagnosis and need to share it, or a client asks what is wrong with them, rejects a label, or worries about who will see it.
10-diagnosis.communicating-a-diagnosis.b: Share a diagnosis as a working description, in plain words, linked straight to what it means for treatment and hope. Ask what the client makes of it, expect relief, fear or disagreement, and tell them who will see it. In the United States the client can usually read the diagnosis in their record, so write it as if they will.
src: HIPAA-45-CFR-164-524 § (a)(1) right of access; (a)(3) reviewable grounds for denial; (b)(2) timeliness
Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 What Is the Case Formulation Approach to Cognitive-Behavior Therapy?

10-diagnosis.comorbidity.s: How often disorders co-occur in CBT clients, common patterns, why comorbidity is the norm, and a decision order for what to treat first when several disorders are present.
10-diagnosis.comorbidity.when: A client meets criteria for more than one disorder, or you must decide which problem to target first and whether one protocol can cover several.
10-diagnosis.comorbidity.b: Comorbidity is the rule in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) practice: most clients with an anxiety or mood disorder have, or have had, another one. Assess for it on purpose, because routine interviews miss it. Then order the work: risk first, then problems that block therapy, then the problem that causes most interference or drives the others, guided by the client's priorities. A single disorder-focused protocol often improves co-occurring problems too.
src: Bradford-etal-2024 § Missed, wrong and delayed diagnoses
Persons-2008 § Ch. 5 Beginning the Therapeutic Relationship and Obtaining a Problem List and Diagnosis; Ch. 6 Developing an Initial Case Formulation and Setting Treatment Goals

10-diagnosis.cultural-formulation-interv.s: What the 16-question Cultural Formulation Interview covers, its four domains, informant version and 12 modules, how long it takes, its evidence, and how to use it in CBT assessment.
10-diagnosis.cultural-formulation-interv.when: You are assessing any new client, especially when culture, language, religion, migration or identity may shape how problems are described, explained or treated.
10-diagnosis.cultural-formulation-interv.b: The Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) is a free, 16-question, semi-structured interview in DSM-5-TR (the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision) that asks the client how they define, explain and cope with their problem and what help they expect. It took about 23 minutes in the field trial and was judged feasible, acceptable and useful. Use it early, for any client, and feed what it yields into both diagnosis and the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) formulation.
src: Lewis-Fernandez-etal-2014 § Outline for Cultural Formulation; CFI structure; Supplementary modules; Indications
Lewis-Fernandez-etal-2017 § Abstract; Results, duration and Table 4

10-diagnosis.diagnosis-vs-formulation.s: What a diagnosis contributes to CBT (protocol choice, prognosis, comorbidity and risk checks, billing) and what only a case formulation supplies, with the limits of diagnostic reliability and validity.
10-diagnosis.diagnosis-vs-formulation.when: You are deciding how much weight to give a diagnosis in planning CBT, or a client, trainee or tool designer asks why CBT needs both a diagnosis and a formulation.
10-diagnosis.diagnosis-vs-formulation.b: A diagnosis tells you which group of people a client resembles, and so which evidence-based protocol, course and risks to expect. A case formulation tells you why this person's problems started and keep going, and so what to change. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) needs both: use the diagnosis to choose the template, and the formulation to fit it to the person. Neither replaces the other.
src: Persons-2008 § Ch. 1 What Is the Case Formulation Approach to Cognitive-Behavior Therapy?; Ch. 5 Beginning the Therapeutic Relationship and Obtaining a Problem List and Diagnosis
NICE-NG222 § Terms used in this guideline, less severe and more severe depression

10-diagnosis.differential-diagnosis-proc.s: A stepwise differential diagnosis for CBT intake covering safety, substance and medical causes, the best-fitting disorder, residual categories and the boundary with no disorder, plus key distinctions to check.
10-diagnosis.differential-diagnosis-proc.when: You are deciding what diagnosis, if any, best explains a client's symptoms, or a working diagnosis no longer fits the picture.
10-diagnosis.differential-diagnosis-proc.b: Work in a fixed order: make sure the client is safe, rule out substance and medical causes, then find the disorder that best explains the picture, then decide between adjustment disorder, a residual category or no disorder. Check the high-cost distinctions every time, especially past hypomania in anyone presenting with depression. Hold the result as a working hypothesis and reassess it.
src: First-2024 § Ch. 1 Differential Diagnosis Step by Step; publisher description

10-diagnosis.dsm-5-tr-overview.s: How DSM-5-TR is organized, how its criteria, subtypes, specifiers and residual categories work, what changed from DSM-5 through the 2025 update, and where the manual is heading.
10-diagnosis.dsm-5-tr-overview.when: You need to read, apply or record a DSM-5-TR diagnosis, or explain how the manual works to a client, trainee or tool designer.
10-diagnosis.dsm-5-tr-overview.b: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) is the United States reference for naming mental disorders. Each diagnosis is a set of criteria (symptoms, duration, distress or impairment, exclusions) applied with clinical judgment, never mechanically. For a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist it supplies shared language, a link to disorder-specific protocols and the codes that payers require. It is updated in place each year, so check the current supplement.

10-diagnosis.icd-10-cm-and-icd-11.s: How US therapists code diagnoses with ICD-10-CM through DSM-5-TR, the annual update cycle, common CBT codes and Z codes, and how ICD-11 differs for UK and international practice.
10-diagnosis.icd-10-cm-and-icd-11.when: You must code a diagnosis for a claim or record, check a code is current, or work with ICD-11 diagnoses from outside the United States.
10-diagnosis.icd-10-cm-and-icd-11.b: In the United States, the code on a claim comes from the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM), and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) lists the matching code for each diagnosis. Codes change every October 1, sometimes April 1, so a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) practice must code from the set in force on the date of service. The UK and most other countries use the World Health Organization (WHO) ICD instead, and ICD-11 has been in effect since January 2022 with different diagnostic concepts in several areas.

10-diagnosis.pitfall-culture-misread-as-.s: Culturally normal beliefs, idioms of distress or justified mistrust are read as symptoms, mood symptoms are underweighted, and racialized clients receive psychosis diagnoses more often than warranted.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-culture-misread-as-.when: The client's culture, religion, language, migration history or racialized identity differs from yours, or you are about to diagnose psychosis or a personality disorder in a client from a historically over-diagnosed group.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-culture-misread-as-.b: Diagnosis is shaped by the clinician's cultural lens. Black clients in the United States have about 2.4 times the odds of a schizophrenia diagnosis that White clients have, and structured interviews do not reliably close the gap. Before labeling unusual beliefs, intense distress or mistrust as pathology, find out how the client's own community would see them, and actively assess mood symptoms.
src: APA-DSM5TR-Update-2025 § III.A Attention to Culture, Racism, and Discrimination

10-diagnosis.pitfall-diagnosis-shaped-by.s: The recorded diagnosis is chosen to secure payment, more sessions or less stigma rather than from the assessment, or is assigned by someone whose license does not allow it.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-diagnosis-shaped-by.when: An insurer, employer, client or colleague is pushing for a particular diagnosis or code, or someone without diagnostic authority is about to record one.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-diagnosis-shaped-by.b: A diagnosis on a claim must be the one your assessment supports, made by someone allowed to make it. Inflating severity to get sessions, inventing a disorder to cover relationship or work problems, or softening a diagnosis to spare a client stigma all make the record false. Discuss the payment and stigma problem openly with the client instead of solving it with the code.
src: ACA-Ethics-2014 § A.2.b; C.2.a; C.6.b; E.5.a; E.5.d

10-diagnosis.pitfall-premature-diagnosti.s: The first diagnosis that fits, often depression or anxiety, is never questioned, so bipolar disorder, substance or medical causes and second disorders go unseen while treatment stalls.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-premature-diagnosti.when: A diagnosis was made quickly or inherited from a referral, treatment is not working as expected, or new information does not fit the label.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-premature-diagnosti.b: Premature closure means accepting the first diagnosis that fits and stopping the search. It is common in mental health care and costly: bipolar disorder treated as depression for years, anxiety hidden behind a depression label, a medical cause missed. The fix is a fixed differential routine, a structured check for the high-cost alternatives, and scheduled reassessment.
src: Bradford-etal-2024 § Missed, wrong and delayed diagnoses; Cognitive biases; Table 1
First-2024 § Ch. 1 Differential Diagnosis Step by Step

10-diagnosis.pitfall-questionnaire-score.s: A PHQ-9, GAD-7 or other screening total above a cutoff is recorded or told to the client as a diagnosis, without a clinical interview of criteria, duration, impairment and exclusions.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-questionnaire-score.when: You or a tool are about to write a diagnosis based mainly on a self-report score, or a client says a questionnaire or app told them they have a disorder.
10-diagnosis.pitfall-questionnaire-score.b: Screening questionnaires such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) flag who needs a diagnostic assessment; they do not make the diagnosis. Using a cutoff as a diagnosis roughly doubles the apparent rate of depression and misses medical, substance and bipolar explanations. Interview every criterion, and say "screened positive" until you have.

10-diagnosis.scope-of-practice-diagnosis.s: Who may make and record a mental health diagnosis in the US and UK by license and role, and what trainees, unlicensed staff and AI tools may say instead.
10-diagnosis.scope-of-practice-diagnosis.when: You are unsure whether your license or role allows you to diagnose, you supervise trainees, or you are designing a tool or service that might label clients.
10-diagnosis.scope-of-practice-diagnosis.b: In the United States, state law decides which licenses may diagnose; physicians, psychologists and psychiatric nurse practitioners generally can, and clinical social workers, counselors and marriage and family therapists can where their state practice act allows. In the UK, regulation is mainly by protected title and employer role, and some diagnoses, such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) at any age, are reserved for specialists. Everyone else, including trainees acting alone, coaches, peer workers and artificial intelligence (AI) tools, describes and screens but does not diagnose.
src: CFR-42-410-73 § (b)(1) Clinical social worker services, State in which the services are performed

adhd.adaptations.s: How to adapt CBT session structure, homework and pacing for clients with ADHD, and how to adjust for comorbidity, age, culture and medication, with rules for stepping up or referring.
adhd.adaptations.when: A client with ADHD, diagnosed or suspected, is in CBT for ADHD or another problem and attendance, homework, focus or comorbidity is getting in the way.
adhd.adaptations.b: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects the very behaviors cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) relies on: arriving on time, remembering homework and holding a thread through the session. Build external structure into therapy itself (reminders, written summaries, short focused homework, one skill at a time) and adjust for comorbidity, age and context. Step up or refer when risk, substance misuse, severe mood problems or lack of progress call for it.

adhd.adult-cbt-modules.s: Module-by-module content, format, dose and evidence for the three main adult ADHD CBT programs, Safren's individual CBT, Solanto's group meta-cognitive therapy, and Ramsay and Rostain's integrative CBT.
adhd.adult-cbt-modules.when: You are choosing or delivering a specific adult ADHD CBT protocol and need to know what each module teaches, how long it runs and how well it is supported.
adhd.adult-cbt-modules.b: Three adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) programs dominate. Safren's individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has the strongest trial support [Safren-etal-2010]; Solanto's group meta-cognitive therapy (MCT) targets time management, organization and planning [Solanto-etal-2010]; Ramsay and Rostain's integrative approach combines CBT with medication and stresses implementation over a longer course [Ramsay-Rostain-2015]. All share a core: an external organizing system, task breakdown, distraction management, and work on thoughts that block action [Knouse-Safren-2010].

adhd.assessment.s: How to assess suspected ADHD across the lifespan, which screening and rating scales to use with their cutoffs, which informants and records to gather, and which look-alikes to rule out.
adhd.assessment.when: A client, parent or teacher raises possible ADHD, a screener is positive, or attention and organization problems keep blocking CBT, and you need to confirm the picture and measure it.
adhd.assessment.b: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is diagnosed from a clinical history, not a test: symptoms meeting the count, childhood onset, presence in two or more settings, impairment, and other causes ruled out [APA-DSM5TR-2022] [Wolraich-etal-2019]. Rating scales screen and track severity; informants and records establish onset and pervasiveness. In many settings only specialist or licensed clinicians may make the diagnosis [NICE-NG87].

adhd.cbt-model.s: The Safren cognitive behavioral model of adult ADHD and the positively valenced avoidance cycle, how they maintain impairment, how to draw them with clients, and the targets implied.
adhd.cbt-model.when: You are formulating an adult client with ADHD and need to explain why skills are not used, why procrastination persists, or why mood and self-esteem have fallen.
adhd.cbt-model.b: In the leading cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) model of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), neurobiological deficits in attention, inhibition, working memory and motivation make it hard to learn and use compensatory skills; the resulting failures breed negative beliefs, low mood and avoidance, which further reduce skill use [Safren-etal-2004] [Knouse-Safren-2010]. A second loop runs through overly optimistic, permission-giving thoughts ("I work better at the last minute") that relieve discomfort now and feed procrastination [Knouse-Mitchell-2015]. Treatment therefore teaches skills and targets whatever stops the client using them.

adhd.children-and-parents.s: Evidence-based behavioral treatments for children and adolescents with ADHD, including parent training, classroom management and daily report cards, organizational skills training, and where CBT fits for teenagers.
adhd.children-and-parents.when: The client is a child or adolescent with ADHD, or a parent or teacher is seeking help, and you need to choose and deliver a psychosocial treatment.
adhd.children-and-parents.b: For children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the best-supported psychosocial treatments work through the adults around the child: behavioral parent training, behavioral classroom management and organization skills training [Evans-etal-2014]. Parent training is first-line for preschoolers; from age 6, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends medication plus parent training and classroom interventions, preferably both [Wolraich-etal-2019]. Child-focused cognitive therapy is not a substitute.
