adhd.emotional-dysregulation-and-associa.s: Emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, delayed sleep and later-life presentation in ADHD, with the evidence, how each appears in sessions, and CBT and DBT-informed adaptations.
adhd.emotional-dysregulation-and-associa.when: A client with ADHD flares quickly into anger or tears, is crushed by criticism, sleeps late and wakes exhausted, or is an older adult, and you need to know whether this belongs to ADHD and how to adapt CBT.
adhd.emotional-dysregulation-and-associa.b: Emotional dysregulation (fast, intense, short-lived frustration, anger and hurt) is common in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and drives much of its impairment, but it is an associated feature, not a diagnostic criterion [Kooij-etal-2019] [Beheshti-etal-2020]. "Rejection sensitive dysphoria" is a popular label, not a diagnosis [VanAsselt-2026]. Delayed sleep timing is estimated to affect most people with ADHD [Bijlenga-etal-2019], and ADHD persists into later life [Dobrosavljevic-etal-2020]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can add emotion skills borrowed from dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), sleep work and age adaptations; evidence for these additions is emerging.

adhd.medication-and-cbt.s: What CBT therapists need to know about stimulant and non-stimulant ADHD medicines, how CBT complements them, and how to talk with clients and prescribers about medication.
adhd.medication-and-cbt.when: A client with ADHD is taking, starting, stopping or questioning medication, or asks whether they need medication or therapy.
adhd.medication-and-cbt.b: Medication is the most effective treatment for core attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms: stimulants have the largest effects and non-stimulants moderate ones [Cortese-etal-2018] [Faraone-etal-2021]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adds what pills do not: organizing habits, coping with avoidance, and help with residual impairment and comorbid mood problems [Knouse-Safren-2010]. Most adult CBT trials were run in people already on medication [Safren-etal-2010]. Therapists inform and support; prescribing decisions belong to licensed prescribers.

adhd.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for ADHD under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with prevalence, course, differential diagnosis, comorbidity, risk notes and where CBT fits for children and adults.
adhd.overview.when: A child, adolescent or adult shows lifelong problems with attention, organization, restlessness or impulsivity and you need to know what ADHD is, how it is defined and what follows.
adhd.overview.b: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder: a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity or both, beginning in childhood, present in more than one setting and impairing daily life [APA-DSM5TR-2022] [WHO-ICD11-2022]. About 5.9% of young people and 2.5% of adults meet criteria worldwide [Faraone-etal-2021]. Medication treats core symptoms best; cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for adults and behavioral parent and classroom programs for children target the functional impairment that remains [Faraone-etal-2021] [Wolraich-etal-2019].
src: Epstein-Loren-2013 § Changes to criteria A to E; Modifiers
WHO-ICD11-2022 § 6A05 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (description and subcodes)

adhd.pitfall-child-cognitive-therapy-fir.s: A young child with ADHD gets individual talk therapy or a social skills group, while parents and teachers get little help and behavior at home and school stays unchanged.
adhd.pitfall-child-cognitive-therapy-fir.when: A child under about 12 with ADHD is referred for therapy and the plan centers on individual sessions with the child.
adhd.pitfall-child-cognitive-therapy-fir.b: For children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the effective psychosocial treatments work through parents and teachers: behavioral parent training, classroom management and organization skills training [Evans-etal-2014]. Individual cognitive or talk therapy with a young child does not change behavior where it happens, and clinic-based social skills training has been tested and found not to work [SCCAP-ADHD-Site].
src: Wolraich-etal-2019 § Key action statements 5a to 5c; Psychosocial treatments

adhd.pitfall-diagnosis-from-self-report-.s: An ADHD label is given or accepted on the strength of a positive questionnaire, a client's self-diagnosis or current symptoms, without childhood onset, informants, other settings or ruling out look-alikes.
adhd.pitfall-diagnosis-from-self-report-.when: An adult arrives saying they have ADHD, a screener is positive, or a referral states ADHD without a documented assessment.
adhd.pitfall-diagnosis-from-self-report-.b: A positive attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) screener or a convincing self-description shows that assessment is worth doing, not that ADHD is present. The diagnosis needs childhood onset, symptoms in more than one setting, impairment, and other causes ruled out [APA-DSM5TR-2022]. Skipping these steps risks missing depression, anxiety, sleep or substance problems and building treatment on the wrong formulation.
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Criteria B to E
FDA-Stimulant-Warning-2023 § Recommendations for health care professionals

adhd.pitfall-disputing-optimistic-though.s: The therapist hunts only for negative thoughts and misses "I'll do it later" style permission-giving thoughts, or debates whether the optimism is accurate, while procrastination continues unchanged.
adhd.pitfall-disputing-optimistic-though.when: An adult with ADHD keeps procrastinating despite skills training, or thought records show no negative thoughts before avoided tasks.
adhd.pitfall-disputing-optimistic-though.b: Adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often avoid tasks through thoughts that sound positive ("I work best at the last minute," "It'll only take 30 minutes"), not only through negative ones [Knouse-Mitchell-2015]. These thoughts bring quick relief and so keep procrastination going. Look for them deliberately, and work on what they do, not on whether they are true.
src: Knouse-Mitchell-2015 § Avoidance function of overly positive thoughts; Why functional analysis?; Applying the model to overly optimistic goals; Case example

adhd.pitfall-skills-without-implementati.s: Sessions explain planners, task lists and timers well, the client agrees they make sense, but between sessions nothing is used, and therapy drifts into talking about ADHD.
adhd.pitfall-skills-without-implementati.when: An adult with ADHD understands the strategies but is not using them a few weeks into CBT, or homework is repeatedly forgotten.
adhd.pitfall-skills-without-implementati.b: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a problem of doing what one knows, not of knowing what to do [Knouse-Safren-2010]. Explaining strategies is not treatment. Skills must be rehearsed in session, cued at the moment they are needed, and checked every session until they are habits [Ramsay-Rostain-2015] [Solanto-etal-2010].
src: Knouse-Safren-2010 § Conceptual model; Active ingredients; Treatment packages

adhd.treatment.s: The best-tested skills-based CBT protocol for adult ADHD, a 12-session outline, core techniques, expected dose, evidence strength, and where NICE and United States guidance place it.
adhd.treatment.when: An adult with diagnosed ADHD still has impaired functioning, on or off medication, and you are planning a course of CBT.
adhd.treatment.b: For adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) means teaching and rehearsing compensatory skills (organizing, planning, managing distraction), then working on the thoughts that block their use. The best-tested protocol is 12 weekly individual sessions [Safren-etal-2010]; a 12-session group alternative exists [Solanto-etal-2010]. It is supported by randomized trials, mostly as an add-on to medication, but the evidence is mostly low quality [Lopez-etal-2018].

adhd.underdiagnosis-in-women-and-adults.s: Why ADHD is missed or diagnosed late in girls, women and adults, how masking, hormones and misdiagnosis shape the picture, and how to assess and support late-diagnosed clients.
adhd.underdiagnosis-in-women-and-adults.when: An adult, often a woman, seeks ADHD assessment for the first time, has anxiety, depression or personality disorder diagnoses that never fully fit, or has just received a late ADHD diagnosis.
adhd.underdiagnosis-in-women-and-adults.b: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is diagnosed less often and later in girls and women, partly through referral bias, quieter symptoms, masking, and anxiety or depression treated in its place [Young-etal-2020b] [Kooij-etal-2025]. Many adults of every gender are now diagnosed for the first time [Staley-etal-2024]. A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist keeps ADHD on the differential when internalizing problems never fully resolve, and helps late-diagnosed clients rework a lifetime of self-blame.

bipolar-and-psychosis.adaptations.s: How to adapt CBT for bipolar and psychotic disorders for trauma, substance use, anxiety, acute severity, youth, culture and ethnicity, pregnancy and medication, with rules for stepping up or referring.
bipolar-and-psychosis.adaptations.when: Standard CBT for a client with bipolar disorder or psychosis needs changing because of comorbidity, illness phase, age, culture, pregnancy, medication issues or poor response.
bipolar-and-psychosis.adaptations.b: Keep the core cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) model but adjust pace, targets and team contact to the illness phase. Trauma-focused therapy is safe and effective in people with psychosis and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) [VanDenBerg-etal-2015]. Black African and Black Caribbean clients received less CBT in a large London provider [Morris-etal-2020], and culturally adapted interventions beat usual care more the more fully they were adapted [Degnan-etal-2018]. Step up whenever mania, acute psychosis or risk appears.

bipolar-and-psychosis.assessment.s: What to ask and record when mania, hypomania or psychosis is possible, which screening and severity measures to use with their cutoffs, differential questions, collateral sources and same-day risk steps.
bipolar-and-psychosis.assessment.when: A depressed client may have had hypomania, or a client describes voices, unusual beliefs, paranoia or disorganized thinking, and you need a structured assessment, baseline measures and a referral decision.
bipolar-and-psychosis.assessment.b: Ask every depressed client about past periods of high energy and reduced need for sleep, because bipolar depression is often misdiagnosed as unipolar depression [Yatham-etal-2018]. Use a validated screener only when suspicion is raised, then confirm by interview and collateral [VADoD-Bipolar-2023]. For psychosis, map each experience, its distress and its timeline, rate severity on a simple dimensional scale, and check risk and medical causes the same day.

bipolar-and-psychosis.at-risk-mental-sta.s: How to recognize an at-risk mental state for psychosis, screen with the PQ-16, explain transition risk honestly, and deliver preventive CBT without antipsychotics, with evidence on transition reduction.
bipolar-and-psychosis.at-risk-mental-sta.when: A young help-seeking client describes attenuated unusual experiences, brief self-limiting psychotic symptoms, or functional decline with a family history of psychosis, but does not meet criteria for a psychotic disorder.
bipolar-and-psychosis.at-risk-mental-sta.b: People at clinical high risk (also called an at-risk mental state) have attenuated or brief psychotic experiences with distress or decline; about 15% develop psychosis within 1 year and 25% within 3 years in the latest meta-analysis [SalazarDePablo-etal-2021]. The United Kingdom (UK) National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), with or without family intervention, and advises against antipsychotics to prevent psychosis [NICE-CG178]. Preventive interventions roughly halved transition at 12 months in pooled trials [VanDerGaag-etal-2013].

bipolar-and-psychosis.bipolar-cbt.s: Session outline for relapse-prevention CBT in bipolar disorder, covering psychoeducation, mood and sleep monitoring, building a personal relapse signature with an action plan, routine regulation, and cognitive work.
bipolar-and-psychosis.bipolar-cbt.when: A client with bipolar I or II disorder who is not acutely manic wants to reduce relapses, spot early warning signs, or manage residual depression between episodes.
bipolar-and-psychosis.bipolar-cbt.b: Relapse-prevention cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for bipolar disorder typically runs about 20 sessions over 6 months plus boosters, alongside mood stabilizers [Yatham-etal-2018]; the positive Lam trial averaged 14 sessions [Lam-etal-2003]. Its core is a personal relapse signature: the client's own early signs of mania and depression, linked to a graded action plan agreed with family and prescriber. At least 80% of people can name one or more early signs, and sleep disturbance is the most common early sign of mania [Jackson-etal-2003].
src: NICE-CG185 § Managing bipolar disorder in the longer term, psychological interventions
Yatham-etal-2018 § 2.6.2 Cognitive behavioural therapy; 4.2.2 Suicide risk

bipolar-and-psychosis.cbt-model.s: The leading CBT maintenance models for psychosis (Garety, Morrison and Freeman appraisal and threat-belief models) and bipolar disorder (integrative cognitive model), their cycles, how to draw them, and targets.
bipolar-and-psychosis.cbt-model.when: You have assessed a client with psychosis or bipolar disorder and need to explain why distressing experiences or mood swings persist and agree treatment targets together.
bipolar-and-psychosis.cbt-model.b: Cognitive models of psychosis hold that unusual experiences become distressing symptoms through how they are appraised: as external, threatening and personally significant, under the influence of emotion, reasoning biases and negative beliefs [Garety-etal-2001] [Strachan-etal-2022]. Persecutory beliefs persist through worry, low self-confidence, poor sleep and safety behaviors that block disconfirmation [Freeman-2016]. In bipolar disorder, the integrative cognitive model proposes that extreme, often conflicting appraisals of internal state changes drive behaviors that push mood further up or down [Kelly-etal-2017a].
src: Strachan-etal-2022 § Positive symptom models, Garety et al. 2001 and Morrison 2001
Freeman-etal-2016 § Background; Methods, the Feeling Safe Programme

bipolar-and-psychosis.cbtp.s: How to deliver CBT for psychosis session by session, from engagement and normalizing to formulation, coping, belief testing for paranoia and voices, and a staying-well plan, with evidence and phrasings.
bipolar-and-psychosis.cbtp.when: You are delivering individual CBT to a client with distressing voices, paranoia or other unusual beliefs and need the concrete session structure, techniques and wording.
bipolar-and-psychosis.cbtp.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (CBTp) helps clients link thoughts, feelings and actions to their experiences, re-evaluate the beliefs that make those experiences distressing, and cope differently, over at least 16 one-to-one sessions according to the United Kingdom National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) [NICE-CG178]. Its stages are engagement, normalizing psychoeducation, shared formulation with targeted work, and relapse prevention [HQO-CBTp-HTA-2018]. Distress and functioning are the targets, not the removal of every belief.

bipolar-and-psychosis.family-work.s: How to run family intervention alongside CBT for psychosis and family-focused therapy for bipolar disorder, covering structure, psychoeducation, communication and problem-solving skills, confidentiality, dose and relapse evidence.
bipolar-and-psychosis.family-work.when: A client with psychosis or bipolar disorder lives with or is in regular contact with relatives or a partner, and you need to involve them to reduce relapse and family strain.
bipolar-and-psychosis.family-work.b: Family intervention is one of the most effective psychosocial treatments for preventing relapse in schizophrenia (odds ratio 0.35 at 1 year versus usual care) [Bighelli-etal-2021]. The United Kingdom (UK) National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends offering it to all families of people with psychosis, over 3 months to 1 year with at least 10 planned sessions [NICE-CG178]. In bipolar disorder, family-focused therapy over 21 sessions reduced relapse and improved medication adherence [Novick-Swartz-2019].

bipolar-and-psychosis.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for bipolar and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, prevalence, onset and course, key differentials, the CBT role in brief, and suicide and safety facts.
bipolar-and-psychosis.overview.when: A client reports periods of elevated or irritable mood with high energy, or hallucinations, fixed unusual beliefs or disorganized thinking, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessment and planning.
bipolar-and-psychosis.overview.b: Bipolar I disorder needs one manic episode; bipolar II needs a hypomanic and a major depressive episode; schizophrenia needs at least a month of active psychotic symptoms within six months of disturbance under the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR) [APA-DSM5TR-2022]. Medication is the base of treatment, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a recommended add-on for both [Yatham-etal-2018] [Serra-etal-2023]. Suicide risk is high in both, so screen at every contact [Palmer-etal-2005] [Yatham-etal-2018].

bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-arguing-wi.s: The therapist tries to prove a persecutory belief false, or goes along with it to keep the peace; the client grows guarded, conviction holds, and sessions stall or end.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-arguing-wi.when: Sessions with a client who holds a strong unusual or persecutory belief turn into debates about whether it is true, or you notice yourself agreeing with it to avoid conflict.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-arguing-wi.b: Debating the truth of a delusion recruits the reasoning biases that maintain it, such as belief inflexibility and confirmation bias [Strachan-etal-2022], and agreeing with it confirms the threat. Cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (CBTp) works on current safety, distress and goals: it builds trust first, then lets the client gather their own evidence through real-world tests [Freeman-etal-2016].

bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-missed-bip.s: A client treated for "depression" improves briefly, then sleeps little, talks fast and spends, or cycles repeatedly, because past hypomania was never asked about and bipolar disorder was missed.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-missed-bip.when: You are about to start CBT or behavioral activation for depression and have not yet asked about past high-energy periods, family history of bipolar disorder, or reactions to antidepressants.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-missed-bip.b: Depression in bipolar disorder is frequently misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder, so a diagnosis of unipolar depression should come only after bipolar disorder has been excluded [Yatham-etal-2018]. The fix takes five minutes: ask every depressed client about past hypomania, family history and antidepressant reactions, and use a validated screener when suspicion is raised [VADoD-Bipolar-2023].

bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-sleep-loss.s: Standard sleep restriction, late-night homework or vigorous activity scheduling is used with a bipolar client, sleep falls and energy climbs, and the client tips into hypomania without anyone noticing.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-sleep-loss.when: You are using CBT for insomnia, behavioral activation or goal-setting homework with a client who has bipolar disorder or possible hypomania.
bipolar-and-psychosis.pitfall-sleep-loss.b: Sleep loss can trigger hypomania or mania [Harvey-etal-2015], and sleep disturbance is the most common early sign of mania, reported by a median 77% of people [Jackson-etal-2003]. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) and activation still help in bipolar disorder, but they need guardrails: time in bed no less than 6.5 hours, regular rhythms, and weekly mood ratings [Harvey-etal-2015]. With these, the adapted CBT-I protocol was followed by 4.6% hypomania or mania relapse versus 31.6% with psychoeducation over 6 months in a pilot trial [Harvey-etal-2015].

bipolar-and-psychosis.treatment.s: Guideline status, typical dose and a phase outline for CBT as an add-on to medication in psychosis and bipolar disorder, with family work, coordinated care and the evidence base.
bipolar-and-psychosis.treatment.when: A client has a psychotic or bipolar disorder and you need to decide which CBT-based treatment to offer, at what dose and alongside which medication and team.
bipolar-and-psychosis.treatment.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an add-on to medication and team care in both conditions, not a replacement. For psychosis, the United Kingdom (UK) National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends offering individual CBT for psychosis (CBTp) over at least 16 planned sessions plus family intervention [NICE-CG178] [BurgessBarr-etal-2023], and the American Psychiatric Association recommends CBTp [Serra-etal-2023]. For bipolar disorder, structured manualized psychological therapy reduces recurrence (odds ratio 0.56 versus control) [Miklowitz-etal-2021].

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.adaptat.s: Decision rules for adapting CBT to pain, diabetes, heart disease, cancer, opioids and health anxiety overlap, and for collaborating with medical teams on roles, information and medication changes.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.adaptat.when: Standard CBT needs adjusting for a client's physical illness, its treatment or its limits, or you need to coordinate with doctors, nurses or a pain team.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.adaptat.b: Keep the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) model, but fit it to the illness: agree roles with the medical team, adjust session length and format to the client's capacity, and separate realistic concerns from catastrophic ones. Where health anxiety overlaps, define with the doctor which checks are medically needed and treat the rest as safety behaviors [Tyrer-etal-2014]. Never change medicines or activity limits yourself.

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.assessm.s: What to ask and record when assessing chronic pain or a long-term condition, which brief measures to use with cutoffs and licensing, and how to involve the medical team.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.assessm.when: A client with chronic pain, diabetes, heart disease, cancer or another long-term condition is referred for distress, low mood, poor coping or disability and you are planning the assessment.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.assessm.b: Assess the person, not just the pain or disease: how the condition affects their life, how life affects the condition, what they believe about it, and what they want [NICE-NG193]. Confirm medical status with the treating team, screen mood and anxiety, and add one or two condition-specific measures such as a pain interference scale or a diabetes distress scale. Always ask about suicidal thoughts.

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.cbt-mod.s: The fear-avoidance model of chronic pain, the role of pain catastrophizing, its goal-based update, and how the same cycles extend to long-term conditions, with how to draw them.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.cbt-mod.when: You have assessed a client with chronic pain or a long-term condition and need a shared maintenance formulation explaining why disability, avoidance or distress persist.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.cbt-mod.b: The fear-avoidance model explains why some people with pain recover and others become disabled: pain read as a sign of harm leads to fear, avoidance, hypervigilance and disuse, which keep pain and disability going [Vlaeyen-Linton-2000; Leeuw-etal-2007]. Pain catastrophizing drives the threatening reading [Quartana-etal-2009]. The update adds goals: avoidance is a costly attempt to protect life goals [Crombez-etal-2012]. The same cycles, plus self-management burden, fit many long-term conditions.

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.overvie.s: How chronic pain and long-term conditions such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer present to CBT, with definitions, prevalence, differentials including health anxiety, suicide risk and the approach in brief.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.overvie.when: A client lives with persistent pain or a long-term physical condition and distress, disability or low mood is the reason for referral, and you need the overall picture first.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.overvie.b: Chronic pain is pain that persists or recurs for more than 3 months [Treede-etal-2019], and about one US adult in four has it [Lucas-Sohi-2024]. Long-term physical conditions such as angina, arthritis, asthma and diabetes raise the rate of depression, and the combination gives the worst health [Moussavi-etal-2007]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) targets distress, disability and coping, not the disease itself. Suicide risk is raised in chronic pain, so ask directly [Tang-Crane-2006].

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.s: The client hears that their pain or symptoms are "in their head", feels blamed or dismissed, argues for the physical cause, and disengages or seeks more tests.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.when: You are explaining a CBT formulation or referral to a client with chronic pain or a long-term condition, especially after normal tests or when they say others have not believed them.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.b: A psychological referral already sounds to many clients like "they think I'm making it up". If your explanation adds to that, the alliance breaks. Pain is defined as a sensory and emotional experience [Raja-etal-2020], and chronic primary pain is a diagnosis in its own right [Nicholas-etal-2019]. Say the pain is real first, then explain what makes it louder.

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.s: Therapy is judged by pain scores, sessions stall when pain stays the same, client and therapist feel they are failing, and activity waits until the pain improves.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.when: Treatment of a client with chronic pain is organized around reducing pain intensity, or the client says life will start again once the pain goes.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) usually reduces pain only a little [Williams-etal-2020], so a plan built on pain relief sets both people up to fail. Set goals in function and valued activity, measure interference as well as intensity, and tell the client early that quality of life can improve even if pain does not [NICE-NG193].

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.s: The therapist sets activity targets, discusses medicines or interprets new symptoms without the treating clinicians, and the client gets mixed messages, flare-ups or missed medical change.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.when: You are treating a client with chronic pain or a long-term condition and have no agreed contact, roles or symptom rule with their doctor, nurse or pain team.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.pitfall.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for people with physical illness works inside a medical plan. Without agreed roles, the therapist may push activity the body cannot take, contradict the doctor, or miss a change that needed review. Agree roles, a symptom rule and information sharing at the start, as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises for shared care [NICE-CG91].

chronic-pain-and-physical-health.treatme.s: CBT and ACT for chronic pain, CBT for depression and distress in diabetes, heart disease and cancer, session outlines, formats, effect sizes and current NICE and US guideline status.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.treatme.when: A client with chronic pain or a long-term condition has a shared formulation and you are choosing, planning or delivering CBT or acceptance-based treatment.
chronic-pain-and-physical-health.treatme.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for chronic pain gives small but reliable gains in pain, disability and distress [Williams-etal-2020], and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) also helps, with its clearest gains in functioning [Ma-etal-2023; Hughes-etal-2017]. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says to consider either for chronic primary pain, alongside supervised exercise [NICE-NG193]. For depression with a long-term condition, offer stepped CBT, usually adapted to the illness and coordinated with medical care [NICE-CG91].

depression.adaptations.s: If-then rules for adapting depression CBT to severity, risk, comorbidity, age, pregnancy, culture and medication, and for stepping up, combining treatment or referring.
depression.adaptations.when: A depressed client's severity, comorbidity, age, pregnancy, culture or medication status means the standard adult protocol needs changing, or progress has stalled.
depression.adaptations.b: Keep the core of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression (activation, testing thoughts, relapse prevention) and change the delivery to fit the person. Severity shifts the balance toward behavioral work, combination treatment and closer monitoring; comorbidity, age, pregnancy and culture change format and content. Refer or step up when there are psychotic features, a bipolar history, risk beyond outpatient care, or no response after 4 to 6 weeks [NICE-NG222].

depression.assessment.s: What to ask and record when assessing depression, covering symptom review, risk, bipolar and medical screens, PHQ-9 and other measures with cutoffs, differential questions and collateral information.
depression.assessment.when: A client presents with low mood, loss of interest or a positive depression screen and you need diagnosis, severity, risk and a baseline before planning treatment.
depression.assessment.b: Confirm the diagnosis by interview, not by questionnaire. Cover symptoms, episode history, suicide risk, past highs, medical and substance causes, and life context. Take a baseline Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and repeat it every session, because scores guide treatment choice and progress review [NICE-NG222; VA-DoD-MDD-2022].

depression.cbt-model.s: Beck's cognitive model and the behavioral activation model of depression, the vicious cycles that maintain it, how to draw them with a client and the targets they imply.
depression.cbt-model.when: You have assessed a depressed client and need a shared maintenance formulation to explain the problem and choose treatment targets.
depression.cbt-model.b: Two models drive cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression. Beck's cognitive model says negative beliefs, activated by stress, produce biased automatic thoughts about self, world and future [Beck-etal-1979; Beck-2008]. The behavioral model says loss of reward, withdrawal and avoidance keep mood low [Dimidjian-etal-2011]. In practice they combine into a few vicious cycles (inactivity, avoidance, rumination, biased thinking, hopelessness) that you draw with the client from a recent low moment and then break, starting with behavior.

depression.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for major and persistent depressive disorder in DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with prevalence, course, differentials, the CBT approach in brief and risk notes.
depression.overview.when: A client reports low mood or loss of interest and you need the diagnostic picture, typical course and overall CBT approach before assessing in detail.
depression.overview.b: Major depressive disorder (MDD) means at least 2 weeks of five or more of nine depressive symptoms, one of them depressed mood or loss of interest, with distress or impairment and no history of mania or hypomania [APA-DSM5TR-2022; Coryell-2026]. Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) means depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years [Coryell-2026]. Depression often recurs and carries suicide risk, so screen for both, and for past highs, before treating. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a guideline-recommended first-line treatment [NICE-NG222; Cuijpers-etal-2023a].

depression.persistent-depression.s: How to recognize persistent depressive disorder and treat chronic depression with CBASP or chronic-focused CBT, including situational analysis, session counts, combination treatment and evidence.
depression.persistent-depression.when: Depressive symptoms have lasted two years or more, began early in life, or have not lifted with standard short-term CBT or medication.
depression.persistent-depression.b: Persistent depressive disorder (PDD) means depressed mood on most days for 2 years or more [Coryell-2026]. Chronic depression responds less to short treatment, so plan longer therapy (about 18 or more sessions) and discuss combining psychotherapy with medication [Cuijpers-etal-2010; Keller-etal-2000]. The Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy (CBASP) was built for chronic depression and has modest advantages over supportive therapy [Schramm-etal-2017; Negt-etal-2016].

depression.pitfall-risk-not-rechecked.s: Suicide risk is screened at intake and then not reassessed as hopelessness, agitation, medication changes or new losses shift it during depression treatment.
depression.pitfall-risk-not-rechecked.when: You are treating depression over several sessions and need to keep suicide risk current, especially early in treatment, after medication changes or after a new loss.
depression.pitfall-risk-not-rechecked.b: Suicide risk in depression moves. It can rise early in treatment, when medication starts or changes, when agitation appears, and after new losses [NICE-NG222]. Check suicidal thinking at every session (for example with Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) item 9 plus a direct question), act on any change the same day, and record what you asked and did.

depression.pitfall-stopping-at-response.s: Therapy ends once the client feels somewhat better, with residual symptoms, no remission check and no written relapse plan, and depression returns within months.
depression.pitfall-stopping-at-response.when: A depressed client has improved and you are deciding when and how to end treatment, or a former client has relapsed soon after discharge.
depression.pitfall-stopping-at-response.b: Feeling better is not the same as being well. Response (about a 50% drop in symptoms) can leave several symptoms in place, and residual symptoms predict earlier relapse [WHO-CDDR-2024; Breedvelt-etal-2021]. Aim for remission, such as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score of 4 or less held for at least a month [VA-DoD-MDD-2022], then end with a written relapse plan, spaced sessions and a route back [NICE-NG222].

depression.pitfall-thought-challenging-t.s: A slowed, hopeless client is given thought records in the first sessions, cannot complete them, and reads the failure as more proof of being useless.
depression.pitfall-thought-challenging-t.when: Early sessions with a moderately or severely depressed client are focused on disputing thoughts while activity, energy and homework completion stay flat.
depression.pitfall-thought-challenging-t.b: In moderate to severe depression, start with behavior. Thought records demand concentration, energy and hope that the client does not yet have, and an unfinished worksheet becomes evidence for "I can't do anything right." Behavioral activation (BA) works as well as the full cognitive package and holds up better in severe depression [Jacobson-etal-1996; Dimidjian-etal-2006]. Bring in cognitive work once the client is moving.

depression.relapse-prevention-mbct.s: Who needs relapse prevention after depression, how the eight-session MBCT group works, alternatives such as preventive and continuation CBT, session counts and evidence versus maintenance antidepressants.
depression.relapse-prevention-mbct.when: A client is in full or partial remission from depression and has recurrent episodes, residual symptoms or other risk factors for relapse.
depression.relapse-prevention-mbct.b: Depression often comes back: about half of people have a recurrence within 5 years, and risk rises with each episode [WHO-CDDR-2024]. After remission, offer relapse prevention to anyone at higher risk. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), an 8-session group, cut relapse compared with usual care (hazard ratio 0.69) [Kuyken-etal-2016b] and in one large trial did not differ from maintenance antidepressants [Kuyken-etal-2015]. Group or individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focused on staying well is the main alternative [NICE-NG222].

depression.treatment.s: First-line CBT for adult depression, covering who it suits, a 16-session outline from activation to relapse prevention, key techniques, session counts, evidence and NICE, APA and VA/DoD guideline status.
depression.treatment.when: An adult with major depression has chosen psychological treatment and you need the structure, session plan and evidence for individual CBT.
depression.treatment.b: Individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression is guideline-recommended first-line care. It usually runs about 8 sessions for less severe and 16 for more severe depression [NICE-NG222]. Start with behavioral activation, then identify and test automatic thoughts, address beliefs if needed, and finish with relapse prevention [Beck-etal-1979; Jacobson-etal-1996]. Measure every session, review progress with the client 2 to 4 weeks in, and change course if there is no response at all by 4 to 6 weeks [NICE-NG222].

eating-disorders.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting eating disorder CBT to comorbidity, severity, age, culture, diabetes, pregnancy, ARFID and medication, and for stepping up care or referring.
eating-disorders.adaptations.when: Standard CBT-E does not fit the client because of age, low weight, comorbidity, diabetes, pregnancy, cultural context, ARFID or medication, or progress is too slow and a step up may be needed.
eating-disorders.adaptations.b: Keep the eating disorder focus and adapt around it. Young people start with family-based treatment; very low weight lengthens treatment and needs medical monitoring; diabetes, pregnancy and severe comorbidity need joint care; and medication is an add-on, never the sole treatment, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) [NICE-NG69]. Step up care when outpatient work cannot stop the decline, judged on the whole picture rather than one weight threshold [NICE-NG69].

eating-disorders.assessment.s: What to ask and record when assessing eating problems, which screens and severity measures to use with their cutoffs, differential questions, and how to involve family and medical colleagues.
eating-disorders.assessment.when: A screen, referral or disclosure suggests an eating problem and the clinician must establish the diagnosis, severity, medical safety and baseline measures.
eating-disorders.assessment.b: Ask every client about eating, weight and shape, because eating disorders are often missed and clients under-report [APA-ED-Guideline-2023]. When a screen is positive, take a full eating and weight history, weigh the client, count behaviors per week, and complete the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) and Clinical Impairment Assessment (CIA). Arrange a medical check in parallel, and never let a screening score alone decide whether someone has a disorder [NICE-NG69].

eating-disorders.cbt-e-stages.s: How to run each stage of enhanced CBT, covering formulation, self-monitoring, collaborative weekly weighing, regular eating, the review, shape and weight work, dietary rules, mood-related eating and ending well.
eating-disorders.cbt-e-stages.when: The clinician is delivering CBT-E or another CBT-ED protocol and needs the concrete procedures, order and decision points for each stage.
eating-disorders.cbt-e-stages.b: Enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) has four stages: an intensive start that establishes formulation, self-monitoring, weekly weighing and regular eating; a brief review; the main body that tackles shape and weight concern, dietary rules and mood-related eating; and an ending focused on relapse prevention [Murphy-etal-2010]. The focused form is the default; the broad form adds modules for perfectionism, low self-esteem or interpersonal problems only when they clearly maintain the disorder [Murphy-etal-2010].
src: Murphy-etal-2010 § Enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy; Stage one; Stage two; Stage three; Stage four

eating-disorders.cbt-model.s: Fairburn's transdiagnostic maintenance model, its core and four additional mechanisms, the vicious cycles it describes, how to draw it with a client, and the treatment targets it implies.
eating-disorders.cbt-model.when: The clinician needs to explain why a client's restriction, binge eating, purging or low weight persists and to build a personal formulation that sets treatment targets.
eating-disorders.cbt-model.b: The leading cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) model of eating disorders is Fairburn's transdiagnostic theory: overevaluation of shape, weight and their control is the core that keeps anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and other eating disorders going [Fairburn-etal-2003]. Strict dieting, binge eating, purging, body checking and the effects of low weight all feed back into that core. In some clients four additional processes block change: clinical perfectionism, core low self-esteem, mood intolerance and interpersonal difficulties [Fairburn-etal-2003].
src: Murphy-etal-2010 § The cognitive behavioral account of eating disorders; Stage one; Stage three; Addressing clinical perfectionism, low self-esteem, and interpersonal problems

eating-disorders.medical-risk.s: Which physical findings signal danger in eating disorders, the MEED and APA thresholds for urgent medical review or admission, what a therapist asks each session, and how to escalate.
eating-disorders.medical-risk.when: A client with an eating disorder is losing weight, purging, restricting fluids or reporting physical symptoms, and the clinician must judge how urgent a medical review is.
eating-disorders.medical-risk.b: Eating disorders can kill through cardiac, electrolyte and refeeding complications at any body weight [RCPsych-CR233] [Vo-Golden-2022]. Most therapists do not take vital signs or bloods, so their job is to ask about warning symptoms each session, make sure a named medical clinician is monitoring, and escalate the same day when red flags appear. Use the Royal College of Psychiatrists' Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders (MEED) framework or the American Psychiatric Association (APA) admission factors to judge urgency; no single number decides it [RCPsych-CR233].
src: RCPsych-CR233 § 2b Risk assessment framework, Table 1 (December 2025 update); 2c Differential diagnosis
APA-ED-Guideline-2023 § Statements 6 to 8; Table 6; Statement 10 Implementation (refeeding)

eating-disorders.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder, ARFID and OSFED, with ICD-11 differences, prevalence, course, mortality and the CBT approach in brief.
eating-disorders.overview.when: A client describes restriction, binge eating, purging, or preoccupation with weight and shape, and the clinician needs the diagnostic picture, course and risk profile before planning CBT.
eating-disorders.overview.b: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder share one core: self-worth judged largely by shape, weight and control of eating, which drives dieting, binge eating and compensatory behavior [Murphy-etal-2010]. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) restricts food without that weight concern [Reed-etal-2019]. Anorexia nervosa has the highest standardized mortality of the group, so every assessment checks medical risk [Arcelus-etal-2011].

Reed-etal-2019 § Binge eating disorder; Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
Murphy-etal-2010 § The cognitive behavioral account of eating disorders

eating-disorders.pitfall-avoiding-in-ses.s: The therapist skips weighing, weighs "blind," or leaves weight to the client or another clinician, so weight fears, checking and unexplained weight loss go unaddressed in therapy.
eating-disorders.pitfall-avoiding-in-ses.when: A therapist delivering CBT for an eating disorder is unsure whether to weigh the client, feels uncomfortable doing it, or the client asks not to know their weight.
eating-disorders.pitfall-avoiding-in-ses.b: Collaborative weekly weighing in session is a core cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) procedure for eating disorders, not an optional extra [Murphy-etal-2010]. Therapists vary widely in whether they weigh, partly from their own reluctance [Waller-Mountford-2015]. Skipping weighing, or weighing without telling the client the number, leaves weight fears untested and safety data missing.
src: Murphy-etal-2010 § Establishing collaborative weekly weighing; Stage four

eating-disorders.pitfall-normal-weight-a.s: A client at average or higher weight who restricts, purges or lost weight fast is told they are not ill enough, goes unchecked medically, or waits behind thinner clients.
eating-disorders.pitfall-normal-weight-a.when: A clinician is judging severity or urgency for a client whose body mass index is in the normal or higher range, including atypical anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and purging disorder.
eating-disorders.pitfall-normal-weight-a.b: Weight status is a poor guide to how ill someone with an eating disorder is. People with atypical anorexia nervosa can have medical complications as severe as those with low weight [Vo-Golden-2022], and people with bulimia nervosa who are not underweight can present in life-threatening emergencies [RCPsych-CR233]. Judge risk from the rate and amount of weight loss, behaviors and physical findings, not body mass index (BMI) alone [NICE-NG69].

eating-disorders.pitfall-therapist-drift.s: Sessions slide into general support, waiting for motivation, or talk about history, while regular eating, monitoring, weighing and food experiments quietly stop and symptoms stay the same.
eating-disorders.pitfall-therapist-drift.when: A course of CBT for an eating disorder has lost its structure, behavior change is not being set or reviewed, or progress has stalled while sessions continue.
eating-disorders.pitfall-therapist-drift.b: Therapist drift is failing to deliver the evidence-based treatment despite having the tools, and it is an important reason evidence-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works less well in routine practice than it should [Waller-Turner-2016]. In eating disorders it usually means dropping the behavioral core: regular eating, self-monitoring, weighing and food experiments. Early change predicts outcome, so drift in the first weeks is especially costly [Murphy-etal-2010].

eating-disorders.pitfall-weight-loss-goa.s: A diet or calorie target is added to treatment for binge eating or bulimia nervosa, binges continue or rebound, and success is judged by the scale instead of eating behavior.
eating-disorders.pitfall-weight-loss-goa.when: A client with binge-eating disorder or bulimia nervosa wants to lose weight during treatment, or a referrer, physician or therapist proposes weight loss as a treatment goal.
eating-disorders.pitfall-weight-loss-goa.b: In the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) model, strict dieting is a main driver of binge eating, so adding a diet to treatment feeds the problem it is meant to fix [Murphy-etal-2010]. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises telling clients that binge-eating treatment has a limited effect on weight, that weight loss is not a therapy target, and that dieting during treatment is likely to trigger binges [NICE-NG69]. Make stopping binge eating the goal, and route weight-loss care through obesity services afterward.
src: Murphy-etal-2010 § The cognitive behavioral account of eating disorders; Addressing dietary rules

eating-disorders.treatment.s: First-line CBT options by diagnosis and age, the CBT-E 20- and 40-session outlines, guided self-help and 10-session CBT-T, and NICE and APA guideline status with evidence strength.
eating-disorders.treatment.when: An eating disorder has been assessed and the clinician must choose a CBT protocol, plan its length and session sequence, and explain the evidence to the client.
eating-disorders.treatment.b: For adults with bulimia nervosa or binge-eating disorder, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) starts with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) based guided self-help and steps up to eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED, most often the enhanced form, CBT-E); for adults with anorexia nervosa, CBT-ED is one of three options [NICE-NG69]. CBT-E runs about 20 sessions over 20 weeks for clients with a body mass index (BMI) above 17.5 and 40 sessions over 40 weeks below that [Murphy-etal-2010]. Young people with anorexia or bulimia nervosa start with family therapy, with CBT-ED as an alternative [NICE-NG69].
src: Murphy-etal-2010 § Enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy; Stage one to Stage four

gad.adaptations.s: If-then rules for adapting CBT for generalized anxiety disorder to comorbidity, severity, older age, children, culture, medication and remote delivery, and for deciding when to step up or refer.
gad.adaptations.when: A client with generalized anxiety disorder also has depression, substance use, physical illness, older or younger age, a different cultural frame or medication, or is not responding to standard CBT.
gad.adaptations.b: Keep the core of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and change delivery, order and pace. Treat the more severe of GAD and comorbid depression first, and treat harmful or dependent substance use before GAD [Kendall-etal-2011]. Older adults and young people benefit from adapted CBT. Step up to medication, combined treatment or specialist care when a full course has not worked or risk is high [Kendall-etal-2011].

NICE-CG113 § 1.2.9 substance misuse; 1.2.26 to 1.2.27; 1.2.30 under-30 monitoring; 1.2.37 step 4

gad.assessment.s: What to ask and record when worry is the complaint, which screening and severity measures to use with their cutoffs, the differential-diagnosis questions, and when to seek collateral information.
gad.assessment.when: A client screens positive for anxiety or reports chronic worry, and you need to confirm generalized anxiety disorder, rate its severity and gather what the formulation needs.
gad.assessment.b: Confirm generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) by mapping a few real worry episodes, then checking duration, controllability, associated symptoms and impairment. Screen with the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), where 10 or more suggests GAD [Spitzer-etal-2006], and track worry with the Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ). Rule out other disorders, substances and medical causes, and screen for suicide risk before formulating [Kendall-etal-2011].
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Generalized Anxiety Disorder, criteria and differential diagnosis (paraphrased)
Kroenke-etal-2007 § Abstract (GAD-7 and GAD-2 detect four anxiety disorders)
AfWinklerfeltHammarberg-etal-2023 § Outcome measures (PSWQ recovery cutoffs and reliable change)

gad.cbt-model.s: The intolerance of uncertainty model and the metacognitive model of generalized anxiety disorder, their vicious cycles, how to draw them from one worry episode, and the treatment targets each implies.
gad.cbt-model.when: You have assessed generalized anxiety disorder and need a shared maintenance formulation that explains why the worry persists and what treatment should target.
gad.cbt-model.b: Two cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) models lead the field for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). The intolerance of uncertainty (IU) model says worry is a way of coping with not knowing, fed by beliefs that worry helps, a threat-focused view of problems, and avoidance of feared images [Dugas-etal-1998]. The metacognitive model says worry persists because of positive beliefs about worrying and negative beliefs that worry is uncontrollable and dangerous [Wells-2009]. Draw either from one recent worry episode and let the model pick the targets.

gad.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials of generalized anxiety disorder in DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with prevalence, onset, course, comorbidity, differentials, suicide risk and the CBT approach in brief.
gad.overview.when: A client describes persistent, hard-to-control worry about several everyday matters with tension, poor sleep or fatigue, and you need to know whether this fits generalized anxiety disorder.
gad.overview.b: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is excessive, hard-to-control worry about several everyday matters, with tension and arousal, lasting at least 6 months under the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) [APA-DSM5TR-2022]. It usually starts in adulthood, waxes and wanes for years, and rarely comes alone: about 8 in 10 people with lifetime GAD have another disorder [Ruscio-etal-2017]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is guideline-recommended, first as low-intensity self-help, then as individual therapy [NICE-CG113].
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Generalized Anxiety Disorder, diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis (paraphrased)
Scheeringa-Burns-2018 § Discussion (criteria A to D as applied; one symptom in children)
NIMH-GAD-Statistics § Prevalence of GAD among adults and adolescents
Ruscio-etal-2017 § Abstract; Results (age of onset, persistence)

gad.pitfall-chasing-worry-content.s: Each session tackles this week's new worry topic with evidence-gathering or reassurance, the client feels briefly better, and next week a different worry has taken its place.
gad.pitfall-chasing-worry-content.when: Sessions with a client who has generalized anxiety disorder keep turning into analysis of one new worry after another, and worry scores do not fall.
gad.pitfall-chasing-worry-content.b: In generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), the topic of worry changes from week to week, while the process stays the same. If therapy keeps testing or answering each new worry, it works like reassurance and leaves the drivers untouched: intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and beliefs about worry [Dugas-etal-1998; Wells-2009]. Work on the process instead.

gad.pitfall-eclectic-anxiety-management.s: Therapy for generalized anxiety disorder samples breathing, thought records, sleep tips and relaxation week by week without a worry model, and worry scores barely move after many sessions.
gad.pitfall-eclectic-anxiety-management.when: You are midway through therapy for generalized anxiety disorder, sessions feel busy, but GAD-7 and worry scores are flat and no single model guides the plan.
gad.pitfall-eclectic-anxiety-management.b: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) responds to coherent, manual-based treatment, not a menu of coping tips. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) asks for cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or applied relaxation based on trial manuals and delivered by trained practitioners [Kendall-etal-2011]. Choose one model, follow its phases, measure worry every session, and change course when scores stall.

gad.pitfall-worry-misread-as-gad.s: A worrier is labeled with generalized anxiety disorder and a worry protocol stalls, because the real driver is obsessions, health anxiety, depression, trauma, substances or a medical problem.
gad.pitfall-worry-misread-as-gad.when: A client reports heavy worry and you are about to diagnose generalized anxiety disorder, or a worry-focused protocol is not working and you suspect the diagnosis.
gad.pitfall-worry-misread-as-gad.b: Worry appears in nearly every anxiety and mood disorder. Diagnose generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) only when worry spans several everyday areas and is not better explained by another disorder, a substance or a medical condition, as the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) requires [APA-DSM5TR-2022]. Comorbidity is the rule (81.9% lifetime) [Ruscio-etal-2017], so look for what else is present, not just whether worry exists.
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Generalized Anxiety Disorder, criteria and differential diagnosis (paraphrased)
Kroenke-etal-2007 § Abstract (GAD-7 detects four anxiety disorders)

gad.treatment.s: First-line CBT for generalized anxiety disorder, with a 12-session intolerance of uncertainty outline, the metacognitive and applied relaxation alternatives, session counts, evidence and NICE and US guideline status.
gad.treatment.when: A client meets criteria for generalized anxiety disorder, has not improved with education or low-intensity self-help or has marked impairment, and you are planning individual CBT.
gad.treatment.b: Offer individual, manual-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or applied relaxation, usually 12 to 15 weekly one-hour sessions, when generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) has not improved with low-intensity help or impairment is marked [NICE-CG113; Kendall-etal-2011]. Follow one model: intolerance of uncertainty (IU) CBT or metacognitive therapy (MCT). Psychotherapy has a large effect against mostly waitlist controls (Hedges' g = 0.84), but gains shrink over the long term [Cuijpers-etal-2014b; VanDis-etal-2020].
src: NICE-CG113 § 1.2.1; 1.2.17 to 1.2.20 (high-intensity interventions); guideline status page (update needed, not scheduled)
AfWinklerfeltHammarberg-etal-2023 § Table 1 treatment content by session

gad.worry-models-compared.s: Side-by-side comparison of the intolerance of uncertainty, metacognitive, cognitive avoidance and contrast avoidance models of worry, with their evidence, critiques, head-to-head trials and treatment targets.
gad.worry-models-compared.when: You need to choose or explain a model of pathological worry, or a client's worry does not fit the formulation you started with.
gad.worry-models-compared.b: Three families of models explain why worry persists. The intolerance of uncertainty (IU) model says worry copes with not knowing; the metacognitive model says beliefs about worry keep it going; avoidance models say worry avoids emotion, either feared images (Borkovec) or a sudden drop into distress (contrast avoidance). All share avoidance of internal experience [Behar-etal-2009]. Head-to-head trials favor metacognitive therapy (MCT) so far, but most are small or developer-led.
src: Hirsch-Mathews-2012 § Discussion of prior models; proposed cognitive model and treatment implications

grief-and-loss.adaptations.s: If-then rules for adapting prolonged grief treatment to cultural and religious mourning, children, older adults, violent or suicide loss, comorbidity, suicide risk, remote delivery and referral.
grief-and-loss.adaptations.when: A bereaved client's culture or faith, age, type of loss, comorbid condition, suicide risk or access needs mean the standard grief protocol needs changing.
grief-and-loss.adaptations.b: Keep the core of grief-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT): facing the loss, working with beliefs and rebuilding life. Adapt the frame. Culture and faith define normal mourning, so judge grief against the client's own norms and work with their rituals [WHO-ICD11-2022; Killikelly-Maercker-2018]. Violent and suicide losses, young people, older adults and comorbidity change the plan; suicidal thinking changes the priority.
src: Killikelly-Maercker-2018 § 4.2 International applicability (mourning periods, examples); 4.3 Therapeutic and interventional implications (mourning rituals)
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

grief-and-loss.assessment.s: How to assess a bereaved client, covering the loss, time since death, cultural mourning norms, prolonged grief symptoms, differentials, suicide risk and baseline measurement with the PG-13-R or ICG.
grief-and-loss.assessment.when: A client has lost someone close and grief, low mood or avoidance of reminders is a presenting problem, or a grief screen is positive.
grief-and-loss.assessment.b: Assess the loss and how it happened, the time since the death, what mourning is expected in the client's culture and faith, the prolonged grief disorder (PGD) symptom pattern, comorbid depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and suicide risk. Use the Prolonged Grief Disorder scale, revised (PG-13-R), or the Inventory of Complicated Grief (ICG) for a baseline and repeat it, but diagnose by interview, because a score cannot show whether grief exceeds the client's norms [Prigerson-etal-2021; WHO-ICD11-2022].
src: Prigerson-etal-2021 § Methods (PG-13-R items and scoring); Results (cutoff, reliability, suicidality)
NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

grief-and-loss.cbt-model.s: The Boelen cognitive behavioral model of prolonged grief, covering poor integration of the loss, negative beliefs, and anxious and depressive avoidance, plus the treatment targets.
grief-and-loss.cbt-model.when: You have assessed prolonged or persistent grief and need a shared formulation that explains why the grief has not eased and what treatment should change.
grief-and-loss.cbt-model.b: Boelen and colleagues propose that grief becomes prolonged through three interacting processes: the loss is not integrated into autobiographical memory, global negative beliefs and catastrophic readings of grief reactions take hold, and anxious and depressive avoidance block both facing the loss and rebuilding life [Boelen-etal-2006]. Background factors such as the type of death or attachment style are thought to act through these processes, so the processes are the treatment targets [Boelen-etal-2006].
src: Boelen-etal-2006 § Abstract (three core processes; mediation of background variables)

grief-and-loss.overview.s: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 essentials for prolonged grief disorder, how it differs from normal grief, prevalence and course, key differentials, the CBT approach in brief, and risk notes.
grief-and-loss.overview.when: A bereaved client describes grief that still dominates daily life many months after a death, and you need to know whether it is normal grief, prolonged grief disorder or another condition.
grief-and-loss.overview.b: Most bereaved people grieve intensely and then adapt without professional help [Stroebe-etal-2007]. Prolonged grief disorder (PGD) describes the minority whose longing for or preoccupation with the person who died stays intense, daily and impairing long after the death: at least 12 months for adults in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), and more than 6 months in the International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (ICD-11) [Prigerson-etal-2021; WHO-ICD11-2022]. It responds to grief-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [Komischke-Konnerup-etal-2024] and carries an independent suicide risk, so always ask [Latham-Prigerson-2004].
src: Prigerson-etal-2021 § Table 1 Proposed DSM criteria for prolonged grief disorder; Introduction (ICD-11 comparison); Results (prevalence, stability)
Szuhany-etal-2021 § Course of grief; Differential diagnosis; Comorbidity; Suicide risk

grief-and-loss.pitfall-colluding-with-av.s: Sessions stay with comforting talk about the person, the story of the death and avoided reminders are never approached, and grief scores stay flat after months of therapy.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-colluding-with-av.when: You are treating prolonged grief disorder and sessions keep circling the same memories or daily problems without revisiting the death, avoided reminders or a return to valued activity.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-colluding-with-av.b: Warm, supportive listening is necessary but not enough for prolonged grief disorder (PGD). Anxious avoidance of the reality of the death maintains the disorder [Boelen-etal-2006], and treatments that include exposure outperform supportive counseling [Boelen-etal-2007]. If the therapist avoids the death story too, therapy repeats the client's avoidance and grief stays stuck.

grief-and-loss.pitfall-missing-suicide-r.s: A client says they want to be with the person who died, and it is heard as ordinary longing, so suicidal thinking is never asked about or planned for.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-missing-suicide-r.when: You are assessing or treating a bereaved client, especially after a suicide or other sudden death, or when the client voices a wish to join the deceased or that life is meaningless.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-missing-suicide-r.b: Prolonged grief disorder (PGD) raises suicide risk on its own: complicated grief, its earlier research name, predicted high suicidality beyond depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) [Latham-Prigerson-2004]. "I just want to be with her" can be longing, a wish to die, or both. Ask directly every time, assess fully, plan for safety, and keep asking as treatment revisits the death.
src: NHS-Urgent-Help § Where to get urgent help

grief-and-loss.pitfall-treating-normal-g.s: A recently bereaved person, or one grieving within their cultural norms, is diagnosed, booked for grief therapy or pushed to process the loss, though most people adapt without professional help.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-treating-normal-g.when: You are deciding whether a bereaved client needs treatment, especially in the first months after a death or when long mourning follows cultural or religious norms.
grief-and-loss.pitfall-treating-normal-g.b: Grief is not a disease, and most bereaved people adjust without professional psychological help [Stroebe-etal-2007]. Preventive interventions offered to all bereaved people have not shown benefit [Wittouck-etal-2011]. Diagnose prolonged grief disorder (PGD) only after the minimum time since the death and only when grief clearly exceeds the client's own cultural and religious norms; until then, support, normalize and monitor.

grief-and-loss.treatment.s: Grief-focused CBT and prolonged grief disorder therapy for adults, covering how they work, a session outline, dose, the role of exposure, medication, and the trial and meta-analytic evidence.
grief-and-loss.treatment.when: An adult meets criteria for prolonged grief disorder, or has persistent impairing grief beyond cultural norms, and you are choosing and delivering a grief-focused treatment.
grief-and-loss.treatment.b: For prolonged grief disorder (PGD), offer grief-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) that includes exposure to the reality of the loss, work on beliefs, and re-engagement with life; prolonged grief disorder therapy (PGDT) has the largest trials, with 95, 151 and 395 adults [Shear-etal-2005; Shear-etal-2014; Shear-etal-2016]. Across 22 randomized trials, grief-focused CBT had a medium effect on grief (Hedges' g 0.65) that was larger at follow-up [Komischke-Konnerup-etal-2024]. Treat people with the disorder, not everyone bereaved: preventive interventions for unselected mourners were not effective [Wittouck-etal-2011].
src: Shear-etal-2016 § Abstract; Methods (CGT sessions); Results (suicidal ideation)

health-anxiety.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting health anxiety CBT to comorbidity, real medical illness, severity and poor insight, age, culture and medication, and for when to step up or refer.
health-anxiety.adaptations.when: Standard health anxiety CBT needs adjusting because of a medical condition, depression or other comorbidity, fixed conviction, age, cultural framing, medication, or poor response.
health-anxiety.adaptations.b: Keep the core of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for health anxiety, which is testing a worry explanation and dropping safety behaviors, and adjust its targets and partners. With real illness, target excessive attention and checking, not the disease. With fixed conviction, invest longer in engagement. Step up to combined treatment or multidisciplinary care when CBT alone is not enough, and check suicide risk throughout [MataixCols-etal-2024].
src: Henningsen-2018 § Abstract; Treatment, the practice principles; Conclusion

health-anxiety.assessment.s: What to ask and record when assessing health anxiety, how to confirm medical status, which screening and severity measures to use with cutoffs, and the differential diagnosis questions.
health-anxiety.assessment.when: A client reports persistent fear of illness, frequent checking or consulting, avoidance of doctors, or distressing bodily symptoms, or a medical clinic refers a frequent attender.
health-anxiety.assessment.b: Assess the worry, not the disease. Confirm with the client's doctor what has been investigated, then map the feared illness, its triggers, the belief strength and every checking, reassurance, searching and avoidance behavior. Score a health anxiety measure such as the Short Health Anxiety Inventory (SHAI) and, when symptoms are prominent, a somatic symptom measure. Screen for depression and suicide risk.
src: Osterman-etal-2022 § Abstract; Discussion, clinical cut-off in the psychiatric setting
Abramowitz-etal-2007a § Abstract, receiver operating characteristic analyses (cut score as reported by Osterman-etal-2022)

health-anxiety.cbt-model.s: The Salkovskis and Warwick model of health anxiety, its threat appraisal and four maintaining cycles, how to draw it with a client, and the treatment targets it implies.
health-anxiety.cbt-model.when: You have assessed a health-anxious client and need to build or share a maintenance formulation that explains why reassurance, tests and checking have not helped.
health-anxiety.cbt-model.b: In the leading cognitive behavioral model, health anxiety comes from misreading bodily sensations and health information as signs of serious illness, driven by learned assumptions about health [Warwick-1998]. Checking, reassurance seeking, searching, avoidance, body-focused attention and arousal then keep the belief alive [Kikas-etal-2024]. Share it as a competing explanation to "I have an undiagnosed disease" and test it, rather than arguing about medical facts.
src: Warwick-1998 § Cognitive factors in health anxiety; Fig. 1 and Fig. 2; Engagement; Cognitive restructuring
Kikas-etal-2024 § Theories; Cognitive components; Behavioural components

health-anxiety.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials, ICD-11 differences, prevalence, course, differentials and risk for health anxiety presenting as illness anxiety disorder or somatic symptom disorder, with the CBT approach in brief.
health-anxiety.overview.when: A client is preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness, or is distressed and consumed by bodily symptoms, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessment.
health-anxiety.overview.b: Health anxiety is persistent, disproportionate fear of having or developing a serious illness, kept going by checking, reassurance seeking, symptom searching or avoidance. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) splits it into illness anxiety disorder (IAD) and somatic symptom disorder (SSD), which in one clinic sample differed mainly in severity [Newby-etal-2017]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best-supported treatment [Axelsson-HedmanLagerlof-2019]. Suicide risk is raised, so ask about it [MataixCols-etal-2024].

health-anxiety.persistent-physical-sympt.s: How to adapt CBT when distressing bodily symptoms such as pain, fatigue or bowel problems dominate, with goals of coping and function, a session approach, and modest evidence.
health-anxiety.persistent-physical-sympt.when: A client with somatic symptom disorder or ICD-11 bodily distress disorder is disabled more by persistent symptoms than by fear of a specific disease, often after many investigations.
health-anxiety.persistent-physical-sympt.b: When persistent bodily symptoms rather than disease fear are the main problem, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) aims at coping and function, not cure. It works on attention to symptoms, symptom expectations, avoidance and boom-and-bust activity, and illness beliefs, in close contact with medical care [Lowe-etal-2024; Henningsen-2018]. Effects are real but small to moderate [VanDessel-etal-2014].
