health-anxiety.pitfall-debating-the-diag.s: Sessions become debates about medical facts, the therapist insists it is "just anxiety", the client feels dismissed and either drops out or seeks more tests elsewhere.
health-anxiety.pitfall-debating-the-diag.when: A client with health anxiety or somatic symptom disorder holds firmly to a disease explanation and the therapist feels pulled to prove otherwise.
health-anxiety.pitfall-debating-the-diag.b: A therapist cannot win an argument about whether a client is ill, and trying confirms the client's fear of being dismissed. Instead, take the symptoms seriously, put two explanations side by side, and agree to test the worry explanation for a set time while medical options stay open [Warwick-1998].

health-anxiety.pitfall-missed-medical-il.s: Once a client is labeled health anxious, a new or changing symptom is put down to anxiety without medical review, or a care-avoidant client's overdue checks go unnoticed.
health-anxiety.pitfall-missed-medical-il.when: A client in treatment for health anxiety or somatic symptom disorder reports a symptom that is new, different, worsening or accompanied by objective signs, or has stopped attending medical care.
health-anxiety.pitfall-missed-medical-il.b: Health anxiety does not protect anyone from real disease. A diagnosis of illness anxiety or somatic symptom disorder can sit alongside medical illness [Lowe-etal-2022], and people with hypochondriasis die of natural causes at a higher rate than matched controls [MataixCols-etal-2024]. Agree a medical review rule at the start of treatment so new symptoms are checked without restarting the reassurance cycle.

health-anxiety.pitfall-reassurance-loop.s: The therapist, family or an app answers each "is this serious?" question, relief lasts hours or days, and requests return more often, about new symptoms, to more people.
health-anxiety.pitfall-reassurance-loop.when: A health-anxious client repeatedly asks for reassurance in or between sessions, or family members, doctors or digital tools routinely answer health questions.
health-anxiety.pitfall-reassurance-loop.b: Answering a health-anxious client's "Is it serious?" feels kind and calms the session, but it works like a compulsion and keeps the fear going [Salkovskis-Warwick-1986]. The fix is to explain the cycle, agree a plan with the client and the people around them, and respond to requests with empathy and a pointer to the plan, while still sending new or urgent symptoms for medical review.
src: Warwick-1998 § Engagement; Exposure and response prevention

health-anxiety.reassurance-seeking.s: How therapists, families and clinical tools should respond when a health-anxious client asks whether a symptom is serious, without colluding, dismissing, or missing a real emergency.
health-anxiety.reassurance-seeking.when: A client asks the therapist, a family member or an app whether a symptom means illness, asks for tests to be sure, or repeats the same health question.
health-anxiety.reassurance-seeking.b: In health anxiety, repeated reassurance works like a compulsion: it brings quick relief, then doubt returns and the next request comes sooner [Salkovskis-Warwick-1986; Abramowitz-Moore-2007]. One clear medical explanation from the responsible doctor is good care [Lowe-etal-2024]; answering the same question again is not. Respond with empathy, name the pattern, point back to the agreed plan, and never let the rule stop a genuinely new or urgent symptom from being checked.
src: Warwick-1998 § Engagement; Exposure and response prevention

health-anxiety.treatment.s: CBT for health anxiety, the best-supported treatment, with a 12-session outline, key techniques, brief and internet-delivered formats, typical session counts, effect sizes, and current guideline status.
health-anxiety.treatment.when: A client meets criteria for illness anxiety disorder, somatic symptom disorder with prominent health anxiety, or ICD-11 hypochondriasis, and you are planning or delivering treatment.
health-anxiety.treatment.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for health anxiety is the best-supported treatment, with moderate to large effects that largely last [Cooper-etal-2017; Axelsson-HedmanLagerlof-2019]. A typical course is about 12 weekly sessions: engage the client in testing a worry explanation, then use behavioral experiments and exposure while dropping checking and reassurance [Axelsson-etal-2020]. Brief versions in medical clinics and therapist-guided internet CBT also work [Tyrer-etal-2017; Axelsson-etal-2020].
src: Warwick-1998 § Box 1 Main components; Engagement; Exposure and response prevention; Treatment studies
NIHR-Alert-2017 § What does current guidance say on this issue

insomnia.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting or delaying CBT-I with depression, bipolar disorder, PTSD, psychosis, substance use, sleep apnea, age, pregnancy, culture and hypnotics, and when to step up or refer.
insomnia.adaptations.when: A client with insomnia also has a mental or medical condition, is older, younger, pregnant or culturally distinct from the protocol population, takes sleep medication, or is not improving.
insomnia.adaptations.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) works with comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions (remission 36.0% versus 16.9% for controls) [Wu-etal-2015], so treat insomnia alongside the other problem. Adapt or delay when sleep loss is dangerous: bipolar disorder, uncontrolled seizures, excessive sleepiness, active substance use disorder, medical instability, acute mental health crises, or during exposure-based trauma therapy [VA-DoD-CPG-Insomnia-2025].
src: VA-DoD-CPG-Insomnia-2025 § Sidebar 3 Conditions requiring adaptations or delay; Recommendation 8 discussion
Harvey-etal-2015 § Method, CBT-I for bipolar disorder; Results

insomnia.assessment.s: What to ask and record in an insomnia assessment, screening and severity measures with cutoffs, how to rule out other sleep disorders, and when to involve a bed partner.
insomnia.assessment.when: A client complains of poor sleep or screens positive for insomnia and you need to confirm the diagnosis, rule out other sleep disorders and measure severity before treatment.
insomnia.assessment.b: Insomnia is diagnosed from a clinical sleep history plus at least 2 weeks of sleep diary; overnight testing is not routine [Schutte-Rodin-etal-2008]. Measure severity with the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and screen every client for sleep apnea, restless legs, circadian timing problems, mood disorder, substances and suicide risk, because each changes the plan [VA-DoD-CPG-Insomnia-2025] [Pigeon-etal-2012].

insomnia.brief-and-digital-cbt-i.s: When and how to use brief behavioral therapy for insomnia, digital CBT-I and group formats, what each contains, how well they work against in-person CBT-I, and when to step up.
insomnia.brief-and-digital-cbt-i.when: Full in-person CBT-I is unavailable, delayed or not wanted, you work in primary care with limited time, or you are choosing or designing a digital insomnia program.
insomnia.brief-and-digital-cbt-i.b: Brief behavioral therapy for insomnia (BBTI, 1 to 4 sessions) and digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) are effective, guideline-supported ways to widen access [Edinger-etal-2021a] [Riemann-etal-2023]. In-person CBT-I by a trained clinician remains the best-studied format, and head-to-head trials show small differences in its favor [Knutzen-etal-2024] [Edinger-etal-2021b]. Step up to full CBT-I when a brief course does not work [VA-DoD-BehaviorChange-2025].
src: Edinger-etal-2021a § Recommendation 2; Table 3; Discussion, delivery options
VA-DoD-BehaviorChange-2025 § Provider guide, formats and stepping up

insomnia.cbt-i-components.s: How to deliver sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene within CBT-I, with titration rules, safety limits and why sleep hygiene alone falls short.
insomnia.cbt-i-components.when: You are delivering CBT-I and need the exact instructions, titration rules and safety limits for each component, or a client asks why sleep hygiene advice has not helped.
insomnia.cbt-i-components.b: Sleep restriction and stimulus control are the behavioral core of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I); cognitive therapy, relaxation and education are added around them [Edinger-etal-2021a]. Set time in bed close to average sleep time, never below 5 hours, and adjust weekly by sleep efficiency [Schutte-Rodin-etal-2008] [Kyle-etal-2014]. Sleep hygiene advice can sit inside CBT-I but should not be offered as the treatment on its own [Edinger-etal-2021a].

Kyle-etal-2014 § Methods, sleep restriction protocol; Results; Discussion

insomnia.cbt-model.s: The 3P behavioral model and Harvey's cognitive model of insomnia, the vicious cycles they describe, how to draw them with a client, and the treatment targets they imply.
insomnia.cbt-model.when: You have assessed insomnia and need a shared formulation that explains why poor sleep has persisted after its original trigger passed.
insomnia.cbt-model.b: Two complementary models guide cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). Spielman's 3P model explains how a short spell of poor sleep becomes chronic through perpetuating habits that weaken sleep drive and condition the bed to wakefulness [Spielman-etal-1987] [Cox-Olatunji-2021]. Harvey's cognitive model explains how sleep-related worry, threat monitoring, misperception and safety behaviors keep arousal high [Harvey-2002]. Together they say: treat what keeps insomnia going now, not what started it.
src: Cox-Olatunji-2021 § The 3P model of insomnia; Perpetuating factors

insomnia.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for insomnia disorder under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with prevalence, course, differential diagnosis, comorbidity, risk notes and the CBT-I approach in brief.
insomnia.overview.when: A client reports trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, and you need to know whether this is insomnia disorder and what follows.
insomnia.overview.b: Insomnia disorder is a persistent complaint of trouble starting sleep, staying asleep or waking too early, despite adequate opportunity to sleep, with daytime distress or impairment, on at least 3 nights a week for at least 3 months [Grima-etal-2019]. About 6% to 10% of adults meet diagnostic criteria [Qaseem-etal-2016]. It is a disorder in its own right even when depression, pain or another sleep disorder is present, and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment [Qaseem-etal-2016] [Riemann-etal-2023].

insomnia.pitfall-insomnia-treated-as-a-s.s: Insomnia alongside depression, anxiety, PTSD or pain is noted as a symptom and left to resolve with the main disorder, and it persists after that disorder improves.
insomnia.pitfall-insomnia-treated-as-a-s.when: A client in treatment for depression, anxiety, trauma, pain or another condition also reports poor sleep, and you are deciding whether to address it directly.
insomnia.pitfall-insomnia-treated-as-a-s.b: Since the 2013 Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), insomnia that occurs with another condition is diagnosed and treated in its own right rather than labeled secondary [Khurshid-2015]. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) works in comorbid insomnia (remission 36.0% versus 16.9% for controls) [Wu-etal-2015] and is first-line for adults with comorbidities [Riemann-etal-2023]. Waiting for sleep to recover on its own leaves a problem that raises depression and suicide risk [Baglioni-etal-2011] [Pigeon-etal-2012].

insomnia.pitfall-judging-progress-by-hou.s: Client and therapist track only total hours of sleep, see little change during CBT-I, extend time in bed to chase more sleep, and abandon a treatment that was working.
insomnia.pitfall-judging-progress-by-hou.when: A client in CBT-I says they are not sleeping any more hours, wants to extend their sleep window early, or is losing faith in treatment despite better diary efficiency.
insomnia.pitfall-judging-progress-by-hou.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) mainly shortens time to fall asleep and time awake at night; total sleep time changes little at the end of treatment (about 8 minutes, not significant, against control) [Trauer-etal-2015]. Judge progress by sleep efficiency, time awake, the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and daytime function, not hours alone, or both of you will wrongly conclude it is failing.

insomnia.pitfall-sleep-hygiene-only.s: A client with chronic insomnia gets a sleep hygiene leaflet or tips about caffeine and screens, follows them, still sleeps badly, and concludes that therapy cannot help.
insomnia.pitfall-sleep-hygiene-only.when: You are about to offer sleep hygiene advice for chronic insomnia, a service pathway starts with a hygiene leaflet, or a client says they have already tried everything.
insomnia.pitfall-sleep-hygiene-only.b: Sleep hygiene is general lifestyle and bedroom advice, and on its own it is not an effective treatment for chronic insomnia. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) and the US Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense (VA/DoD) both advise against using it as a stand-alone therapy [Edinger-etal-2021a] [VA-DoD-CPG-Insomnia-2025]. Offer cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), brief behavioral therapy or digital CBT-I instead, with hygiene points folded in where relevant.

insomnia.pitfall-unscreened-sleep-restri.s: A sleep window is prescribed without checking for sleep apnea, bipolar disorder, seizures, sleepiness or driving, and the client becomes dangerously sleepy, has a mood episode or drops out.
insomnia.pitfall-unscreened-sleep-restri.when: You are about to start sleep restriction or a brief behavioral program, or a digital program will set the client's sleep window for them.
insomnia.pitfall-unscreened-sleep-restri.b: Sleep restriction, a core part of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), works by making people mildly sleep-deprived at first, so it carries real risks: daytime sleepiness and slowed reactions in the first weeks [Kyle-etal-2014], and possible harm for drivers, people prone to mania and people with poorly controlled seizures [Edinger-etal-2021a]. Screen before you prescribe a window, adapt or delay when a risk is present, and agree a no-driving-when-sleepy plan.
src: VA-DoD-CPG-Insomnia-2025 § Sidebar 3 Conditions requiring adaptations or delay; Recommendation 8 discussion
Harvey-etal-2015 § Method, CBT-I for bipolar disorder; Results

insomnia.sleep-diary.s: How to collect and score a sleep diary, calculate total sleep time and sleep efficiency with a worked example, and use weekly averages to adjust the sleep window.
insomnia.sleep-diary.when: You are assessing insomnia or delivering CBT-I and need baseline sleep data, a sleep efficiency figure, or a rule for adjusting the client's sleep window.
insomnia.sleep-diary.b: A prospective sleep diary, kept each morning for at least 2 weeks before treatment, is the core insomnia measure and the basis for every sleep window decision [Schutte-Rodin-etal-2008] [Carney-etal-2012]. Sleep efficiency is total sleep time divided by time in bed, times 100; under 85% is a common complaint threshold and the main titration signal [Schutte-Rodin-etal-2008] [Kyle-etal-2014].
src: Carney-etal-2012 § Core consensus sleep diary; Versions; Derived variables

insomnia.treatment.s: The first-line CBT-I protocol for chronic insomnia, session by session, with typical session counts, effect sizes, and guideline status from the AASM, ACP, VA/DoD, European guideline, NICE and APA.
insomnia.treatment.when: An adult has chronic insomnia, alone or with another condition, and you are planning or delivering a course of psychological treatment for it.
insomnia.treatment.b: Offer cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the first treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, including older adults and people with psychiatric or medical comorbidity [Qaseem-etal-2016] [Riemann-etal-2023]. It typically runs 4 to 8 weekly sessions guided by a sleep diary, built around sleep restriction and stimulus control, with cognitive therapy and education [Edinger-etal-2021a]. Medication is a second step when CBT-I alone has not worked [Qaseem-etal-2016].

ocd.adaptations.s: How to adapt CBT for OCD for severity, poor insight, depression, tics, autism, children, culture and religion, medication and remote delivery, and when to step up or refer.
ocd.adaptations.when: Standard ERP-based CBT for OCD needs changing because of severity, age, comorbidity, culture or faith, medication, or poor response.
ocd.adaptations.b: Keep exposure and response prevention (ERP) at the core of every adaptation and change the format, intensity or supports around it. Step up to combined treatment or intensive formats when impairment is severe or response stalls, bring in families for children, and treat poor insight as obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), not psychosis [NICE-CG31] [Reed-etal-2019].
src: NICE-CG31 § 1.5.1.1 to 1.5.1.4 adults; 1.5.1.8 to 1.5.1.9, 1.5.5.2 to 1.5.5.3 and 1.5.6.1 children and young people; 1.6.1.1 to 1.6.1.2 specialist and inpatient services
Hezel-Simpson-2019 § Efficacy; New directions, access to care

ocd.assessment.s: How to screen for OCD, map obsessions, overt and mental compulsions, avoidance and accommodation, rate severity with the Y-BOCS and self-report scales, and rule out key differentials.
ocd.assessment.when: A client reports intrusive thoughts, rituals, checking, washing, reassurance seeking or hours lost to "getting it right," and you need a diagnosis, a severity baseline and material for the formulation.
ocd.assessment.b: Ask directly about washing, checking, unwanted thoughts, slowness and order, because people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) rarely volunteer them. Then map each obsession to its feared consequence and to every way the client neutralizes it, including mental acts, avoidance and reassurance. Rate severity with the clinician-rated Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) at baseline and track a self-report weekly [Storch-etal-2015] [Mataix-Cols-etal-2016].
src: Stein-etal-2019 § Diagnosis, screening and prevention; Box 2

ocd.cbt-model.s: The responsibility appraisal model of OCD, its belief domains, and the neutralizing, reassurance, suppression and attention cycles that maintain obsessions, with how to draw it and what to target.
ocd.cbt-model.when: You have mapped a client's obsessions and rituals and need to explain why they persist and choose treatment targets together.
ocd.cbt-model.b: Most people have odd, unwanted thoughts: 93.6% of students across six continents reported at least one in 3 months [Radomsky-etal-2014]. In obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), an intrusion becomes an obsession when the person reads it as meaning they could cause or fail to prevent harm, and so must act [Salkovskis-1999] [Rachman-1997]. Rituals, reassurance, avoidance and suppression bring quick relief but stop the person learning the appraisal is wrong, so the obsession returns stronger. Treatment targets the meaning and the neutralizing, not the thought itself.
src: Hezel-Simpson-2019 § Elements of ERP; Mechanisms of change
Veale-2007 § Compulsions and safety-seeking behaviours; Therapy in practice (The formulation, Box 4; Safety behaviours and compulsions); Hazards of cognitive therapy in OCD (Box 5)

ocd.erp-protocol.s: Step-by-step OCD exposure and response prevention, covering rationale, written ritual rules, in vivo and imaginal exposure, mental rituals, inhibitory learning tactics, and cognitive techniques for inflated responsibility.
ocd.erp-protocol.when: You are running OCD treatment and need the concrete in-session procedure for exposures, response prevention and responsibility-focused cognitive work.
ocd.erp-protocol.b: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) means planned, repeated contact with the triggers and feared consequences of the client's core fear while all rituals, including mental ones and reassurance, are dropped. Stay with the exposure, block distraction and reassurance, and aim the hierarchy at the core fear [Gillihan-etal-2012]. Add cognitive work on inflated responsibility when the client's belief in harm or blame stays high [Salkovskis-1999].
src: Gillihan-etal-2012 § Abstract; pitfall sections 1 to 7 (Not Encouraging Patient to Go Far Enough in Exposures through Ineffectively Handling Mental Compulsions)

ocd.family-accommodation.s: How to assess and reduce family accommodation in OCD, teaching relatives to swap reassurance and ritual participation for supportive statements, with scripts, a stepwise plan and evidence.
ocd.family-accommodation.when: Partners, parents or housemates answer reassurance questions, join or wait for rituals, or change household routines because of a client's OCD.
ocd.family-accommodation.b: Family accommodation means relatives helping the obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) run: answering reassurance questions, joining rituals, helping avoid triggers, or reorganizing the household. It tracks severity (r = .42 across 41 studies) [Wu-etal-2016] and is listed among factors linked to poorer treatment outcome [Stein-etal-2019]. With the client's consent, bring relatives into the plan, teach them to give comfort without reassurance, and withdraw accommodation step by step in line with the exposure hierarchy.
src: Gillihan-etal-2012 § Working With the Patient's Significant Others

ocd.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials of OCD under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, prevalence, onset and course, main differentials and comorbidity, the CBT approach in brief, and suicide risk facts.
ocd.overview.when: A client describes unwanted repetitive thoughts, urges or images, or repetitive rituals or mental acts, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessment and planning.
ocd.overview.b: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is diagnosed when obsessions, compulsions or both take a lot of time (for example, more than an hour a day) or cause marked distress or impairment [Stein-etal-2019]. About 1.2% of United States (US) adults have it in a given year and mean onset is about 19.5 years [Ruscio-etal-2010]; the course is often long, though many people remit [Stein-etal-2019]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with exposure and response prevention (ERP) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the first-line treatments [APA-Psychiatry-OCRD-Site]. Suicide risk is raised, so screen for it at intake [FernandezDeLaCruz-etal-2017].
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
Stein-etal-2019 § Box 2 DSM-5 criteria; Epidemiology; Diagnosis, screening and prevention

APA-Psychiatry-OCRD-Site § What is obsessive-compulsive disorder, Treatment
NICE-CG31 § 1.5.1.1 to 1.5.1.4 stepped care for adults

ocd.pitfall-misreading-intrusions-as-ris.s: A client discloses unwanted harm, sexual or violent thoughts, and the clinician responds with alarm, a risk report or a paraphilia diagnosis instead of assessing OCD.
ocd.pitfall-misreading-intrusions-as-ris.when: A client reports horrifying, unwanted thoughts or images about harming others, sexual content involving children, or blasphemy, and you must decide whether this is risk or an obsession.
ocd.pitfall-misreading-intrusions-as-ris.b: Unwanted thoughts of harming someone, sexual images involving children, or blasphemous urges are common obsessional themes in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). They distress the person because they clash with the person's values [Rachman-1997] [Veale-2007]. Assess them with the same structured questions you use for any risk, but do not treat the content itself as evidence of intent. Alarm, unnecessary reports or misdiagnosis confirm the client's worst fear and drive disclosure underground.
src: Veale-2007 § Therapy in practice, The formulation (Box 4)
Gillihan-etal-2012 § Treating the Peripheral Symptoms and Not the Core Fear

ocd.pitfall-missed-mental-compulsions.s: Exposures are completed and overt rituals stop, but symptoms barely change because the client is neutralizing in their head, distracting, or substituting quieter rituals.
ocd.pitfall-missed-mental-compulsions.when: An OCD client reports doing exposures with little distress or little gain, or Y-BOCS scores plateau despite good attendance and homework.
ocd.pitfall-missed-mental-compulsions.b: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) fails quietly when rituals move out of sight: mental reviewing, praying, counting, replacing an image, telling oneself "it's just OCD," or drifting attention away. Covert compulsions are harder to resist or monitor than overt ones [Veale-2007], and mishandling them is a recognized therapist error [Gillihan-etal-2012]. Before deciding obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is "treatment resistant," hunt for hidden neutralizing.
src: Gillihan-etal-2012 § Encouraging Distraction During Exposure; Ineffectively Handling Mental Compulsions; Not Encouraging Patient to Go Far Enough in Exposures

ocd.pitfall-therapist-reassurance.s: The client asks the therapist whether the feared outcome could happen, the therapist explains why it is unlikely, relief lasts minutes, and the same question returns in a new form.
ocd.pitfall-therapist-reassurance.when: Sessions with an OCD client keep circling back to "But are you sure?" questions, probability debates or requests to review whether something bad happened.
ocd.pitfall-therapist-reassurance.b: In obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), reassurance seeking is a compulsion, and a therapist who answers "Could I have...?" questions becomes part of the ritual [Gillihan-etal-2012]. Debating how unlikely the feared outcome is works the same way [Veale-2007]. Give warmth and validation of the distress, decline to answer the content, and turn the moment into practice with uncertainty.
src: Gillihan-etal-2012 § Providing Reassurance; Working With the Patient's Significant Others
Veale-2007 § Hazards of cognitive therapy in OCD (Box 5)

ocd.related-disorders.s: CBT essentials for body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, and trichotillomania with skin picking, covering diagnostic features, prevalence, measures, maintenance models, treatment dose and risks.
ocd.related-disorders.when: A client is preoccupied with a perceived flaw in appearance, cannot discard possessions, or repeatedly pulls hair or picks skin, and you need the CBT approach that differs from OCD.
ocd.related-disorders.b: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), hoarding disorder and the body-focused repetitive behavior disorders (hair pulling and skin picking) sit with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in both diagnostic systems, but each needs its own cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus [Reed-etal-2019]. BDD responds to CBT with exposure, ritual prevention and attention retraining; hoarding to skills, motivation and graded discarding at home; hair pulling to habit reversal [Harrison-etal-2016] [Steketee-etal-2010] [McGuire-etal-2014]. Skin picking uses the same behavioral methods, on thinner controlled evidence [Selles-etal-2016].
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Body Dysmorphic Disorder; Hoarding Disorder; Trichotillomania; Excoriation Disorder
APA-Psychiatry-OCRD-Site § Body dysmorphic disorder; Hoarding disorder; Trichotillomania; Excoriation disorder

ocd.treatment.s: First-line CBT with exposure and response prevention for adult OCD, with guideline status, stepped care by impairment, a session-by-session outline, typical dose and the evidence base.
ocd.treatment.when: An adult has a confirmed OCD diagnosis and you need to choose the treatment, its intensity and format, and plan the course of sessions.
ocd.treatment.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) built around exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the first-line psychological treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), with large effects in many randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [Ost-etal-2015]. Match intensity to impairment: up to 10 therapist hours of guided work for mild OCD, more than 10 therapist hours or a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for moderate, and both for severe [NICE-CG31]. Courses usually run 6 to 20 sessions depending on severity and chronicity, with daily homework [Veale-2007].

panic-and-phobias.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting panic and phobia treatment for comorbidity, severity, age, culture and medication, and for when to step up, coordinate with prescribers or refer.
panic-and-phobias.adaptations.when: Standard panic or phobia CBT needs changing because of comorbidity, severity, age, culture, medication or poor progress.
panic-and-phobias.adaptations.b: Keep the core of exposure and testing catastrophic predictions, and change the delivery: who joins sessions, where exposure happens, how meaning is framed, and how medication is handled. The biggest risks are as-needed benzodiazepines working as safety behaviors, untreated depression or alcohol use, and suicide risk that goes unasked. Step up or refer when the formulation, not the session count, says the treatment is not reaching the problem.
src: NICE-CG113 § 1.3.9 Step 2 self-help; 1.3.20 benzodiazepines; 1.3.35 Step 4 referral after 2 interventions

panic-and-phobias.agoraphobia.s: Agoraphobia as a diagnosis separate from panic disorder, with its situations, feared outcomes, course, differentials, how exposure is planned and guided, and work with housebound clients.
panic-and-phobias.agoraphobia.when: A client avoids or needs company for public transport, open or enclosed places, crowds or leaving home alone, with or without panic attacks.
panic-and-phobias.agoraphobia.b: Agoraphobia is fear and avoidance of several kinds of everyday situations because escape might be hard or help unavailable if panic-like or embarrassing symptoms strike. Since 2013 it has been diagnosed on its own, with or without panic disorder [APA-DSM5TR-2022]. It carries more comorbidity and impairment than panic alone [Kessler-etal-2006], and the treatment is in vivo exposure, ideally therapist-guided at first, with companions and other safety behaviors faded [Gloster-etal-2011].

panic-and-phobias.assessment.s: What to ask and record when assessing panic, agoraphobia and phobias, including attack mapping, avoidance and safety behavior inventories, medical screening, differential questions and measures with cutoffs.
panic-and-phobias.assessment.when: A client describes panic attacks, sudden fear, or avoidance of places, objects or body sensations, and you need to assess, measure and rule out other causes.
panic-and-phobias.assessment.b: Map one recent attack or phobic encounter in detail, then inventory avoidance and safety behaviors, screen for medical and substance causes, ask what the client fears will happen, and measure severity at baseline. The Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) and the free severity measures from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) track change; in panic disorder, a Mobility Inventory avoidance-alone score of 1.61 or more suggests agoraphobia.
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Panic Disorder; Panic Attack Specifier; Differential Diagnosis
APA-DSM5TR-Severity-Measures § Instructions to clinicians; Rights granted
Chambless-etal-1984 § Body Sensations Questionnaire; Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire
Kessler-etal-2006 § Results, cued and uncued attacks

panic-and-phobias.cbt-model.s: Clark's cognitive model of panic, the learning theory account, and the phobic avoidance and safety behavior cycle, with how to draw each with the client and the targets implied.
panic-and-phobias.cbt-model.when: You need to formulate why a client's panic attacks or phobic fear keep going and share a diagram that sets up exposure and behavioral experiments.
panic-and-phobias.cbt-model.b: In Clark's cognitive model, panic attacks come from catastrophically misinterpreting normal bodily sensations as signs of imminent disaster, which raises anxiety and the sensations further in a fast vicious circle. Body scanning, safety behaviors and avoidance keep the misinterpretation alive by blocking disconfirmation. Phobias follow the same logic: avoidance and safety behaviors stop the person from learning that the feared outcome does not happen or can be tolerated.
src: Clark-1986 § The cognitive model of panic

panic-and-phobias.interoceptive-exposure.s: How to run interoceptive exposure, deliberately bringing on feared body sensations, to test catastrophic predictions in panic, with exercise choice, steps, safety checks and evidence.
panic-and-phobias.interoceptive-exposure.when: A client with panic fears body sensations such as a racing heart, dizziness or breathlessness, and you are ready to move from discussing the model to testing it.
panic-and-phobias.interoceptive-exposure.b: Interoceptive exposure means deliberately bringing on the body sensations a client fears, such as dizziness or a pounding heart, and staying with them without safety behaviors so the predicted catastrophe can be tested. It is the cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) component most consistently linked to better outcomes in panic disorder [Pompoli-etal-2018]. Choose exercises that reproduce the client's own attack sensations.

panic-and-phobias.one-session-treatment.s: How to deliver Öst's one-session treatment, a single massed exposure session of up to 3 hours after a functional assessment, for adults and children, with steps, adaptations and evidence.
panic-and-phobias.one-session-treatment.when: A client of any age from about 7 has a specific phobia whose feared stimulus can be safely presented, and a brief intensive treatment would suit them or the service.
panic-and-phobias.one-session-treatment.b: One-session treatment (OST) is a functional assessment followed by a single exposure session of up to 3 hours that combines graduated in vivo exposure, therapist modeling, testing of catastrophic beliefs and reinforcement [Zlomke-Davis-2008]. In children it was as effective as multi-session cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and cheaper [Wright-etal-2023]. Use it when the feared stimulus can be presented safely and the client agrees to an intensive session.
src: Wright-etal-2023 § Methods; Results; Exclusions; Economic evaluation
Ollendick-etal-2021 § Abstract, standard OST and adaptations

panic-and-phobias.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials, ICD-11 differences, prevalence, course, differentials and risk notes for panic disorder, agoraphobia and specific phobia, with routes to assessment and treatment pages.
panic-and-phobias.overview.when: A client reports sudden attacks of fear, avoids places or objects out of fear, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessing or planning treatment.
panic-and-phobias.overview.b: Panic disorder is recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus at least 1 month of worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behavior. Agoraphobia and specific phobia are separate diagnoses of out-of-proportion fear and avoidance of situations or objects, typically lasting 6 months or more. All three are common, start early, persist without treatment, and respond to exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).

panic-and-phobias.pitfall-exposure-stopp.s: Exposure tasks are cut short at peak fear, kept too easy, or ended once anxiety dips, so the feared outcome is never tested and avoidance returns.
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-exposure-stopp.when: Exposure is happening but progress stalls, the client leaves tasks at peak fear, the hierarchy stays at the bottom, or gains do not last.
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-exposure-stopp.b: Exposure works when the client's specific feared outcome is tested and fails to happen, not merely when anxiety goes up and down [Craske-etal-2014]. Stopping a task at peak fear teaches that escape was necessary, and tasks that are too easy or too short never reach the prediction. Write the prediction, design the task to test it, and finish only when the test is done.
src: Craske-etal-2014 § Expectancy violation; Variability; Multiple contexts

panic-and-phobias.pitfall-hidden-safety-.s: The client completes exposure and anxiety drops, but catastrophic beliefs barely move and fear returns, because a companion, pill, breathing routine or other safety behavior stayed in use.
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-hidden-safety-.when: Exposure appears to go well but belief ratings stay high, gains do not generalize, or the client says "I managed because...
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-hidden-safety-.b: Exposure done while the client keeps a safety behavior teaches "I was safe because of the safety behavior", not "the catastrophe does not happen". Dropping safety behaviors during exposure reduced catastrophic beliefs and anxiety more than the same exposure with them [Salkovskis-etal-1999]. Ask about safety behaviors before, during and after every task.
src: Clark-1986 § The cognitive model of panic
NICE-CG113 § 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder

panic-and-phobias.pitfall-reassurance-in.s: The client keeps asking whether sensations are dangerous or seeks repeated tests, the therapist keeps reassuring, and the fear returns each time while panic does not improve.
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-reassurance-in.when: A client with panic repeatedly asks you or doctors whether they are safe, or you notice yourself reassuring rather than setting up experiments.
panic-and-phobias.pitfall-reassurance-in.b: Reassurance ("your heart is fine") brings quick relief, then the doubt returns and the client needs more, so it works like a safety behavior. Education and reassurance alone rarely settle panic-related health fears [Tunnell-etal-2024]. Do one appropriate medical check, then let behavioral experiments, not the therapist's word, answer the question.
src: Clark-1986 § The cognitive model of panic

panic-and-phobias.specific-phobia.s: Specific phobia subtypes, prevalence, course and differentials, with exposure as the treatment of choice, one-session treatment, applied tension for blood-injection-injury phobia, and the role of medication.
panic-and-phobias.specific-phobia.when: A client fears and avoids one kind of object or situation, such as animals, heights, flying, enclosed spaces, needles or vomiting.
panic-and-phobias.specific-phobia.b: Specific phobia is marked, out-of-proportion fear of one kind of object or situation, avoided or endured, typically for 6 months or more. It is common, usually starts in childhood, and is rarely treated [Eaton-etal-2018]. Exposure, especially in vivo, is the treatment of choice [Wolitzky-Taylor-etal-2008], often in a single session of up to 3 hours [Ost-1989; Wright-etal-2023], with applied tension added when blood or needles cause fainting [Ost-etal-1991].
src: Barnhill-2026c § Symptoms and Signs; Diagnosis; Treatment
Eaton-etal-2018 § Summary; Prevalence; Age of onset; Persistence; Treatment

panic-and-phobias.treatment.s: First-line CBT for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, with a session-by-session outline, key techniques, typical dose, and the evidence and guideline status behind it.
panic-and-phobias.treatment.when: A client has panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia, and you are planning or delivering a course of CBT.
panic-and-phobias.treatment.b: Panic-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best-supported psychological treatment for panic disorder: about 7 to 14 hours over up to 4 months, built on psychoeducation, cognitive work on catastrophic misinterpretations, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure without safety behaviors [NICE-CG113; Clark-1986]. Interoceptive exposure and face-to-face delivery are the components most linked to good outcomes, while muscle relaxation is linked to worse ones [Pompoli-etal-2018].

personality-disorders.adaptations.s: How to adapt CBT for personality disorder by comorbidity, severity, age, culture, learning disability and medication, with step-up and referral rules in If-then form.
personality-disorders.adaptations.when: A client with personality disorder or borderline features also has another disorder, is young or older, comes from a different cultural context, has a learning disability or takes medication, and the standard plan needs changing.
personality-disorders.adaptations.b: Keep one structured plan for borderline personality disorder (BPD) and fit other problems into it, rather than running separate treatments side by side [NICE-CG78]. Refer out for major psychosis, alcohol or Class A drug dependence and severe eating disorders [NICE-CG78]. Raise intensity with severity, weigh development and culture before diagnosing, and treat medication as a time-limited adjunct [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024].

personality-disorders.assessment.s: How to screen for and assess personality disorder and borderline features in CBT, with screening cutoffs, interviews, severity measures, differential questions, collateral sources and what to record.
personality-disorders.assessment.when: A client has repeated self-harm, marked emotional instability, chronic relationship problems or a poor response to standard CBT, and you need to check for personality disorder.
personality-disorders.assessment.b: Screen when you see repeated self-harm, marked emotional instability or persistent risk-taking [NICE-CG78], then confirm with a structured interview and history across time, contexts and informants. Rate severity with a repeatable measure so you can track change [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Assess chronic and acute risk separately, and share the diagnosis with the client [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024].

personality-disorders.cbt-model.s: Beck's belief-and-strategy model, Linehan's biosocial theory and the schema mode model, the vicious cycles that keep borderline and other personality patterns going, how to draw them, and targets.
personality-disorders.cbt-model.when: You have assessed a client with personality disorder or borderline features and need a shared formulation that explains why the pattern persists and what treatment should target.
personality-disorders.cbt-model.b: Three cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) models explain personality disorder: Beck's view of exaggerated beliefs and strategies, Linehan's biosocial theory of emotion dysregulation, and Young's schema mode model. All three describe short-term relief that keeps long-term patterns going, and all three expect the pattern to show up with the therapist. Draw one recent episode first, add origins later, and set targets for safety, emotion regulation, beliefs, relationships and functioning.

personality-disorders.chronic-risk-and-c.s: How to tell chronic from acute risk in borderline personality disorder, respond to crises in session, build crisis plans, and decide on escalation, admission and between-session contact.
personality-disorders.chronic-risk-and-c.when: A client with borderline personality disorder has long-standing suicidal thoughts or repeated self-harm, arrives in crisis, asks for admission, or contacts you between sessions.
personality-disorders.chronic-risk-and-c.b: In borderline personality disorder (BPD), suicidal thoughts can be a long-standing baseline while risk still rises sharply in a crisis, so assess chronic and acute risk separately and plan for both [NICE-CG78]. Respond to crises calmly and with validation, use the agreed crisis plan, and choose the least restrictive safe setting [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Decide your between-session contact rules before the first crisis.

personality-disorders.dbt-informed-skill.s: How to bring dialectical behavior therapy skills, chain analysis, diary cards and validation into CBT for emotion dysregulation and self-harm, and when to refer for comprehensive DBT.
personality-disorders.dbt-informed-skill.when: A CBT client with borderline features or emotion dysregulation acts on intense emotions through self-harm, substance use, outbursts or impulsive acts, and you need skills-based work inside your CBT.
personality-disorders.dbt-informed-skill.b: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) skills give cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) clients concrete alternatives to self-harm and other emotion-driven actions. Use daily monitoring, chain analysis of each target behavior, and skills from four modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness [Linehan-2025]. Skills training is the component linked to fewer self-injury episodes [Linehan-etal-2015]. Call it DBT-informed CBT, not DBT, and refer for comprehensive DBT when risk is high and persistent.

personality-disorders.other-personality-.s: CBT-relevant essentials for avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive, paranoid, schizotypal, antisocial and narcissistic personality disorders, with prevalence, differentials, evidence-based approaches and risk notes.
personality-disorders.other-personality-.when: A client's long-standing pattern looks avoidant, dependent, perfectionistic and rigid, suspicious, eccentric, antisocial or grandiose rather than borderline, and you need to plan CBT around it.
personality-disorders.other-personality-.b: People with personality disorders other than borderline usually come to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression, anxiety or the fallout of their behavior, not for the personality pattern itself [Zimmerman-2023a]. Cluster C disorders have randomized trial support for cognitive therapy and for schema therapy [Svartberg-etal-2004] [Bamelis-etal-2014]. Evidence for antisocial personality disorder is weak; use group-based cognitive and behavioral programs and watch risk to others [NICE-CG77] [Gibbon-etal-2020].

personality-disorders.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials of personality disorders and borderline personality disorder under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, prevalence, course, differentials, the CBT approach in brief, and suicide risk facts.
personality-disorders.overview.when: A client describes long-standing problems with identity, relationships, emotions or impulse control across many situations, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessment and planning.
personality-disorders.overview.b: A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible pattern of experience and behavior that begins by adolescence or early adulthood and causes distress or impairment across situations [Zimmerman-2023a]. Borderline personality disorder (BPD), the most researched type in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [Beck-etal-2015], affects 1.4% to 2.7% of United States adults over a lifetime and about 10% to 25% of psychiatric outpatients and inpatients [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Most people with BPD remit over time [Zanarini-etal-2010]. Suicide risk is high, so assess it from the first contact.

personality-disorders.pitfall-brief-or-u.s: A client with borderline personality disorder gets a short standard CBT course or a plan that changes each crisis, then drops out or relapses and is called treatment-resistant.
personality-disorders.pitfall-brief-or-u.when: You are about to offer a client with borderline personality disorder a standard short CBT course, or your current therapy has no agreed model, framework or end point.
personality-disorders.pitfall-brief-or-u.b: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) needs a structured therapy with an explicit model, a framework and enough time; most structured programs run 6 to 18 months [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Short courses of standard cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for BPD itself, or open-ended sessions that follow each week's crisis, are not what the evidence supports [NICE-CG78]. Choose a structured approach at the start and share it with the client.
src: APA-BPD-Guideline-2024 § Statement 5; Psychotherapy recommended for BPD; Comparison of psychotherapies for BPD

personality-disorders.pitfall-change-bef.s: The therapist challenges thoughts or sets behavior goals while the client is flooded, the client feels dismissed, escalates or shuts down, and the session ends in rupture or missed homework.
personality-disorders.pitfall-change-bef.when: A client with borderline features reacts to thought challenging, homework or problem solving with anger, tears, silence or "you don't get it," and sessions keep stalling.
personality-disorders.pitfall-change-bef.b: For clients who grew up with emotions dismissed, a fast move to "let's look at the evidence" can feel like one more invalidation and can escalate the very emotion you want to reduce [Crowell-etal-2009]. Validate what is valid first, then move to change, and keep switching between the two [Linehan-2025]. The goal is balance, not validation instead of change.

personality-disorders.pitfall-crisis-dri.s: Each crisis changes the plan, adds a medication, extends contact or triggers admission, so the agreed treatment never runs and the therapist ends up exhausted, resentful or rescuing.
personality-disorders.pitfall-crisis-dri.when: Treatment with a client with borderline personality disorder has become a series of emergencies, with growing medication lists, admissions, extra contact and no progress on agreed goals.
personality-disorders.pitfall-crisis-dri.b: In borderline personality disorder (BPD), reacting to every crisis with a new plan, a new drug or an admission replaces the treatment it was meant to protect. Agree a framework and crisis plan at the start, keep medication time-limited and reviewed, and take your own reactions to supervision [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Crises then become material for the planned work.

personality-disorders.pitfall-withholdin.s: The clinician avoids naming borderline personality disorder, or uses it as a pejorative or reason to exclude, so the client lacks an explanation, a matched treatment and hope.
personality-disorders.pitfall-withholdin.when: You suspect or have confirmed borderline personality disorder and are unsure whether to tell the client, or you notice the label being used to dismiss, blame or exclude someone.
personality-disorders.pitfall-withholdin.b: Clients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) prefer to be told their diagnosis, telling them does not lower satisfaction, and discussing it is part of good practice [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Naming it, with compassion and with the facts that most people improve, opens the door to matched treatment. Never use the label to blame or to exclude [NICE-CG78].
src: APA-BPD-Guideline-2024 § Statement 4 collaborative discussion of diagnosis and treatment; Rationale for this guideline (stigma)

personality-disorders.schema-therapy-lin.s: When to consider schema therapy for personality disorder within or after CBT, what it adds, its evidence and dose, and rules for referring or integrating schema-informed techniques.
personality-disorders.schema-therapy-lin.when: A client with personality disorder or long-standing characterological problems has not responded fully to standard CBT, or you are choosing between structured therapies for borderline or cluster C personality disorder.
personality-disorders.schema-therapy-lin.b: Schema therapy extends cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for clients whose problems are chronic, pervasive and part of who they are, adding childhood origins, experiential techniques, the therapy relationship and coping styles [Young-etal-2003]. Consider it for borderline personality disorder (BPD) and for cluster C, paranoid, histrionic or narcissistic personality disorder, where trials show it beats usual care [Arntz-etal-2022] [Bamelis-etal-2014]. It is long and needs specific training, so refer or train rather than improvise.
src: Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Conceptual Model (assumptions of CBT violated; development of schema therapy; schema domains; coping styles; schema modes; overview of treatment)
APA-BPD-Guideline-2024 § Statement 5; Schema-focused therapy; Comparison of psychotherapies for BPD

personality-disorders.treatment.s: Guideline-recommended structured psychotherapy for borderline personality disorder within CBT, covering guideline status, choosing DBT, schema therapy or CBT, a phased session outline, typical dose and evidence.
personality-disorders.treatment.when: An adult has a confirmed diagnosis of borderline personality disorder and you need to choose a structured treatment, plan its dose and format, and outline the course of sessions.
personality-disorders.treatment.b: Treat borderline personality disorder (BPD) with a structured psychotherapy that has research support and targets the core features [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has the most trials; schema therapy, mentalization-based treatment and other structured models also have trial support, and no type is clearly best [Storebo-etal-2020]. Plan for months, not weeks: most structured programs run 6 to 18 months [APA-BPD-Guideline-2024]. Medication is an adjunct only.
src: APA-BPD-Guideline-2024 § Statements 3, 5, 7 and 8; Psychotherapy recommended for BPD; Establishing a therapeutic framework; Treating co-occurring PTSD; Comparison of psychotherapies for BPD; Overall evidence for psychotherapy

ptsd.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting trauma-focused CBT to depression, substance use, suicide risk, dissociation, psychosis, ongoing danger, culture, age, medication and remote delivery, and when to step up or refer.
ptsd.adaptations.when: A client with PTSD has a comorbid condition, raised risk, dissociation, a cultural or language need, medication questions or access barriers, or is not responding to standard trauma-focused treatment.
ptsd.adaptations.b: Comorbidity, substance use, dissociation and even psychosis are reasons to adapt trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), not to withhold it. Treat posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) first unless depression or risk blocks the work, integrate substance use care rather than requiring abstinence first, and keep medication as an option for those who prefer it. Step up through more sessions or intensive formats, and refer for acute danger, acute psychosis or mania, or medically unsafe substance use.
src: APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025 § PTSD and substance use disorder; Pharmacological interventions; Discussion, individual differences and cultural adaptation

ptsd.assessment.s: How to screen for trauma and PTSD, take a trauma history without flooding the client, confirm diagnosis, rate severity with the PCL-5, and record risks and complicating factors.
ptsd.assessment.when: A client reports or shows signs of trauma-related symptoms, a screen is positive, or you are about to start and then monitor trauma-focused treatment.
ptsd.assessment.b: To assess posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), ask about traumatic events directly, using concrete examples, but take only the headline of each event. Screen briefly, confirm the diagnosis by interview, and rate severity with a validated checklist at baseline and every session. Record the index (worst) event, current danger, suicide risk, dissociation, substance use and complex PTSD features, because each changes the plan.
src: VA-CSP591-2018 § V.B Cognitive Processing Therapy, Session 1

ptsd.cbt-model.s: The Ehlers and Clark model of persistent PTSD, with the CPT and emotional processing views, how they maintain symptoms, how to draw them with the client, and treatment targets.
ptsd.cbt-model.when: You have assessed PTSD and need a shared, individual formulation that explains why symptoms persist and points to what treatment must change.
ptsd.cbt-model.b: In the Ehlers and Clark model, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) persists when the trauma is processed in a way that creates a sense of serious current threat. That threat comes from two sources: negative appraisals of the trauma or its aftermath, and a poorly integrated trauma memory that is easily triggered. Avoidance, suppression, rumination and safety behaviors stop both from changing [Ehlers-Clark-2000]. Treatment targets all three.
src: Wild-etal-2020 § Formulation; Memory work; Changing appraisals; Safety behaviors and rumination
VA-CSP591-2018 § I.C Theoretical background; V.A Prolonged Exposure; V.B Cognitive Processing Therapy

ptsd.children-and-adolescents.s: Treating PTSD in young people, covering NICE age and timing rules, TF-CBT components and phases, caregiver involvement, cognitive therapy for youth, safeguarding, and why NICE advises against drug treatment.
ptsd.children-and-adolescents.when: A child or adolescent has PTSD or clinically important trauma symptoms and you need to choose, adapt and deliver a trauma-focused treatment with caregivers.
ptsd.children-and-adolescents.b: Individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the treatment of choice for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in children and young people, delivered with a non-offending caregiver involved. The United Kingdom (UK) National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says to offer it to ages 7 to 17 presenting more than 3 months after a trauma, typically over 6 to 12 sessions, and not to offer drug treatment under 18 [NICE-NG116]. Check for ongoing abuse before anything else.
src: Pollio-Deblinger-2017 § Overview of TF-CBT; Empirical support

ptsd.cognitive-processing-therapy.s: The 12-session CPT protocol session by session, stuck points and worksheets, the optional written account, variable-length delivery, therapist moves, and the trial and guideline evidence.
ptsd.cognitive-processing-therapy.when: You are delivering or considering CPT for PTSD, especially when self-blame, guilt, shame or shattered beliefs about safety and trust dominate.
ptsd.cognitive-processing-therapy.b: Cognitive processing therapy (CPT) treats posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) by finding and testing "stuck points", the beliefs that keep the trauma unresolved, first about blame for the event and then about safety, trust, power and control, esteem and intimacy. It runs 12 weekly sessions, about 60 minutes individually or 90 minutes in groups [VA-NCPTSD-CPT]. Writing a trauma account is optional [VA-NCPTSD-CPT]. It is a first-line, strongly recommended treatment [APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025] [VA-DoD-PTSD-CPG-2023].
src: Resick-etal-2024 § Part II CPT Manual, Sessions 1 to 12; Ch. 18 Variations in CPT; Ch. 19 Group CPT
VA-CSP591-2018 § V.B Cognitive Processing Therapy; VIII.B.3 Early completion and additional sessions

ptsd.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.s: The Ehlers and Clark CT-PTSD protocol, covering formulation, reclaiming life, updating hot spots, then-versus-now trigger discrimination, site visits, appraisal work, dropping safety behaviors, dose and evidence.
ptsd.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.when: You are delivering or considering cognitive therapy for PTSD, especially when intrusions feel like they are happening now and appraisals of shame, guilt, danger or permanent change dominate.
ptsd.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.b: Cognitive therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), abbreviated CT-PTSD, applies the Ehlers and Clark model directly. It aims to reduce the sense of current threat by updating the trauma memory at its worst moments, changing the appraisals that make the trauma and its aftermath feel threatening, and dropping the strategies that maintain both, while the client reclaims their life [Ehlers-Clark-2000] [Wild-etal-2020]. Standard delivery is about 12 weekly sessions, with 90 minutes for memory sessions, plus up to 3 optional monthly boosters [Ehlers-etal-2014] [Wild-etal-2020].

ptsd.complex-ptsd.s: ICD-11 complex PTSD criteria, prevalence and differential from borderline personality disorder, and what the evidence says about stabilization-first phased treatment versus starting trauma-focused work directly.
ptsd.complex-ptsd.when: A client with PTSD after prolonged or repeated trauma, often in childhood, also has severe emotion dysregulation, a deeply negative self-concept and relationship difficulties, and you must decide how to sequence treatment.
ptsd.complex-ptsd.b: In the International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (ICD-11), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) becomes complex PTSD when severe, persistent disturbances in emotion regulation, self-concept and relationships are also present. Most evidence now shows that standard trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and related treatments work for these clients and that a mandatory stabilization phase is not required. Add skills, time and practical support where they help engagement, but start trauma-focused work early and set a limit on any preparatory phase.
src: WHO-ICD11-2022 § 6B41 Complex post traumatic stress disorder
WHO-CDDR-2024 § 6B41 Complex post-traumatic stress disorder, boundary with personality disorder
NICE-NG116 § 1.7.3; Terms used in this guideline, complex PTSD
APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025 § Background, complex PTSD; Discussion, individual differences

ptsd.early-intervention.s: What to do in the first weeks after trauma, with practical support and monitoring, no debriefing, trauma-focused CBT for acute stress disorder or marked symptoms, and no preventive medication.
ptsd.early-intervention.when: A person was exposed to a traumatic event within roughly the last month, or within 3 months with marked symptoms, and you must decide whether to watch, support or treat.
ptsd.early-intervention.b: Most people recover from early stress reactions, so the first weeks call for practical help, accurate information and active monitoring, not routine therapy. Do not offer single-session psychological debriefing. Offer individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) within the first month only to people with acute stress disorder or clinically important posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, and do not use medication, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD [NICE-NG116].

ptsd.overview.s: DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 diagnostic essentials for PTSD and acute stress disorder, with prevalence, course, key differentials, the CBT approach in brief, and risk notes.
ptsd.overview.when: A client describes a frightening or horrific event followed by intrusive memories, avoidance or a constant sense of threat, and you need the diagnostic picture before assessing or treating.
ptsd.overview.b: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a persistent reaction to an extremely threatening event, built around intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, negative changes in thinking and mood, and heightened arousal lasting more than a month. About 6% of United States (US) adults meet criteria at some point [Goldstein-etal-2016]. Many recover in the first months, but a large minority stay unwell for years [Morina-etal-2014], so offer trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) rather than waiting.

ptsd.pitfall-indefinite-stabilization.s: Months of coping skills, grounding and supportive sessions pass, the trauma memory is never processed because the client never seems stable enough, and PTSD symptoms stay unchanged.
ptsd.pitfall-indefinite-stabilization.when: Treatment for PTSD or complex PTSD has spent more than a few sessions on skills or support, memory work keeps being postponed, and PCL-5 scores are flat.
ptsd.pitfall-indefinite-stabilization.b: In posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) treatment, a preparatory skills phase can help some clients, but when it has no end date it becomes a way of avoiding effective treatment. Trials show that people with complex presentations, dissociation and even psychosis benefit from trauma-focused therapy without a long stabilization phase. Set a time limit, name the trauma-focused plan from the start, and move to memory work.

ptsd.pitfall-routine-debriefing.s: After an incident everyone is asked to talk through the event in one session, or offered therapy regardless of symptoms, while people with real early disorder go unfollowed.
ptsd.pitfall-routine-debriefing.when: An employer, school or service asks for a debriefing session after a critical incident, or a clinician is about to treat everyone exposed to a trauma in the first weeks.
ptsd.pitfall-routine-debriefing.b: Single-session psychological debriefing, in which people recount the event and their emotions soon after it, does not prevent posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and may increase it. Treating everyone exposed has no proven benefit either. Offer practical support, information and active monitoring to all, and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to those with acute stress disorder or marked symptoms.

ptsd.pitfall-therapist-avoidance-of-trau.s: Sessions drift into general support or problem-solving, imaginal exposure is shortened, hot spots and stuck points are skipped, and the protocol is delivered in name only.
ptsd.pitfall-therapist-avoidance-of-trau.when: You are delivering a trauma-focused protocol and notice that sessions rarely reach the memory or the worst moments, or that you feel relief when the client brings another topic.
ptsd.pitfall-therapist-avoidance-of-trau.b: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is maintained by avoidance, and therapists avoid too. When the therapist steers away from the memory, accepts every crisis as a reason to skip the protocol, or softens the hardest moments, the client learns that the memory is too dangerous to touch. Trauma-focused treatment is safe; temporary symptom rises are expected. Plan the memory work, protect its time, and use supervision to spot your own avoidance.
src: VA-CSP591-2018 § VIII.B.4 Adjunctive services, stressor sessions; V.A Prolonged Exposure

ptsd.prolonged-exposure.s: The PE protocol session by session, covering breathing, psychoeducation, the in vivo hierarchy, imaginal exposure with processing, hot spots, recorded homework, massed delivery and evidence.
ptsd.prolonged-exposure.when: You are delivering or considering PE for PTSD, particularly when fear, avoidance of reminders and a fragmented memory dominate.
ptsd.prolonged-exposure.b: Prolonged exposure (PE) helps people with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) stop avoiding by repeatedly revisiting the trauma memory aloud (imaginal exposure) and approaching safe but avoided situations (in vivo exposure), then talking through what they learned. It usually takes 8 to 15 weekly sessions of 60 to 90 minutes [VA-NCPTSD-PE] and is a first-line, strongly recommended treatment [APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025] [VA-DoD-PTSD-CPG-2023].
src: Foa-etal-2019 § Therapist guide, 2nd edition (cited for the manual only)
VA-CSP591-2018 § V.A Prolonged Exposure, Sessions 1 to termination
APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025 § Psychological interventions, first-line; Appendix G Table G1

ptsd.treatment.s: First-line trauma-focused CBT for adult PTSD, with how to choose between CPT, PE and CT-PTSD, a generic session outline, typical dose, and NICE, APA and VA/DoD guideline status.
ptsd.treatment.when: An adult has PTSD or clinically important PTSD symptoms more than 1 month after a trauma and you are planning which trauma-focused treatment to offer and how to run it.
ptsd.treatment.b: Offer adults with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) more than 1 month after the trauma an individual, manualized trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), such as cognitive processing therapy (CPT), prolonged exposure (PE) or cognitive therapy for PTSD (CT-PTSD). Plan for about 8 to 12 weekly sessions, more for multiple traumas. Every major guideline rates these above medication, and none has been shown reliably better than the others, so let client preference and therapist training decide.
src: APA-PTSD-Guideline-2025 § Treatment recommendations, psychological and pharmacological interventions; Appendix G Table G1

social-anxiety.adaptations.s: Decision rules for adapting social anxiety treatment to comorbid depression and substance use, severity, children and adolescents, culture, autism and medication, and for when to step up or refer.
social-anxiety.adaptations.when: A client with social anxiety disorder also has depression, substance use, autism, a different cultural frame, is a child or adolescent, takes or wants medication, or is not improving.
social-anxiety.adaptations.b: Keep the core of cognitive therapy for social anxiety disorder (CT-SAD) and adapt around it: sequence treatment when depression is present, do not let drinking delay treatment, involve parents for young people, read fears against cultural norms, and broaden the formulation for autistic clients [NICE-CG159] [Hofmann-etal-2010] [Lei-etal-2024]. Medication is the client's informed choice.
src: Katzman-etal-2014 § Table 19; Table 21; Pharmacotherapy for SAD
Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § General points; Addressing unconditional negative beliefs

social-anxiety.assessment.s: How to screen for and assess social anxiety disorder, which measures to use with their cutoffs, what to ask to separate it from look-alikes, and what to record.
social-anxiety.assessment.when: A client reports shyness, fear of judgment, avoidance of people or performance fears, or screens positive for anxiety, and you need to confirm social anxiety disorder and measure its severity.
social-anxiety.assessment.b: Screen with the three-item Mini Social Phobia Inventory (Mini-SPIN, positive at 6 or more) or two plain questions about avoidance and embarrassment, then assess fear, avoidance, distress, impairment and comorbidity in a full interview [NICE-CG159] [Connor-etal-2001]. Measure severity every session with the Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN, clinical cutoff 19) or the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS, cutoff 30) [Connor-etal-2000] [Mennin-etal-2002]. The core question for diagnosis is what the person fears others will think.
src: Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § Questionnaires to guide therapy; Table 2

social-anxiety.behavioral-experiments-an.s: How to design social anxiety behavioral experiments that drop safety behaviors and test specific predictions, run decatastrophizing experiments and surveys, and handle post-event rumination and socially traumatic memories.
social-anxiety.behavioral-experiments-an.when: A client with social anxiety holds a specific feared prediction or belief (I'll blush, I'm boring, people will stare) and you need a concrete in-session or homework test.
social-anxiety.behavioral-experiments-an.b: In cognitive therapy for social anxiety disorder (CT-SAD), behavioral experiments are the main engine of change: the client states a specific, observable prediction, enters the situation without safety behaviors and with attention on the interaction, and checks what others actually do [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. Early experiments drop safety behaviors; later ones deliberately show the feared sign (decatastrophizing). Surveys, rumination work and memory work support the experiments but do not replace them.
src: Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § Behavioral experiments; Table 3; Surveys; Using virtual audiences; Dealing with anticipatory worry and post-event rumination; Techniques for working on socially traumatic memories; Table 4

social-anxiety.cbt-model.s: The Clark and Wells model of social anxiety disorder, its cycles of self-focus, distorted self-image and safety behaviors, how to draw it with a client, and its treatment targets.
social-anxiety.cbt-model.when: You have assessed social anxiety disorder and need a shared, individualized formulation that explains why the fear persists despite repeated social contact.
social-anxiety.cbt-model.b: In the Clark and Wells model, people with social anxiety disorder (SAD) enter social situations predicting they will come across badly, then shift attention inward and judge how they look from their own anxious feelings and a distorted self-image [Clark-Wells-1995] [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. Safety behaviors and worry before and rumination after events stop them from discovering that others see them more favorably than they think. Draw the model from one recent situation in the first session; every later technique targets one of its loops.

social-anxiety.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials for social anxiety disorder under DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with prevalence, onset, course, comorbidity, differential diagnosis, risk notes and the CBT approach in brief.
social-anxiety.overview.when: A client fears being judged, embarrassed or rejected in social or performance situations and you need to know whether this is social anxiety disorder and what follows.
social-anxiety.overview.b: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is a marked, persistent fear of social or performance situations where the person might be scrutinized, driven by the fear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety, that will be judged negatively [APA-DSM5TR-2022] [Katzman-etal-2014]. It is common (about 7% of US adults in a year), starts early, and often stays chronic without treatment [NIMH-SAD-Statistics] [Leigh-Clark-2018]. Individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best-supported first treatment [Mayo-Wilson-etal-2014].
src: APA-DSM5TR-2022 § Anxiety Disorders, Social Anxiety Disorder
Katzman-etal-2014 § Social anxiety disorder; Table 19; Table 32

social-anxiety.pitfall-brief-or-group-de.s: Social anxiety disorder is routed by default to a short course of standard sessions, a general anxiety group or self-help, and the client drops out or improves little.
social-anxiety.pitfall-brief-or-group-de.when: You are deciding the format, length or intensity of treatment for a client with social anxiety disorder, or a service pathway sends all anxiety referrals to the same first step.
social-anxiety.pitfall-brief-or-group-de.b: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is one of the few common disorders for which the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends going straight to high-intensity individual therapy rather than stepped care [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. NICE advises against routinely preferring group cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and reserves supported self-help for people who decline CBT [NICE-CG159]. Offer the full individual protocol, or a proven internet version, unless the client chooses otherwise.
src: Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § Introduction; General points about remotely delivered CT-SAD
Katzman-etal-2014 § Social anxiety disorder, psychological treatment

social-anxiety.pitfall-safety-behaviors-.s: The client keeps entering feared social situations, anxiety eases a little, but belief in the feared outcome stays high because rehearsing, hiding or self-monitoring continued throughout.
social-anxiety.pitfall-safety-behaviors-.when: Repeated social exposure or homework is producing little change in belief ratings, or the client says situations "went fine because I was careful.
social-anxiety.pitfall-safety-behaviors-.b: People with social anxiety disorder (SAD) face social situations every day without getting better, because safety behaviors and self-focus stop them from learning that the feared outcome does not happen [Wells-etal-1995] [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. Exposure that keeps these behaviors in place repeats the client's everyday experience. Name the safety behaviors, drop them deliberately, and test a specific prediction each time.
src: Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § The cognitive model of SAD; Behavioral experiments

social-anxiety.pitfall-skills-deficit-as.s: The therapist sees a quiet, stilted client, assumes poor social skills, and coaches scripts and conversation techniques that become new safety behaviors while fear of evaluation stays untouched.
social-anxiety.pitfall-skills-deficit-as.when: A socially anxious client seems awkward, monotone or withdrawn in session and you are tempted to teach conversation skills or give them scripts.
social-anxiety.pitfall-skills-deficit-as.b: Most apparent social skill problems in social anxiety disorder (SAD) are the visible side of safety behaviors and self-focus, not a lack of ability: treated adults do not show ongoing skills deficits, and performance problems tend to appear only when the person is anxious [Leigh-Clark-2018]. Teaching scripts gives the client more things to monitor and rehearse. Test what happens when the client drops the safety behaviors before deciding a skill is missing.
src: Leigh-Clark-2018 § Safety behaviors and social skills
Warnock-Parkes-etal-2017 § Processing biases; Gaining insight into the impressions safety behaviors convey
Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020 § The cognitive model of SAD

social-anxiety.pitfall-unprepared-video-.s: The therapist plays a recording without predictions or viewing instructions, the client watches through their feelings and inner critic, spots flaws, and leaves more convinced they look odd.
social-anxiety.pitfall-unprepared-video-.when: You plan to show a socially anxious client a recording of themselves, or a previous video review left them more upset or unconvinced.
social-anxiety.pitfall-unprepared-video-.b: Video feedback changes a distorted self-image only when the client predicts in detail how they will look, is set up to watch "as a stranger", and compares predictions with the footage afterwards [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2017]. Without this, social anxiety biases take over the viewing, and studies that skipped preparation found no benefit [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2017]. Never let the client watch a recording alone before the joint session [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020].

social-anxiety.treatment.s: The first-line individual CBT protocol for social anxiety disorder (CT-SAD), session by session, with the Heimberg alternative, session counts, guideline status and the evidence behind it.
social-anxiety.treatment.when: An adult has social anxiety disorder as a main problem and you are planning or delivering a course of psychological treatment.
social-anxiety.treatment.b: Offer individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) built on the Clark and Wells model or the Heimberg model as the first treatment for adults; the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) does not recommend group CBT in preference or a low-intensity first step [NICE-CG159] [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. Cognitive therapy for social anxiety disorder (CT-SAD) runs up to 14 weekly sessions of up to 90 minutes, with in-session behavioral experiments, some outside the office [NICE-CG159] [Clark-etal-2023]. In one trial, 84% of patients no longer had the diagnosis after treatment [Clark-etal-2006].

Warnock-Parkes-etal-2017 § Effectiveness of current version of video feedback

social-anxiety.video-feedback-and-attent.s: How to run video feedback that corrects a distorted self-image and externally focused attention training that reverses self-focus, with preparation steps, therapist questions and evidence, including computerized attention bias modification.
social-anxiety.video-feedback-and-attent.when: A client with social anxiety believes they look visibly anxious, odd or boring, judges how they come across from their feelings, or is absorbed in self-monitoring during conversations.
social-anxiety.video-feedback-and-attent.b: Video feedback works when the client first makes specific, rated predictions of how they will look, is coached to watch themselves "as a stranger", and then compares predictions with what the recording shows; prepared this way, 98% of patients saw they came across better than predicted [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2017]. Externally focused attention training follows, so the client can attend to the interaction and collect real evidence during behavioral experiments [Warnock-Parkes-etal-2020]. Computerized attention bias modification is not ready for routine use [Heeren-etal-2015].
