substance-use.adaptations.s: If-then rules for adapting CBT for substance use to co-occurring depression, anxiety, trauma and psychosis, severity, age, culture, medication, relationships and cognitive limits, and for stepping up care.
substance-use.adaptations.when: A client with a substance use problem also has another mental disorder, severe dependence, is a young person or older adult, takes addiction medication, or is not improving with standard CBT.
substance-use.adaptations.b: Keep the core of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for substance use and change the order, intensity and partners. Treat co-occurring disorders alongside the substance use rather than waiting for sobriety, except that the United Kingdom's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises treating alcohol misuse first when depression or anxiety may be alcohol-related [VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021; NICE-CG115]. Step up the setting when dependence is severe, support is thin or treatment is not working [NICE-CG115].
src: VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021 § Patients with Multiple Substance Use Disorders; Substance Use Disorder and Other Co-occurring Conditions; Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Care; Recommendations 10, 28 and 29
Babor-etal-2001 § Scoring and interpretation (cutoff for women and men over 65)

substance-use.addiction-medications.s: Which medications treat opioid and alcohol use disorders and withdrawal, how strongly guidelines back them, the overdose risk of stopping, and what a CBT therapist does to support them.
substance-use.addiction-medications.when: A client with opioid or alcohol use disorder is taking, starting, refusing or wanting to stop an addiction medication, or you are deciding whether to suggest a medical referral.
substance-use.addiction-medications.b: For opioid use disorder, staying on buprenorphine or methadone sharply lowers death from any cause and from overdose [Sordo-etal-2017], and guidelines strongly recommend it [VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021]. For moderate to severe alcohol use disorder, naltrexone and other medications are recommended alongside psychological treatment [VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021; NICE-CG115]. Few people receive them: in 2024, 17.0 percent of people in the United States (US) with opioid use disorder and 2.5 percent with alcohol use disorder did [SAMHSA-NSDUH-2024]. A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist does not prescribe, but should support these treatments and never undermine them.
src: VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021 § Recommendations 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 to 14, 16, 17, 22, 25; Overdose Education and Naloxone Distribution; Patients with Multiple Substance Use Disorders

substance-use.assessment.s: What to ask and record when alcohol or drug use is a concern, with screening and severity measures and their cutoffs, withdrawal and overdose checks, differential questions and collateral sources.
substance-use.assessment.when: A client screens positive for alcohol or drug use, mentions drinking or drug use as a problem, or you suspect use is driving another presenting problem.
substance-use.assessment.b: Screen briefly, then measure consumption, count the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) criteria per substance, and check withdrawal and overdose risk before anything else [Hasin-etal-2013; NICE-CG115]. The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) gives risk zones and guides referral [Babor-etal-2001]. A history of withdrawal seizures or delirium, or heavy daily alcohol or sedative use, means medical assessment before the client stops [ASAM-Alcohol-Withdrawal-2020].

substance-use.cbt-model.s: The functional analysis and Beck cognitive models of substance use, the reinforcement and craving cycles that maintain it, how to map an episode with the client, and treatment targets.
substance-use.cbt-model.when: You have assessed a substance use problem and need a shared explanation of why use continues despite harm, to choose what treatment should target.
substance-use.cbt-model.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) explains continued use as learned behavior kept going by its short-term payoff: triggers set off expectations and cravings, use brings quick relief or pleasure, and the later costs arrive too late to steer behavior [Carroll-Kiluk-2017; Larimer-etal-1999]. Map this as a functional analysis of real episodes, and add the Beck cognitive model when beliefs about using carry the episode [Beck-etal-1993]. Each link in the chain is a treatment target.

substance-use.motivational-interviewing.s: How motivational interviewing and motivational enhancement therapy fit with CBT for substance use, covering when to use them, the four tasks, evoking change talk, formats, common errors and evidence.
substance-use.motivational-interviewing.when: A client with a substance use problem is unsure about changing, argues against change, misses sessions or homework, or you are starting treatment and need commitment before skills work.
substance-use.motivational-interviewing.b: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative way of talking that draws out the client's own reasons to change. In substance use care it opens assessment, stands alone as motivational enhancement therapy (MET), and serves as the front end of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) [NICE-CG115; VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021]. It reduces use compared with no treatment, mainly in the short term, and is no better than usual care or other active treatments [Schwenker-etal-2023]. The skill that matters most is evoking change talk and not provoking sustain talk [Magill-etal-2018].

substance-use.overview.s: Diagnostic essentials of substance use disorders in DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, with US prevalence, onset, recovery rates, comorbidity, differentials, overdose and suicide risk, and the CBT approach in brief.
substance-use.overview.when: A client reports alcohol or drug use that causes problems, loss of control or failed attempts to cut down, and you need to know whether it fits a substance use disorder and how serious it is.
substance-use.overview.b: A substance use disorder (SUD) in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) is a problem pattern of use shown by at least 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months, graded mild (2 to 3), moderate (4 to 5) or severe (6 or more) [Hasin-etal-2013; APA-DSM5TR-2022]. In 2024, 48.4 million people aged 12 or older in the United States (US), 16.8 percent, had one [SAMHSA-NSDUH-2024]. Recovery is common, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of several guideline-supported psychosocial treatments [Kelly-etal-2017b; VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021].

WHO-CDDR-2024 § Harmful pattern of psychoactive substance use; Substance dependence, essential features; Course specifiers for alcohol dependence

ASAM-Alcohol-Withdrawal-2020 § Recommendations II.5 to II.8; Table 1

substance-use.pitfall-confrontation-and-.s: The therapist argues the client has a problem, calls it denial or uses labels like addict, the client defends use harder, and sessions become debates or end in dropout.
substance-use.pitfall-confrontation-and-.when: Sessions with a client who uses alcohol or drugs keep turning into arguments about whether there is a problem, or the client becomes defensive when use is discussed.
substance-use.pitfall-confrontation-and-.b: Arguing a client into admitting a problem backfires. A confrontational counseling style produces more resistance, and in one trial the more the therapist confronted, the more the client drank a year later [Miller-etal-1993]. Labels such as "substance abuser" also make clinicians more punitive [Kelly-Westerhoff-2010]. Replace confrontation with reflection, permission-based information and the client's own reasons.

substance-use.pitfall-lapse-treated-as-f.s: After a slip, the client hides it or gives up, the therapist shows disappointment, resets the count or ends treatment, and one episode of use grows into full relapse.
substance-use.pitfall-lapse-treated-as-f.when: A client in treatment has used again after a period of abstinence or reduced use, or you notice the client concealing use from you.
substance-use.pitfall-lapse-treated-as-f.b: A lapse is a single episode of use; relapse is a return to the old pattern. Whether one becomes the other depends a great deal on how the client explains the lapse: blaming a stable personal flaw leads to guilt and giving up, while seeing it as a coping failure in one situation leads to learning [Larimer-etal-1999]. Therapists can feed the first explanation without meaning to. Treat each lapse as data and plan for it before it happens.
src: Larimer-etal-1999 § The abstinence violation effect; Lapse management; Cognitive restructuring; Theoretical and practical support
VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021 § Working Toward Successful Treatment of Substance Use Disorders

substance-use.pitfall-missed-withdrawal-.s: A therapist encourages a heavy daily drinker or sedative user to stop abruptly, or celebrates opioid abstinence without warning about lost tolerance, and the client has withdrawal seizures or overdoses.
substance-use.pitfall-missed-withdrawal-.when: A client plans to stop alcohol, sedatives or opioids, has recently stopped, is leaving a detoxification unit, prison or opioid treatment, or mixes depressants.
substance-use.pitfall-missed-withdrawal-.b: Stopping is not always the safe option. Alcohol and sedative withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium [ASAM-Alcohol-Withdrawal-2020], and people who lose opioid tolerance after detoxification, prison or leaving treatment face a spike in overdose death [Strang-etal-2003; Sordo-etal-2017]. Check withdrawal and overdose risk before agreeing any plan to stop, and again at every transition.
src: ASAM-Alcohol-Withdrawal-2020 § Recommendations II.5 to II.8; Table 1; Discussion of withdrawal timeline
VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021 § Recommendations 5, 7 and 10; Overdose Education and Naloxone Distribution

substance-use.pitfall-waiting-for-sobrie.s: A client with trauma, depression or anxiety plus substance use is told to get sober first, bounces between mental health and addiction services, and neither problem gets treated.
substance-use.pitfall-waiting-for-sobrie.when: A client has substance use plus another mental disorder and someone proposes to delay treatment of one until the other is fixed.
substance-use.pitfall-waiting-for-sobrie.b: Co-occurrence is common: 21.2 million adults in the United States (US) had both a mental illness and a substance use disorder in 2024 [SAMHSA-NSDUH-2024]. Making sobriety a condition of mental health care, or the reverse, leaves both untreated. The US Veterans Affairs and Defense (VA/DoD) guideline says substance use should not block treatment of co-occurring conditions [VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021], and integrated trauma treatment works during active substance use disorder [Back-etal-2019]. The one sequencing rule with support is narrower: reassess alcohol-related depression and anxiety after 3 to 4 weeks of abstinence [NICE-CG115].
src: VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021 § Patients with Multiple Substance Use Disorders; Substance Use Disorder and Other Co-occurring Conditions
NICE-CG51 § 1.4.6 Cognitive behavioral therapy and psychodynamic therapy

substance-use.relapse-prevention-model.s: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse model and its dynamic revision, covering high-risk situations, coping, self-efficacy, expectancies, the abstinence violation effect, covert antecedents, mapping it and the interventions it implies.
substance-use.relapse-prevention-model.when: A client has stopped or cut down and you need to anticipate how a slip could happen, or a lapse has happened and you need to stop it becoming a full relapse.
substance-use.relapse-prevention-model.b: In Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention (RP) model, relapse is a process, not an event. A high-risk situation meets a weak coping response, confidence drops, positive expectations of using rise, a first lapse follows, and self-blame for that lapse (the abstinence violation effect) turns it into relapse [Larimer-etal-1999]. Lifestyle imbalance and small "apparently irrelevant" choices set up the situation. Each step is a place to intervene, and RP-based treatment reduces substance use with a small effect and improves functioning more [Hendershot-etal-2011].

substance-use.treatment.s: Skills-based CBT for alcohol and drug use disorders, with a 12-session outline, session structure, key techniques, combinations with other treatments, effect sizes, and NICE and US guideline status.
substance-use.treatment.when: A client has a substance use disorder or harmful use, has some willingness to change, and you are planning structured individual CBT.
substance-use.treatment.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for substance use teaches a functional analysis of use and a set of coping skills, usually in about 12 weekly one-hour sessions [NICE-CG115; Project-MATCH-1997]. It beats minimal or no treatment, but not other specific therapies such as motivational enhancement or contingency management, so combine rather than compete [Magill-etal-2019]. Guidelines differ by substance: CBT is an option for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, while contingency management leads for stimulants [VA-DoD-SUD-CPG-2021; NICE-CG51].

12-medical-pharmacology.adhd-medications.s: How stimulant and non-stimulant ADHD medicines differ, their first-choice status, side effects and warnings, and what a CBT therapist monitors, schedules around and reports.
12-medical-pharmacology.adhd-medications.when: A child, adolescent or adult with ADHD takes or is considering ADHD medication and you are planning or delivering CBT alongside it.
12-medical-pharmacology.adhd-medications.b: Stimulants (methylphenidate and amphetamines) are the most effective short-term medicines for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD); a large network meta-analysis favored methylphenidate first for children and adolescents and amphetamines for adults [Cortese-etal-2018]. Non-stimulants such as atomoxetine and guanfacine are alternatives. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adds benefit for adults whose symptoms persist on medication [Safren-etal-2010]. The therapist tracks sleep, appetite, mood, misuse risk and timing, and reports concerns to the prescriber.

12-medical-pharmacology.antidepressants.s: What SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine and older antidepressants do, how long they take, their main side effects and warnings, and what a non-prescribing therapist watches for.
12-medical-pharmacology.antidepressants.when: A client is taking, starting, changing or asking about an antidepressant and you need to know what to expect and what to report to the prescriber.
12-medical-pharmacology.antidepressants.b: All 21 antidepressants compared in the largest network meta-analysis beat placebo for adult major depression, with modest differences between them [Cipriani-etal-2018]. For a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist the practical points are: benefit is judged over about 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose, early weeks bring side effects and a warning about suicidal thinking in young people, stopping needs a taper, and every change is the prescriber's decision.

12-medical-pharmacology.anxiolytics-and-.s: What benzodiazepines and z-drug sleeping pills do, their dependence, withdrawal and overdose risks, why as-needed use can undermine exposure work, and how CBT supports tapering.
12-medical-pharmacology.anxiolytics-and-.when: A client takes or is offered a benzodiazepine, z-drug or other sedative for anxiety or sleep, especially before or during exposure work or CBT for insomnia.
12-medical-pharmacology.anxiolytics-and-.b: Benzodiazepines and z-drug sleeping pills work fast but carry risks of dependence, withdrawal, falls, next-day impairment and dangerous interactions with opioids and alcohol. As-needed use for anxiety predicted poorer cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) outcomes in panic disorder [Westra-etal-2002], and gains made on alprazolam were lost after stopping [Marks-etal-1993]. CBT gains last, and adding CBT to a slow taper roughly tripled the rate of coming off a benzodiazepine [Otto-etal-1993].

12-medical-pharmacology.discontinuation-.s: How common antidepressant and benzodiazepine withdrawal is, how tapering works, how to tell withdrawal from relapse, and how a CBT therapist supports a prescriber-led taper.
12-medical-pharmacology.discontinuation-.when: A client is reducing or stopping an antidepressant, benzodiazepine or other psychiatric medicine, has missed doses, or reports new symptoms that might be withdrawal or relapse.
12-medical-pharmacology.discontinuation-.b: Stopping antidepressants or benzodiazepines should be a planned, gradual taper led by the prescriber. Withdrawal symptoms are common, usually begin within days, and are easily mistaken for relapse [Henssler-etal-2024; RCPsych-Stopping-Antidepressants-2024]. The therapist's job is to help the client plan with the prescriber, recognize withdrawal, keep cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) skills active, and have a relapse plan ready.

12-medical-pharmacology.medical-mimics.s: The physical conditions, substances and medicines most likely to cause or worsen low mood, anxiety or panic, with the clues that should prompt a medical check.
12-medical-pharmacology.medical-mimics.when: A client's symptoms are new, atypical or strongly physical, began after a new medicine or substance, or are not responding to well-delivered CBT.
12-medical-pharmacology.medical-mimics.b: Thyroid disease, anemia, sleep apnea, neurological illness, heart rhythm problems, alcohol or drug use and withdrawal, and many prescribed medicines can produce symptoms that look like depression, anxiety or panic. A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist does not diagnose these, but should know them, ask about them, and refer when clues appear. A physical cause rarely ends the psychological work; often both need treatment.

12-medical-pharmacology.medication-and-c.s: How psychiatric medicines can help, blunt or complicate CBT techniques, how CBT changes medication outcomes and attributions, and how to time therapy around starting or stopping medicines.
12-medical-pharmacology.medication-and-c.when: A client in CBT is starting, taking, changing or stopping psychiatric medication, or attributes their progress to a pill, and you need to adjust techniques or timing.
12-medical-pharmacology.medication-and-c.b: Antidepressants usually sit comfortably alongside cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), but as-needed benzodiazepines and the belief that "the pill did it" can undermine exposure and raise relapse risk after medication stops. CBT, in turn, protects against relapse when medication ends. Map each medicine's role in the case formulation, keep doses stable during exposure blocks where possible, help clients credit their own efforts, and plan any stopping with the prescriber.

12-medical-pharmacology.medication-histo.s: A step-by-step medication, supplement and substance history for non-prescribing therapists, with adherence and side-effect questions, what to record, and how to keep it current.
12-medical-pharmacology.medication-histo.when: You are completing an intake or review and need an accurate picture of the client's medicines, supplements, caffeine, alcohol and drug use, side effects and adherence.
12-medical-pharmacology.medication-histo.b: Ask about every medicine the client takes, not just psychiatric ones, plus supplements, contraception, caffeine, alcohol and drugs. For each psychiatric medicine record the purpose, dose as the client reports it, prescriber, start date, adherence, side effects, past trials and what the client believes it does. Recheck at every review, because a stale list hides the most common medical explanations for change.

12-medical-pharmacology.mood-stabilizers.s: What lithium, valproate, lamotrigine and antipsychotics are used for, the monitoring each needs, the toxicity and side-effect signs a therapist should recognize, and when to alert the prescriber.
12-medical-pharmacology.mood-stabilizers.when: A client with bipolar disorder, psychosis or treatment-resistant depression takes lithium, an anticonvulsant mood stabilizer or an antipsychotic while in CBT.
12-medical-pharmacology.mood-stabilizers.b: Lithium, valproate, lamotrigine and antipsychotics treat bipolar disorder and psychosis, and some are added for treatment-resistant depression. Each needs specific monitoring, and each has warning signs a therapist may be the first to see: lithium toxicity, a rash on lamotrigine, restlessness from akathisia, weight gain, or new compulsive behaviors. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works alongside these medicines, and the therapist's role is to notice, support adherence conversations and alert the prescriber.

12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-advising.s: The therapist suggests skipping, reducing, stopping or starting a medicine, or gives opinions on doses, and the client acts on it without the prescriber.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-advising.when: A client asks whether to stop, reduce or change a medicine, or you notice yourself offering views on drugs or doses.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-advising.b: A non-prescribing therapist does not advise starting, changing or stopping medication. The fix is a fixed response: acknowledge the question, explain whose decision it is, help the client take it to the prescriber, and offer to share progress data. Abrupt changes can cause seizures, withdrawal or relapse [FDA-Benzodiazepine-DSC-2020; Lewis-etal-2021].

12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-medicati.s: Exposure seems to succeed, but the client carries or takes an as-needed pill before each task, credits the pill for coping, and relapses when it is stopped.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-medicati.when: A client with anxiety, panic or phobia uses an as-needed benzodiazepine, beta-blocker or other medicine around feared situations during exposure work.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-medicati.b: An as-needed pill taken before or carried during exposure can work like any other safety behavior: it prevents the client from learning that they can cope and that the feared outcome does not happen. As-needed benzodiazepine users gained least from cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for panic [Westra-etal-2002]. Put the medicine in the case formulation, and plan any change with the prescriber.
src: Katzman-etal-2014 § Overview of pharmacological treatment; panic disorder combined treatment

12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-side-eff.s: New restlessness, agitation, sleepiness, low libido, confusion or low mood after a medication change is formulated as anxiety, depression or poor motivation, and nobody tells the prescriber.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-side-eff.when: A client's symptoms change within weeks of starting, raising or switching a medicine, or a symptom does not fit the case formulation.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-side-eff.b: Many common side effects look like the problems cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) treats: akathisia looks like anxiety, sedation looks like depression or low motivation, sexual side effects look like relationship problems, and low sodium or lithium-related thyroid changes look like cognitive slowing or relapse. Ask about medication changes whenever symptoms shift, and pass the observation to the prescriber.

12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-withdraw.s: Days after a dose cut or missed doses, a client feels dizzy, anxious and low, and the therapist and client conclude the depression or anxiety has returned.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-withdraw.when: A client reports new or returning symptoms soon after reducing, stopping or missing doses of an antidepressant, benzodiazepine or other psychiatric medicine.
12-medical-pharmacology.pitfall-withdraw.b: Withdrawal usually starts within days of a reduction or missed dose, includes unfamiliar physical sensations, and eases quickly when the dose is restored; relapse usually takes weeks and repeats the original pattern. Misreading withdrawal as relapse can lead to unnecessary long-term medication [Horowitz-Taylor-2019], lost confidence in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) skills, or a sense that the client "can't cope without pills."

12-medical-pharmacology.when-to-refer-me.s: Red flags that call for medical assessment, sorted into emergency, same-day and routine referrals, with the route for each and what to say, send and record.
12-medical-pharmacology.when-to-refer-me.when: A client reports new physical symptoms, a reaction after a medication change, signs of withdrawal or confusion, or symptoms that do not fit the case formulation or do not respond to CBT.
12-medical-pharmacology.when-to-refer-me.b: Refer for medical assessment when symptoms are new, sudden, atypical, accompanied by physical or neurological signs, linked to a medicine or substance, or not responding to good cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Sort each concern by urgency: emergency (call emergency services now), same day (contact the prescriber or urgent care today), or routine (primary care within weeks). Tell the client why, send specifics, and follow up.

12-medical-pharmacology.working-with-pre.s: How a non-prescribing CBT therapist sets up consent, agrees roles, shares measures and concerns with prescribers in a structured way, and stays within scope and privacy law.
12-medical-pharmacology.working-with-pre.when: A client in CBT has a prescriber, or needs one, and you need to communicate about medication, side effects, risk or progress.
12-medical-pharmacology.working-with-pre.b: A cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) therapist should treat the prescriber as a teammate: get consent early, agree who does what, share brief structured updates with measure scores, and pass on side effects, adherence concerns and risk promptly. Never advise on starting, changing or stopping a medicine; help the client take those questions to the prescriber. Collaborative care, where roles and information are shared by design, improves depression and anxiety outcomes compared with usual care [Archer-etal-2012].

13-context-culture-development.autism-ad.s: How to adapt CBT for autistic children and adults with anxiety or depression, covering structure, concrete language, visual materials, emotion literacy, sensory needs, family support and suicide risk.
13-context-culture-development.autism-ad.when: The client is autistic (diagnosed or self-identified) and has co-occurring anxiety, depression or another problem that CBT treats.
13-context-culture-development.autism-ad.b: Adapted cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) helps autistic people with anxiety, most clearly on clinician and parent ratings. Keep the CBT model but change the delivery: predictable structure, concrete language, visual material, emotion-recognition work, behavior first, supporter involvement and sensory adjustments. Screen for suicide risk, which is markedly raised.

13-context-culture-development.child-anx.s: Child anxiety presentations including separation anxiety and selective mutism, the SCAS, RCADS and SCARED, family accommodation, and CBT from Coping Cat style programs to parent-led CBT and SPACE.
13-context-culture-development.child-anx.when: A child has fears, worries, separation distress, school refusal or does not speak outside the home, and you must assess it and choose between child-focused and parent-led CBT.
13-context-culture-development.child-anx.b: About 6.5% of children and adolescents have an anxiety disorder [Polanczyk-etal-2015]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) built around graded exposure is the guideline-recommended psychological treatment, supported by randomized trials [Walter-etal-2020; James-etal-2020], and can be delivered to the child, through parents as coaches, or by changing parents' accommodation alone. Use child and parent forms; scores are screens, not diagnoses.

13-context-culture-development.children-.s: Developmental adaptations of CBT for children and adolescents, when and how to involve parents, consent and confidentiality basics, and what the guidelines and trials say works.
13-context-culture-development.children-.when: The client is under 18, or a young adult whose developmental stage or family involvement shapes how CBT should be delivered.
13-context-culture-development.children-.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works for young people, most clearly for anxiety, but it must be pitched at the child's cognitive and emotional level: more concrete, behavioral and visual for younger children, and more autonomy and confidentiality for adolescents. Involve parents as coaches when the child is young or parent behavior maintains the problem; adding parents by default does not reliably improve outcomes.

13-context-culture-development.cultural-.s: How to hold a culturally humble stance in CBT by asking rather than assuming, broaching identity and power, repairing cultural missteps, and recording what matters to the client.
13-context-culture-development.cultural-.when: Any client, and especially when the client's culture, identity, language, faith or social position differs from yours or seems relevant to the problem.
13-context-culture-development.cultural-.b: Cultural humility is a stance, not a body of facts about groups. Stay curious about how this client defines their identity, notice your own assumptions, name power differences, and repair missteps openly. Clients' ratings of their therapist's cultural humility and competence track outcomes, while therapists' self-ratings do not, so ask the client instead of trusting your own sense of being competent.

13-context-culture-development.culturall.s: Frameworks and evidence for culturally adapting CBT, from the eight-dimension ecological validity model to meta-analyses, with steps for adapting content and delivery for an individual client.
13-context-culture-development.culturall.when: A client's language, explanatory model, values or community context make the standard protocol a poor fit, or a service is designing CBT for a specific cultural group.
13-context-culture-development.culturall.b: Cultural adaptation means systematically changing how cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is delivered (language, metaphors, explanation of the problem, goals, methods and context) while keeping its active ingredients. Adapted interventions outperform unadapted versions of the same therapy in several meta-analyses, though effects shrink after correction for publication bias and one large youth meta-analysis found standard therapy worked as well for minority samples. Adapting the explanation of the illness so it fits the client's own beliefs appears to matter most.

13-context-culture-development.identity-.s: The minority stress model (distal stressors, proximal processes, coping) and how to use it in CBT formulation and affirmative treatment for LGBTQ+, racially minoritized and other stigmatized clients.
13-context-culture-development.identity-.when: The client belongs to a stigmatized group and discrimination, concealment, expected rejection or internalized stigma may be part of the problem.
13-context-culture-development.identity-.b: Stigma adds ongoing stress for members of minority groups: outside events such as discrimination, violence and rejection, and inside processes such as expecting rejection, concealing identity and internalized stigma. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), map these as real stressors and as maintaining processes, validate the reality of discrimination, and target the avoidance, rumination and self-blame that follow. The identity itself is never the treatment target.

13-context-culture-development.intellect.s: How to simplify CBT materials and methods for clients with intellectual disability or low literacy, including accessible measures, supporter involvement, teach-back checks and behaviorally weighted treatment.
13-context-culture-development.intellect.when: The client has an intellectual disability, limited reading or numeracy, or struggles with written worksheets, abstract questions or standard questionnaires.
13-context-culture-development.intellect.b: People with mild to moderate intellectual disability benefit from adapted cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and behavioral activation, and low literacy is common in the general population. Use plain spoken language, pictures and simple rating scales, short chunks checked with teach-back, more doing than verbal reasoning, measures built for the population, and a supporter for between-session practice when the client agrees.

13-context-culture-development.older-adu.s: Evidence that CBT helps older adults with depression and anxiety, plus practical adaptations for sensory, cognitive, health, ageism and cohort factors, including mild dementia.
13-context-culture-development.older-adu.when: The client is an older adult, or age-related health, sensory, cognitive or life-stage changes affect how CBT can be delivered.
13-context-culture-development.older-adu.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works for depression and anxiety in later life; effects for depression are similar to those in midlife, and effects for anxiety are somewhat smaller. Adapt the delivery (pace, sensory access, memory aids, booster contacts, coordination with medical care) more than the content. Check cognition and physical health early, and challenge ageist beliefs, including your own.

13-context-culture-development.perinatal.s: How to screen and treat perinatal depression, anxiety and OCD with CBT, respond calmly to intrusive infant-harm thoughts, handle postpartum psychosis as an emergency, and route medication and safeguarding questions.
13-context-culture-development.perinatal.when: The client is pregnant or within a year of giving birth, or a new parent reports low mood, anxiety, or frightening thoughts about harm coming to the baby.
13-context-culture-development.perinatal.b: Perinatal depression and anxiety are common, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a guideline-recommended first-line treatment [Vigod-etal-2025; NICE-CG192]. Ask every perinatal client about unwanted thoughts of harm to the baby: they are very common, and in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) they do not signal danger [Collardeau-etal-2024; Fairbrother-etal-2022]. Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency [RCPsych-Postpartum-Psychosis]. Medication decisions belong to the prescriber, and safeguarding referrals rest on evidence of risk, not on intrusive thoughts alone.

13-context-culture-development.pitfall-a.s: The therapist infers a client's values, problems or preferences from their ethnicity, faith, age, sexuality or disability, and the client feels stereotyped, misread or quietly disengages.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-a.when: You catch yourself predicting what a client believes or needs from a group label, or a client seems guarded, corrects you, or drops out after early sessions.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-a.b: Group knowledge is a starting hypothesis, never a description of the person in front of you. Ask before you assume, use the client's own words for their identity, and when you get it wrong, say so and repair. The opposite error, ignoring culture entirely, fails clients in the same way.

13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.s: New distress or symptoms are put down to a client's autism, intellectual disability, age, gender identity or culture, so treatable depression, anxiety, trauma or medical illness goes unassessed.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.when: A client with a known disability, neurodivergence, older age or minority identity shows a change in mood, behavior, sleep or functioning, and the explanation offered is "that's just their condition.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.b: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing a new problem to a condition or identity the client already has. Treat every change from the client's own baseline as something to assess: mental health, physical health, medication, pain and life events. Autism, intellectual disability, age and minority identity raise the risk of treatable problems; they do not explain them away.

13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.s: The therapist treats thoughts about discrimination, poverty or danger as cognitive distortions to dispute, and the client feels invalidated, blamed or unsafe, and disengages.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.when: A client's negative thought refers to discrimination, money, housing, violence or another real adversity, and you are about to look for evidence against it.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-d.b: Some negative thoughts are accurate. When a thought describes real discrimination, poverty or danger, validate it, then problem-solve the situation and examine only the extra meanings the client adds, such as self-blame or hopelessness. Disputing the fact itself invalidates the client and can blame them for their circumstances.
src: APA-LowIncome-Guidelines-2019 § Guidelines 5 and 6, treatment considerations and respecting client priorities

13-context-culture-development.pitfall-f.s: A relative, friend, child or untrained staff member interprets therapy, so content is filtered, risk and abuse go unspoken, and errors with clinical consequences slip through.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-f.when: A client with limited English arrives with a relative or friend to interpret, no professional interpreter is booked, or a bilingual colleague is asked to help informally.
13-context-culture-development.pitfall-f.b: Do not let family, friends, children or untrained staff interpret therapy except as a brief emergency stopgap. Ad hoc interpreters make more clinically serious errors, cannot be neutral, and may be the very people the client cannot speak freely in front of. Book a qualified interpreter and document any exception.
src: NHSE-Interpreting-2018 § Principle 1 items 5 and 6; Principle 4 items 6 to 9

13-context-culture-development.religion-.s: How to assess religious and spiritual life in CBT, integrate faith resources when clients want it, respect beliefs while testing unhelpful appraisals, and handle value conflicts.
13-context-culture-development.religion-.when: Faith, spirituality or religious community matters to the client, shapes how they understand the problem, or could be a resource or a source of distress in therapy.
13-context-culture-development.religion-.b: Ask every client whether faith or spirituality matters to them, and if it does, how it bears on the problem and on coping. When a client wants it, weaving their beliefs and practices into cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works about as well as standard CBT for symptoms and adds spiritual wellbeing. Respect the belief itself, and test only the unhelpful appraisals and behaviors around it.

13-context-culture-development.socioecon.s: How poverty, debt, housing, work and access barriers affect CBT engagement and outcomes, and how to assess them, adapt delivery, problem-solve practical needs and avoid blaming clients.
13-context-culture-development.socioecon.when: The client faces low income, debt, unstable housing, unemployment, insecure work or practical barriers to attending and using therapy.
13-context-culture-development.socioecon.b: Socioeconomic deprivation goes with more mental health problems and somewhat poorer therapy outcomes, yet low-income clients benefit from evidence-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) when services remove barriers. Ask about money, housing, work and food as routinely as about sleep, put real stressors in the formulation, fix logistics, use problem solving and small acts of advocacy for practical problems, and keep cognitive restructuring for interpretations, not for the hardship itself.

13-context-culture-development.working-w.s: Step-by-step procedure for interpreter-mediated CBT, covering booking a qualified interpreter, pre-session briefing, seating and turn-taking, adapting materials, debriefing, legal duties and what to record.
13-context-culture-development.working-w.when: The client prefers or needs to receive therapy in a language you do not speak fluently, including a signed language.
13-context-culture-development.working-w.b: Use a trained, qualified interpreter, not family, friends, children or untrained staff. In one service comparison, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for refugees delivered through interpreters worked as well as CBT without them. Book about double time, brief the interpreter beforehand, speak directly to the client in short segments, use professionally translated materials, debrief afterward, and record the language, interpreter and any decisions about who interprets.

14-ethics-law.administrative-and-billing.s: Psychotherapy Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes and time rules, prior authorization, Good Faith Estimates for self-pay clients, fee and cancellation agreements, release forms, and UK equivalents.
14-ethics-law.administrative-and-billing.when: A clinician is choosing a billing code, documenting session time, seeking insurer authorization, quoting fees to an uninsured or self-pay client, setting a cancellation policy, or preparing a release form.
14-ethics-law.administrative-and-billing.b: Bill the code matching the face-to-face time spent and record start and stop or total time: Medicare contractors treat 90832 as 16 to 37 minutes, 90834 as 38 to 52 and 90837 as 53 or more [CMS-A57520]. Give uninsured and self-pay clients a written Good Faith Estimate (GFE) on the federal timetable [CFR-45-149-610]. Put fees, billing and nonpayment terms in writing first [ACA-Ethics-2014]. Send payers only the minimum they need [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-502], and never let billing shape a diagnosis [ACA-Ethics-2014].

14-ethics-law.ai-documentation-and-recor.s: How to use AI note-taking, transcription and session recording lawfully, covering vendor checks, state consent rules, a client consent script, note review and data deletion.
14-ethics-law.ai-documentation-and-recor.when: A clinician or service is considering, or already using, an AI scribe, transcription tool, note generator or audio or video recording of therapy sessions.
14-ethics-law.ai-documentation-and-recor.b: Recording or transcribing a session needs the client's permission before you start [APA-Ethics-2017], and in several states an artificial intelligence (AI) recording or transcription tool needs advance, written, informed consent that names the tool and its purpose [BakerDonelson-2025] [CO-HB26-1195]. Use only vendors that sign a business associate agreement, read and correct every AI-drafted note, and let clients decline without losing care. You, not the tool, remain responsible for the record.

14-ethics-law.boundaries-and-dual-relati.s: How to tell harmless boundary crossings from harmful violations, the absolute rules on sexual contact, and how to handle gifts, social media, small communities and out-of-office contact.
14-ethics-law.boundaries-and-dual-relati.when: A client offers a gift, invitation, friend request or business deal, a clinician meets a client socially or in a small community, or a clinician feels pulled toward a personal relationship.
14-ethics-law.boundaries-and-dual-relati.b: A boundary crossing (accepting a small gift, attending a graduation) is not automatically wrong; it is wrong when it risks impairing your objectivity or exploiting or harming the client [APA-Ethics-2017]. Sexual or romantic contact with a current client is always prohibited, and with former clients psychologists must wait at least 2 years, counselors 5 years, and social workers should not at all [APA-Ethics-2017] [ACA-Ethics-2014] [NASW-Code-2021]. When you extend a boundary, consult and document beforehand.

14-ethics-law.competence-and-supervision.s: How to judge whether a case or technique is within your competence, what to do if not, what supervision must provide, and rules for trainees, delegation and impairment.
14-ethics-law.competence-and-supervision.when: A clinician is offered a client or technique outside their training, is supervising or being supervised, is a trainee, or notices personal problems affecting their work.
14-ethics-law.competence-and-supervision.b: Treat only populations and problems you are competent to treat by education, training, supervised experience, consultation or study, and get training, supervision or consultation before taking on new ones, or refer [APA-Ethics-2017]. Supervision is how competence is built and checked: it should be regular, matched to experience and caseload, independent of line management, and clear about who holds clinical responsibility [BACP-Ethical-Framework-2026]. Trainees must tell clients they are supervised and name the supervisor [APA-Ethics-2017].

14-ethics-law.confidentiality-and-limits.s: What therapy confidentiality covers, the standard exceptions (harm, abuse, court, supervision, billing, minors), how to explain them at the start, and how to disclose the minimum when required.
14-ethics-law.confidentiality-and-limits.when: A clinician is explaining confidentiality at intake, a client asks who will find out what they say, or a possible disclosure without consent is being considered.
14-ethics-law.confidentiality-and-limits.b: What a client says in therapy stays private except in a short list of situations that the client should hear about at the start: serious risk of harm to self or others, suspected abuse of a child or adult at risk, a court order or other legal requirement, and routine sharing for supervision, billing or care coordination. Discuss these limits at the outset and again when circumstances change [APA-Ethics-2017]. When disclosure is needed, share only what the purpose requires, with someone able to act, and record why.

14-ethics-law.digital-and-ai-tools.s: Evidence for internet CBT and AI chatbots, their ethical risks, the 2025 to 2026 US state laws restricting AI therapy, and how to discuss a client's AI use.
14-ethics-law.digital-and-ai-tools.when: A client uses or asks about a mental health app or AI chatbot, a clinician considers recommending one, or someone is designing or deploying an AI tool that talks with clients.
14-ethics-law.digital-and-ai-tools.b: Guided internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works about as well as face-to-face CBT across the trials that compared them directly [Carlbring-etal-2018]. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots show early, short-term benefits but no proof of safety, and the American Psychological Association (APA) advises against using them in place of a qualified clinician [APA-AI-Advisory-2025]. Since 2025, several United States (US) states have banned or restricted AI that delivers therapy, so check the client's state before recommending or building such a tool.

14-ethics-law.duty-to-warn-and-protect.s: The Tarasoff duty and how US states differ (mandatory, permissive, none), what triggers it, the lawful ways to discharge it, HIPAA's serious-threat rule, and the UK public interest position.
14-ethics-law.duty-to-warn-and-protect.when: A client threatens serious violence against an identifiable person, or a clinician must decide whether law requires or permits warning a victim or police.
14-ethics-law.duty-to-warn-and-protect.b: Since the 1976 Tarasoff ruling, United States (US) therapists who determine, or should determine, that a client poses a serious danger of violence to another person must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim [Tarasoff-1976]. States now differ: in the 2022 National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) chart, 28 states make the duty mandatory, 16 permissive, 3 mixed, and 3 impose none, while the District of Columbia is permissive [NCSL-Duty-to-Warn-2022]. Know your state's trigger and approved actions before you need them, consult the same day, and document. The United Kingdom (UK) has no Tarasoff statute; disclosure is a public interest judgment.

14-ethics-law.hipaa-and-gdpr.s: The privacy rules a CBT clinician must know, covering who HIPAA covers, permitted disclosures, psychotherapy notes, access rights, breaches and business associates, plus UK and EU GDPR equivalents.
14-ethics-law.hipaa-and-gdpr.when: A clinician needs to know whether a disclosure, records request, vendor or data breach is lawful and what deadline applies, in the US under HIPAA or in the UK or EU under GDPR.
14-ethics-law.hipaa-and-gdpr.b: For cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) clinicians in the United States (US), the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule lets you share protected health information (PHI) for treatment, payment and operations without authorization, but separately kept psychotherapy notes need a specific authorization [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-508]. Clients can get copies of their record within 30 days, extendable once by 30 days [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-524]. In the United Kingdom (UK) and European Union (EU), the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) treats health data as a special category, gives access within one month, and requires breach reports to the regulator within 72 hours [EU-GDPR-2016].

14-ethics-law.informed-consent.s: How to obtain and maintain informed consent for CBT assessment and treatment, including exposure, trainees, recording, minors and capacity, with what to say and record.
14-ethics-law.informed-consent.when: A clinician is starting assessment or therapy, proposing a new technique such as exposure, recording sessions, or treating a minor or an adult whose capacity is in doubt.
14-ethics-law.informed-consent.b: Informed consent is a conversation that starts before assessment and is revisited whenever the plan changes, not a signature on a form. Tell the client, in language they understand, the nature and likely course of therapy, fees, third-party involvement and the limits of confidentiality, and give them time to ask questions [APA-Ethics-2017]. For exposure, explain the rationale, the expected temporary rise in anxiety, the alternatives and the right to stop, then agree each step together.

14-ethics-law.mandatory-reporting.s: Who must report child or adult abuse, to whom, how fast and on what standard, in the US and England and Wales, including FGM and child sexual abuse duties.
14-ethics-law.mandatory-reporting.when: A client discloses, or the clinician suspects, abuse or neglect of a child or an adult at risk, or a clinician must check what their jurisdiction legally requires them to report.
14-ethics-law.mandatory-reporting.b: In the United States (US), every state requires therapists to report suspected child abuse or neglect, either by naming mental health professionals (38 states and the District of Columbia) or by requiring everyone to report; the usual standard is suspicion or reason to believe, and you do not need proof [CWIG-Mandatory-Reporting-2023]. Report yourself, promptly, to the agency your state names, even if you also tell your employer. Adult abuse duties vary by state [NAPSA-Site]. In England and Wales, regulated health professionals and teachers must report female genital mutilation (FGM) in a girl under 18 to police [FGM-Act-2003-s5B]; a 2026 child sexual abuse reporting duty for England is not yet in force [UK-Crime-Policing-Act-2026].

14-ethics-law.pitfall-investigating-befo.s: The clinician delays a required abuse report to gather proof, question the family, wait a session, or let a manager decide, so the report is late or never made.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-investigating-befo.when: A clinician suspects child or adult abuse but feels unsure, wants more evidence, or has passed the concern to a supervisor or institution instead of reporting.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-investigating-befo.b: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion; they do not need proof, and the investigation belongs to the agency [CWIG-Mandatory-Reporting-2023]. Questioning a child in detail, confronting a parent, or waiting a week can contaminate evidence and leave a child at risk. In many states, telling your manager does not discharge your own duty [CWIG-Mandatory-Reporting-2023].

14-ethics-law.pitfall-practicing-where-n.s: A clinician keeps holding telehealth sessions after a client moves, travels or starts college in another state or country, without checking licensure there.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-practicing-where-n.when: A telehealth client mentions being away, moving, or living part of the year elsewhere, or a service accepts out-of-state or overseas clients.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-practicing-where-n.b: For telehealth, the practice is treated as happening where the client is, so a provider typically needs a license or privilege in the client's state [CCHP-Cross-State-2026]. Unlicensed sessions risk board discipline, uninsured practice and unclear duties if a crisis occurs. Check the client's location every session and plan for moves before they happen.

14-ethics-law.pitfall-unqualified-confid.s: The clinician tells a client that everything said stays in the room, or skips the limits at intake, then must break that promise when risk or abuse emerges.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-unqualified-confid.when: A clinician, intake script or AI intake tool describes therapy as completely confidential, or a disclosure of risk or abuse arrives before limits were explained.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-unqualified-confid.b: "Everything you say here is confidential" is untrue, because law and ethics codes require or permit disclosure for serious harm, abuse and legal process [APA-Ethics-2017]. Clients who disclose on that promise and then learn you must report feel betrayed, and the alliance can break. Explain the limits at the outset, in plain words, before the client tells their story.

14-ethics-law.pitfall-unvetted-ai-and-ap.s: The clinician pastes session content into a consumer AI assistant, uses an app or scribe without a business associate agreement or consent, or recommends a chatbot as therapy.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-unvetted-ai-and-ap.when: A clinician or service uses AI or apps to draft notes, summarize sessions, message clients, or support clients between sessions, without having checked the vendor and the law.
14-ethics-law.pitfall-unvetted-ai-and-ap.b: Any vendor that handles protected health information (PHI) for a covered clinician needs a written business associate agreement [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-502], and client data should not enter an artificial intelligence (AI) tool without the client's informed consent [BACP-Ethical-Framework-2026]. Consumer chatbots are not therapists, and several states now penalize presenting them as such [BakerDonelson-2025] [CO-HB26-1195].

14-ethics-law.professional-codes.s: Which ethics codes bind US and UK CBT clinicians (APA, ACA, NASW, BABCP, BACP, HCPC), their current editions, where they differ, and a short process for ethical decisions.
14-ethics-law.professional-codes.when: A clinician needs to know which code applies to them, check what a code says on a dilemma, or compare rules across professions and countries.
14-ethics-law.professional-codes.b: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is practiced by many professions, so the code that binds you depends on your license or membership, not on the therapy you deliver. In the United States (US) that is usually the American Psychological Association (APA), American Counseling Association (ACA) or National Association of Social Workers (NASW) code plus your state board's rules; in the United Kingdom (UK) it is the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies (BABCP), the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP), or the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) for psychologists. Codes agree on most things but differ on details such as relationships with former clients.

14-ethics-law.record-keeping.s: How to keep a lawful CBT record, covering what belongs in the clinical record versus psychotherapy notes, retention, access requests, corrections and secure storage.
14-ethics-law.record-keeping.when: A clinician is setting up a record system, deciding where a note belongs, receiving a request for records, correcting an entry, or deciding how long to keep or when to destroy files.
14-ethics-law.record-keeping.b: Keep one clinical record that a client, a covering clinician or a court could read: dates, diagnosis, plan, progress, measures, risk decisions and disclosures. Psychotherapy notes, if you keep them at all, are a narrow, separately stored category under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and get extra protection [HIPAA-45-CFR-164-501]. Where no law or contract sets a period, the American Psychological Association (APA) 2007 guidelines suggest keeping full records for 7 years after the last service for adults, or 3 years after a minor reaches majority, whichever is later [APA-RecordKeeping-2007]. State law, employer policy and payer contracts override this, and the guidelines may have been superseded.

14-ethics-law.telehealth-law.s: The legal checklist for remote CBT, covering licensure where the client is, interstate compacts, HIPAA-compliant platforms, telehealth consent, emergency planning, prescribing rules and international clients.
14-ethics-law.telehealth-law.when: A clinician offers video or phone sessions, a client moves or travels to another state or country, or a service is choosing a telehealth platform or setting telehealth policy.
14-ethics-law.telehealth-law.b: Telehealth is treated as happening where the client is, so you typically need a license, or a compact privilege, in the client's state at the time of each session [CCHP-Cross-State-2026]. Use a platform whose vendor signs a business associate agreement, add telehealth-specific items to consent, and set an emergency plan for the client's location before the first session. 15-transdiagnostic-processes.assessing-t.s: Step-by-step method for screening, functionally analyzing and measuring transdiagnostic processes, with a table of common self-report measures, what to record, and how to feed results into the formulation.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.assessing-t.when: The clinician suspects that worry, rumination, avoidance, safety behaviors, perfectionism, uncertainty intolerance, self-criticism or emotion regulation problems are maintaining a client's difficulties and needs to confirm and measure them.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.assessing-t.b: Assess processes the same way you assess symptoms: ask about them directly, analyze a recent example, and measure them before and during treatment. Use a content-independent measure such as the Perseverative Thinking Questionnaire (PTQ) when repetitive thinking spans several topics [Ehring-etal-2011], add a process-specific measure only where it will change the plan, and back every questionnaire with idiographic ratings of the client's own behaviors.

15-transdiagnostic-processes.attention-p.s: Explains self-focused attention, threat-related attentional bias and threat monitoring as transdiagnostic processes, how they supply false evidence for fears, and how to work with attention in session.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.attention-p.when: A client scans for danger, checks their body, or watches themselves during social situations, and the clinician needs to show how where attention goes keeps fear or low mood going.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.attention-p.b: Where attention goes shapes what a person concludes. Heightened self-focused attention appears across almost every disorder studied [Ingram-1990], and anxious people preferentially attend to threat (d = 0.45 across 172 studies) [Bar-Haim-etal-2007]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), the practical work is to notice where attention goes in feared situations, show how it creates misleading evidence, and practice flexible, outward attention, rather than to rely on computerized bias training, whose clinical effects are small and uncertain [Fodor-etal-2020].

15-transdiagnostic-processes.avoidance.s: How behavioral, cognitive and experiential avoidance keep anxiety, depression and related problems going through short-term relief, how to judge an avoidance by its function, and which treatments target it.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.avoidance.when: A client stays away from situations, tasks, people, feelings, memories or thoughts, and the clinician needs to show how this keeps the problem going and choose what to target.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.avoidance.b: Avoidance is any action, overt or mental, that keeps a person away from something they expect to be threatening or painful. It brings quick relief, so it is reinforced, and it stops the person learning that the feared outcome is unlikely or bearable [Krypotos-etal-2015; Craske-etal-2014]. Judge each avoidance by its function, not its form: the same act can be avoidance for one client and healthy coping for another [Hofmann-Hay-2018].

15-transdiagnostic-processes.cognitive-d.s: Explains what cognitive distortions are, where the idea comes from, its limits as evidence, and how this wiki's cognitive distortions vocabulary scheme is structured and used for tagging.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.cognitive-d.when: A clinician or tool designer needs to know what counts as a cognitive distortion, how the named categories relate, and how to tag a client's thought with the cd vocabulary.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.cognitive-d.b: A cognitive distortion is a systematic bias in information processing that shows up in an automatic thought, such as all-or-nothing thinking or mind reading. It describes how a thought is biased, not what it is about. Beck introduced the idea from clinical observation of depression [Beck-1963], and Burns popularized a list of named distortions [Burns-1980]. Treat a distortion label as a hypothesis that guides testing, never as proof the thought is false.
src: Beck-1963 § Idiosyncratic content and cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 Definitions of cognitive distortions

15-transdiagnostic-processes.emotion-reg.s: Defines emotion regulation and its difficulties, summarizes evidence that maladaptive strategies and dysregulation cut across disorders and change with treatment, and gives concrete ways to assess and work with them.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.emotion-reg.when: A client's emotions feel overwhelming, confusing or unacceptable to them, or they manage feelings with avoidance, suppression, rumination, substances, bingeing or self-harm.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.emotion-reg.b: Emotion regulation is how people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them [Gross-1998]. Difficulties show up as low awareness or clarity about feelings, not accepting them, losing control of behavior when upset, and relying on strategies such as avoidance, suppression and rumination. These strategies are associated with symptoms across anxiety, depression, eating and substance-related disorders [Aldao-etal-2010], and dysregulation falls after effective treatment for many disorders [Sloan-etal-2017]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), it is a formulation target in its own right.
src: Gross-1998 § Process model of emotion regulation
Gratz-Roemer-2004 § Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale dimensions

15-transdiagnostic-processes.intolerance.s: Defines intolerance of uncertainty, summarizes evidence that it is a transdiagnostic factor across anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, depressive and eating disorders, and shows how to spot and target it in session.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.intolerance.when: A client cannot settle until they know for sure, seeks reassurance or checks repeatedly, delays decisions, or treats any chance of a bad outcome as unacceptable.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.intolerance.b: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is the tendency to find the possibility of a negative event unacceptable, however unlikely it is [Carleton-etal-2007]. A meta-analysis of 181 studies found moderate associations between IU and symptoms of generalized anxiety, social anxiety, panic, agoraphobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), depression and eating disorders (r = 0.51) [McEvoy-etal-2019]. Treatments, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), reduce IU, and greater reductions go with greater symptom change [Miller-McGuire-2023].
src: Behar-etal-2009 § Abstract, Intolerance of Uncertainty Model

15-transdiagnostic-processes.perfectioni.s: The cognitive behavioral model of clinical perfectionism, how it maintains eating, anxiety and depressive problems, how to draw it with a client, its suicide risk links, and treatment targets.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.perfectioni.when: A client's self-worth rides on meeting demanding standards in work, study, eating, appearance or another valued area, and they keep pursuing them despite clear costs.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.perfectioni.b: Clinical perfectionism is the overdependence of self-evaluation on the determined pursuit and achievement of self-imposed, personally demanding standards in at least one valued area, despite adverse consequences [Shafran-etal-2002]. It is a risk and maintaining factor across eating disorders, anxiety disorders and depression [Egan-etal-2011]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for perfectionism has medium to large effects on perfectionism and medium effects on eating disorder and depressive symptoms [Galloway-etal-2022].
src: Shafran-etal-2002 § Abstract; Definition and maintenance model

15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-cop.s: The client faithfully uses breathing, distraction, reassuring self-talk or a companion during exposures and homework, yet fear and threat beliefs barely change and setbacks follow whenever the strategy is unavailable.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-cop.when: A client completes exposures or practice tasks reliably but belief in the feared outcome stays high, or they say they can only cope if they use a particular strategy.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-cop.b: A coping skill becomes a safety behavior when the client uses it to prevent a feared catastrophe or to escape distress during exposure. Then the non-occurrence of disaster is credited to the skill and the threat belief survives [Salkovskis-etal-1999; Blakey-Abramowitz-2016]. Judge each strategy by its function, and plan for it to be dropped during exposures.
src: Craske-etal-2014 § Removal of safety signals; Expectancy violation

15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-dis.s: Each session the therapist disputes a new worry or ruminative topic; the client feels briefly reassured, a fresh topic appears next week, and time spent worrying does not fall.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-dis.when: Sessions keep turning into evidence-for-and-against debates about whatever the client is currently worrying or ruminating about, without change in how much they do it.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-dis.b: Worry and rumination are processes that attach to whatever content is available. Disputing each topic in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) leaves the process untouched and can turn the therapist into a reassurance source. Formulate and target the process, its beliefs and its functions instead [Ehring-etal-2011; Behar-etal-2009].
src: Ehring-etal-2011 § Introduction, process features of repetitive negative thinking

15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-tel.s: The therapist advises "try not to think about it," thought stopping or distraction as escape; intrusions keep returning, distress rises, and the client concludes their mind is out of control.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-tel.when: A client is troubled by intrusive thoughts, images, urges or memories, and the plan, the client or the therapist relies on blocking them out.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.pitfall-tel.b: Advising a client to push thoughts away is advice to suppress, and suppression is effortful, unreliable and tends to bring the thought back and raise distress [Wegner-etal-1987; Najmi-etal-2009]. Replace it with allowing the thought while engaging in a chosen activity, and test the switch as an experiment.

15-transdiagnostic-processes.rumination.s: How rumination works as a repetitive, abstract, self-focused process, why it deepens and prolongs low mood across disorders, how to map it with a client, and which treatments target it.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.rumination.when: A client spends long periods going over why they feel bad, what is wrong with them or what went wrong, and this thinking leaves them feeling worse rather than solving anything.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.rumination.b: Rumination is repetitive, passive focus on one's distress and its possible causes and consequences, without moving to action [Nolen-Hoeksema-1991]. It deepens low mood, biases thinking, impairs problem solving and erodes social support, and it is linked to depression, anxiety, binge eating, binge drinking and self-harm [Nolen-Hoeksema-etal-2008]. Treat it as a habit with triggers and functions, not as a set of thoughts to dispute.

15-transdiagnostic-processes.safety-beha.s: What safety behaviors are, how they stop threat beliefs being disconfirmed across anxiety and related disorders, how to spot subtle and mental ones, and when gradual fading is reasonable.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.safety-beha.when: A client keeps facing a feared situation but the fear does not shrink, or they rely on actions, objects, people or mental routines to stop a feared outcome.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.safety-beha.b: A safety behavior is an action a person takes in or around a feared situation to prevent, escape or reduce a feared catastrophe or the distress that comes with it [Blakey-Abramowitz-2016]. Because the catastrophe does not happen, the person credits the safety behavior, so the threat belief survives every exposure. In small experiments in social phobia and in panic disorder with agoraphobia, exposure with safety behaviors dropped produced larger falls in belief and anxiety than exposure with them kept [Wells-etal-1995; Salkovskis-etal-1999].

15-transdiagnostic-processes.self-critic.s: Defines self-criticism and shame, distinguishes shame from guilt, summarizes evidence that both cut across depression, anxiety, eating and personality problems, and shows how to assess and respond to them.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.self-critic.when: A client attacks or belittles themselves after setbacks, feels fundamentally flawed or exposed, or says they understand balanced thoughts but cannot feel them.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.self-critic.b: Self-criticism is a habitual, hostile way of relating to oneself after setbacks; shame is the painful sense that the whole self is flawed or exposed. Both are transdiagnostic: self-criticism is linked to depression, eating disorders, social anxiety, personality disorders and psychotic symptoms [Werner-etal-2019], and shame is more strongly linked to depressive symptoms than guilt is (r = 0.43 versus 0.28) [Kim-etal-2011]. Harsh forms resist logical challenge, so cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adds work on a warmer inner stance.
src: Gilbert-2009 § Summary; Three affect regulation systems; Logic is not enough

15-transdiagnostic-processes.thought-sup.s: Explains thought suppression and its rebound effects, what the meta-analyses actually show, why suppression maintains intrusive thoughts and distress across disorders, and what to do instead in session.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.thought-sup.when: A client tries hard to push unwanted thoughts, images, urges or memories out of mind and reports that they keep coming back or feel out of control.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.thought-sup.b: Thought suppression is deliberately trying not to think about something. It tends to backfire: people cannot hold the thought away, and it often returns more often afterward (the rebound effect) [Wegner-etal-1987]. Meta-analysis shows a small to moderate rebound [Abramowitz-etal-2001], and in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) the main harm of suppression is more distress rather than more intrusions [Najmi-etal-2009]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), replace suppression with allowing the thought, or with focused, absorbing activity, and test this with the client.

15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.s: Explains the transdiagnostic view from Harvey and colleagues, the shared processes that maintain problems across diagnoses, and how to use them alongside disorder-specific models in formulation.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.when: A client has several diagnoses, no clear diagnosis, or problems that keep changing form, and the clinician wants to formulate what keeps them going across labels.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.b: Many disorders are kept going by the same small set of processes: avoidance, safety behaviors, repetitive negative thinking (worry and rumination), biased attention, intolerance of uncertainty, perfectionism, self-criticism and difficulty regulating emotion. Harvey and colleagues identified cognitive and behavioral processes, such as selective attention and repetitive negative thinking, that are implicated across four or more disorders [Harvey-etal-2004; Dalgleish-etal-2020]. In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), formulating at the level of process helps when a client has several diagnoses or none, but it adds to the disorder-specific model with trial evidence rather than replacing it.
src: Harvey-etal-2004 § Ch. 1 Introduction; Chs. 2 to 6 on attention, memory, reasoning, thought and behavior
Dalgleish-etal-2020 § Defining transdiagnostic approaches; Transdiagnostic processes; Challenges and a way forward

15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.s: Describes universal, modular and process-targeted transdiagnostic treatments such as the Unified Protocol and rumination-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, when to choose them over single-disorder protocols, and what the trial evidence shows.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.when: A client has several co-occurring emotional disorders, a service must treat mixed presentations with one protocol, or a single maintaining process such as rumination or perfectionism drives several problems.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.transdiagno.b: Transdiagnostic treatments apply the same treatment principles across disorders [Dalgleish-etal-2020]. They outperform control conditions for anxiety and depression [Newby-etal-2015], and the Unified Protocol matched single-disorder cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) protocols for four anxiety disorders with less dropout [Barlow-etal-2017]. Choose one when comorbidity is high or a shared process is the main driver, and keep disorder-specific protocols where they are the established first choice for a single clear problem.
src: Dalgleish-etal-2020 § Transdiagnostic interventions, universal and modular approaches

15-transdiagnostic-processes.worry.s: How worry works as repetitive, verbal, future-focused thinking, the beliefs and avoidance functions that keep it going across disorders, how to map it, and what it implies for treatment.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.worry.when: A client describes chains of "what if" thoughts about things that might go wrong, finds them hard to stop, and the worry spreads across topics or disorders.
15-transdiagnostic-processes.worry.b: Worry is repetitive, mostly verbal thinking about possible future threats, an attempt at mental problem solving on an issue whose outcome is uncertain [Borkovec-etal-1983b; Ehring-etal-2011]. It persists because it feels useful, because it dampens emotional imagery and body arousal, and because people come to fear the worry itself [Borkovec-Inz-1990; Behar-etal-2009]. Target the process and the beliefs about worry, not each worry topic.
src: Ehring-etal-2011 § Introduction, worry and rumination compared

bf.childhood-criticism.def: Growing up with frequent criticism, harsh standards, or approval that depended on performance or behavior.
bf.childhood-criticism.cw: Growing up being criticized a lot, or feeling loved only when you did well.
bf.childhood-criticism.ex: A parent who pointed out what was wrong with every school report.

bf.childhood-emotional-neglect.def: Caregivers persistently failed to notice, comfort or respond to the child's emotional needs, even if physical needs were met.
bf.childhood-emotional-neglect.cw: Growing up without enough comfort, attention or warmth, even if you were fed and clothed.
bf.childhood-emotional-neglect.ex: No one at home asked how the child felt after being bullied.

bf.childhood-physical-neglect.def: Caregivers failed to provide adequate food, clothing, shelter, hygiene, medical care, safety or supervision.
bf.childhood-physical-neglect.cw: Growing up without enough food, care, safety, or someone looking out for you.
bf.childhood-physical-neglect.ex: Regularly going to school hungry and in unwashed clothes.

bf.childhood-emotional-abuse.def: Repeated insults, threats, humiliation, rejection or terrorizing by a caregiver or other adult during childhood.
bf.childhood-emotional-abuse.cw: Being insulted, threatened, humiliated, or made to feel worthless by an adult as a child.
bf.childhood-emotional-abuse.ex: A parent who regularly said they wished the child had never been born.

bf.childhood-physical-abuse.def: Being deliberately hit, kicked or otherwise physically hurt by a caregiver or other adult during childhood.
bf.childhood-physical-abuse.cw: Being hit or physically hurt by an adult when you were a child.
bf.childhood-physical-abuse.ex: Being beaten with a belt for minor misbehavior.

bf.childhood-sexual-abuse.def: Any sexual contact with, or sexual exploitation of, a child by an adult or by a significantly older or more powerful young person.
bf.childhood-sexual-abuse.cw: Being touched or used sexually as a child by someone older or more powerful.
bf.childhood-sexual-abuse.ex: Recorded briefly, without detail: sexual abuse by a relative between ages 8 and 11.

bf.childhood-domestic-violence-exposure.def: Seeing or hearing violence or threats between caregivers or other household members during childhood.
bf.childhood-domestic-violence-exposure.cw: Seeing or hearing adults at home hurt or threaten each other when you were growing up.
bf.childhood-domestic-violence-exposure.ex: Hiding upstairs while a father hit the child's mother.

bf.bullying.def: Repeated harassment, exclusion, ridicule or aggression by peers in childhood or adolescence, in person or online.
bf.bullying.cw: Being picked on, teased, left out, or hurt by other kids, in person or online.
bf.bullying.ex: Mocked daily about weight throughout middle school.

bf.early-loss-or-separation.def: Death of, or prolonged separation from, a parent or main caregiver in childhood, including parental divorce or placement in care.
bf.early-loss-or-separation.cw: Losing a parent or main caregiver as a child, through death, divorce, or being placed elsewhere.
bf.early-loss-or-separation.ex: Mother died when the client was nine.

bf.overprotective-parenting.def: Caregivers limited independence, solved problems for the child, and discouraged age-appropriate risk-taking and independent coping.
bf.overprotective-parenting.cw: Growing up with parents who did things for you and stopped you trying things yourself.
bf.overprotective-parenting.ex: Not allowed to take the bus alone until age 16.

bf.unstable-home.def: Childhood marked by unpredictability, such as frequent moves, changing caregivers, household chaos, or a household member imprisoned.
bf.unstable-home.cw: A childhood where home life kept changing or felt unpredictable and unsafe.
bf.unstable-home.ex: Changed schools six times before age twelve.

bf.caregiver-mental-illness-or-substance.def: Growing up with a caregiver who had serious mental health problems, suicidal behavior, or alcohol or drug problems.
