em.longing.def: Aching wish for an absent person, place or time that is not lost for good, as in separation or homesickness.
em.longing.cw: Missing someone or somewhere so much it aches.
em.longing.ex: Holidays far from my family back home. Longing 70.

em.jealous.def: Fear and anger about losing a valued relationship, or a person's attention, to a rival; involves three people.
em.jealous.cw: Afraid someone will take away a person who matters to me.
em.jealous.ex: My partner laughs at a coworker's message: "They'd rather be with them." Jealous 80.

em.envious.def: Painful wish for another person's advantage, success or possession, often with resentment or inferiority; involves two people.
em.envious.cw: Wanting what someone else has, and feeling worse because they have it.
em.envious.ex: Scrolling past a friend's promotion announcement. Envious 60.

em.hopeless.def: Expectation that the future is bleak and nothing will improve; a key suicide risk marker that always prompts risk assessment.
em.hopeless.cw: Like nothing will ever get better.
em.hopeless.ex: "There's no point trying, it'll always be like this." Hopeless 90.

em.helpless.def: Feeling that one's actions cannot influence important outcomes.
em.helpless.cw: Powerless, like nothing I do makes a difference.
em.helpless.ex: Watching my father's illness get worse. Helpless 85.

em.defeated.def: Sense of having lost a struggle for valued goals, status or self-worth, with a pull to give up.
em.defeated.cw: Beaten down, like I've lost and there's no fight left.
em.defeated.ex: Rejected for the tenth job in a row. Defeated 80.

em.trapped.def: Strong wish to escape a painful situation or inner state combined with sensing no way out; central to suicide risk models.
em.trapped.cw: Stuck in how things are, with no way out.
em.trapped.ex: "I can't leave this marriage and I can't stand staying." Trapped 90.

em.discouraged.def: Loss of confidence and motivation after setbacks; milder and more situation-bound than hopelessness.
em.discouraged.cw: Losing heart after things keep going wrong.
em.discouraged.ex: Third week of therapy and still low: "This isn't working." Discouraged 55.

em.numb.def: Reduced capacity to feel emotions, especially positive or loving ones; common after trauma and in depression.
em.numb.cw: Can't feel much of anything, as if my feelings are switched off.
em.numb.ex: At my friend's wedding I felt nothing at all. Numb 80.

em.empty.def: Chronic sense of inner hollowness or lack of substance, distinct from sadness; a feature of borderline personality disorder and depression.
em.empty.cw: Hollow inside, like something important is missing.
em.empty.ex: Home alone after work, scrolling with no sense of who I am. Empty 75.

em.anhedonic.def: Markedly reduced interest in, or pleasure from, activities once enjoyed; a core symptom of depression.
em.anhedonic.cw: Nothing feels enjoyable or interesting anymore.
em.anhedonic.ex: I went fishing, which I used to love, and felt nothing. Enjoyment 0.

em.bored.def: Aversive state of wanting, but being unable, to engage attention in satisfying activity.
em.bored.cw: Restless and fed up because nothing holds my attention.
em.bored.ex: A long empty Sunday with nothing planned: "A drink would help." Bored 70.

em.happy.def: Pleasant feeling of joy, gladness or satisfaction when things go well or valued needs are met.
em.happy.ex: My daughter called with good news. Happy 70.

em.enjoyment.def: Pleasure taken in an activity itself; recorded as the pleasure rating in activity monitoring and scheduling.
em.enjoyment.cw: How much I liked doing something.
em.enjoyment.ex: Walk in the park with the dog: pleasure rated high, even though I was tired.

em.accomplished.def: Satisfaction from completing a task or meeting a challenge, judged against current ability; recorded as the achievement or mastery rating.
em.accomplished.cw: Feeling I got something done or handled something hard.
em.accomplished.ex: On a low day I paid one overdue bill: achievement rated high.

em.proud.def: Pleasant self-evaluation after an achievement or after acting in line with one's values.
em.proud.cw: Pleased with myself for something I did.
em.proud.ex: I spoke up in the meeting even though I was nervous. Proud 65.

em.calm.def: Low-arousal state of physical and mental ease; the target state of relaxation and arousal-reduction techniques.
em.calm.cw: Relaxed and settled in body and mind.
em.calm.ex: After ten minutes of slow breathing on the porch. Calm 60.

em.soothed.def: Felt safeness and warmth from care or self-compassion, linked to the soothing affect system in compassion-focused therapy.
em.soothed.cw: Comforted and safe, like someone, or I, am looking after me.
em.soothed.ex: Putting a hand on my chest and speaking kindly to myself after a mistake. Soothed 50.

em.hopeful.def: Expectation that valued goals are reachable and things can improve, with a sense of pathways to get there; protective against despair.
em.hopeful.cw: Things could get better, and I can help make that happen.
em.hopeful.ex: After making a plan with my therapist: "This might actually help." Hopeful 55.

em.confident.def: Expectation that one can carry out a task or handle a situation successfully (self-efficacy).
em.confident.cw: Sure that I can handle this.
em.confident.ex: Before my third practice presentation. Confident 70.

em.interested.def: Engaged curiosity that draws a person toward exploring and learning; the opposite pull to boredom and withdrawal.
em.interested.cw: Curious and drawn in by something.
em.interested.ex: Lost track of time reading about bird migration. Interested 70.

em.connected.def: Warmth and closeness with others, including love and a sense of belonging; the counterpart of loneliness.
em.connected.cw: Close to people, cared about and belonging.
em.connected.ex: Cooking dinner with my sister and laughing. Connected 80.

em.relieved.def: Drop in distress when a feared outcome passes or is escaped; relief after avoidance or a safety behavior can keep fear going.
em.relieved.cw: The weight lifting when something I feared is over or avoided.
em.relieved.ex: I cancelled the party at the last minute. Relieved 80, and the next invite felt even harder.

em.elated.def: Intense, expansive happiness; when persistent, out of proportion or with reduced need for sleep, assess for hypomania or mania.
em.elated.cw: Extremely high or on top of the world, more than usual for me.
em.elated.ex: Three nights of little sleep, full of plans: "I can do anything." Elated 95.

em.yearning.def: Intense, persistent longing for a person who has died; a core symptom of prolonged grief when it stays daily and impairing.
em.yearning.cw: Aching to have the person who died back, again and again.
em.yearning.ex: Hearing his favorite song in a shop. Yearning 85.

ib.must-be-perfect.def: Rule demanding flawless performance and no mistakes, with self-evaluation hinging on meeting rigid, very high standards.
ib.must-be-perfect.cw: I have to do everything perfectly; mistakes aren't okay.
ib.must-be-perfect.ex: "I must never hand in work with a single error."

ib.must-be-liked.def: Rule that one must win everyone's approval and avoid any disapproval, so self-esteem rests on others' reactions.
ib.must-be-liked.cw: I need everyone to like me; I can't bear anyone being displeased with me.
ib.must-be-liked.ex: "If even one person is annoyed with me, I've failed."

ib.must-put-others-first.def: Rule that others' needs must always come before one's own, so saying no or self-care feels selfish or guilt-inducing.
ib.must-put-others-first.cw: I should always put other people first, whatever it costs me.
ib.must-put-others-first.ex: "I can't rest until everyone else is taken care of."

ib.must-stay-in-control.def: Rule that one must keep tight control of oneself, others or events, because losing control would be intolerable or dangerous.
ib.must-stay-in-control.cw: I have to stay in control at all times.
ib.must-stay-in-control.ex: "If I'm not on top of everything, it will all fall apart."

ib.must-cope-alone.def: Rule that one should solve problems without help, because needing or asking for help would expose weakness or incompetence.
ib.must-cope-alone.cw: I should be able to sort this out myself; asking for help means I'm weak.
ib.must-cope-alone.ex: "I should be able to do this on my own."

ib.others-must-be-fair.def: Rule that other people must behave fairly or as expected, so breaches are judged intolerable and provoke anger.
ib.others-must-be-fair.cw: People should treat me fairly, and it's unacceptable when they don't.
ib.others-must-be-fair.ex: "He should have called. It's completely out of line."

ib.self-criticism-motivates.def: Assumption that harsh self-criticism is needed to improve or avoid mistakes, and that self-kindness would lead to laziness or failure.
ib.self-criticism-motivates.cw: If I go easy on myself, I'll get lazy and fail.
ib.self-criticism-motivates.ex: "If I stop beating myself up, I'll never get anything done."

ib.worth-depends-on-achievement.def: Assumption that personal worth depends on achievement, so any failure or poor performance shows one is worthless or a failure.
ib.worth-depends-on-achievement.cw: If I don't succeed, I'm worthless.
ib.worth-depends-on-achievement.ex: "If I don't get this promotion, it proves I'm nothing."

ib.closeness-leads-to-rejection.def: Assumption that if others get close or see one's true self, they will discover one's flaws and reject one.
ib.closeness-leads-to-rejection.cw: If people really got to know me, they'd leave.
ib.closeness-leads-to-rejection.ex: "If I open up to her, she'll see what I'm really like and go."

ib.assertion-leads-to-rejection.def: Assumption that expressing needs, opinions or anger, or refusing requests, will lead to conflict, retaliation or abandonment.
ib.assertion-leads-to-rejection.cw: If I say no or stand up for myself, people will get angry or leave.
ib.assertion-leads-to-rejection.ex: "If I tell my partner I'm upset, he'll walk out."

ib.trying-leads-to-failure.def: Assumption that attempting difficult things will expose inadequacy and end in failure, while avoiding them keeps one safe.
ib.trying-leads-to-failure.cw: If I try anything hard, I'll just fail, so it's safer not to.
ib.trying-leads-to-failure.ex: "If I apply for that job, I'll only prove how useless I am."

ib.high-social-standards.def: Excessively high standards for social performance, such as always appearing confident, interesting and free of visible anxiety.
ib.high-social-standards.cw: I must always come across as confident and never look nervous.
ib.high-social-standards.ex: "I must always look cool and calm."

ib.visible-anxiety-brings-rejection.def: Conditional belief that any visible sign of anxiety or social slip will lead others to judge, reject or humiliate one.
ib.visible-anxiety-brings-rejection.cw: If anyone notices I'm nervous, they'll think I'm weird or weak.
ib.visible-anxiety-brings-rejection.ex: "If my hands shake, everyone will think I'm pathetic."

ib.worry-is-helpful.g: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
ib.worry-is-helpful.def: Positive metacognitive belief that worrying helps one prepare, solve problems or prevent bad outcomes, motivating its use as a coping strategy.
ib.worry-is-helpful.cw: Worrying helps me be ready for whatever might go wrong.
ib.worry-is-helpful.ex: "If I worry about it now, I won't be caught off guard."

ib.rumination-is-helpful.g: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
ib.rumination-is-helpful.def: Positive metacognitive belief that dwelling on problems, feelings and the causes of low mood will produce insight or solutions.
ib.rumination-is-helpful.cw: If I keep thinking about why I feel bad, I'll figure it out.
ib.rumination-is-helpful.ex: "I need to work out why I'm like this before I can move on."

ib.worry-is-uncontrollable.g: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
ib.worry-is-uncontrollable.def: Negative metacognitive belief that worrying, once started, cannot be stopped or controlled.
ib.worry-is-uncontrollable.cw: Once I start worrying, I can't stop.
ib.worry-is-uncontrollable.ex: "My mind just runs away with me and I can't switch it off."

ib.worry-is-dangerous.g: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
ib.worry-is-dangerous.def: Negative metacognitive belief that worrying itself is harmful, for example causing madness, illness or a breakdown.
ib.worry-is-dangerous.cw: All this worrying is going to make me ill or drive me crazy.
ib.worry-is-dangerous.ex: "If I keep worrying like this, I'll have a breakdown."

ib.must-control-thoughts.g: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
ib.must-control-thoughts.def: Belief that one must control or suppress unwanted thoughts, and that failing to do so is dangerous, abnormal or blameworthy.
ib.must-control-thoughts.cw: I should be able to control my thoughts, and it's bad if I can't.
ib.must-control-thoughts.ex: "If I can't push this thought away, something must be wrong."

ib.inflated-responsibility.def: Belief that one has pivotal power and duty to prevent harm, so failing to prevent it equals causing it.
ib.inflated-responsibility.cw: If I could prevent something bad and don't, it's my fault.
ib.inflated-responsibility.ex: "If I don't check the stove again and there's a fire, I'll have killed them."

ib.thought-action-fusion-likelihood.def: Belief that thinking about an unwanted event makes it more likely to happen, to oneself or to others.
ib.thought-action-fusion-likelihood.cw: If I think about something bad happening, it's more likely to happen.
ib.thought-action-fusion-likelihood.ex: "If I picture Mom in a car crash, it could make it happen."

ib.thought-action-fusion-moral.def: Belief that having an unacceptable thought is morally equivalent to carrying out the act.
ib.thought-action-fusion-moral.cw: Having a terrible thought is as bad as actually doing it.
ib.thought-action-fusion-moral.ex: "Thinking about hurting him makes me as bad as someone who would."

ib.thoughts-reveal-true-self.def: Belief that unwanted intrusive thoughts are significant, revealing one's true character or hidden wishes, such as being secretly dangerous.
ib.thoughts-reveal-true-self.cw: If I have this thought, it must mean I'm secretly a bad person.
ib.thoughts-reveal-true-self.ex: "Why would I think that unless part of me wants it?"

ib.need-for-certainty.def: Rule that one must be completely certain, and things must be exactly right, before stopping, deciding or feeling safe.
ib.need-for-certainty.cw: I have to be 100 percent sure before I can stop or move on.
ib.need-for-certainty.ex: "I can't leave until I'm totally sure the door is locked."

ib.emotions-unacceptable.def: Belief that experiencing or showing negative emotions is unacceptable, weak or shameful, and must be hidden or controlled.
ib.emotions-unacceptable.cw: Showing my feelings is a sign of weakness.
ib.emotions-unacceptable.ex: "I can't let anyone see me upset. They'd think less of me."

ib.emotions-overwhelming.def: Belief that strong emotions are uncontrollable, will last indefinitely or will overwhelm one if allowed.
ib.emotions-overwhelming.cw: If I start crying, I'll never stop.
ib.emotions-overwhelming.ex: "If I let myself feel the grief, I'll fall apart completely."

ib.anxiety-sensations-dangerous.g: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
ib.anxiety-sensations-dangerous.def: Belief that the physical, mental or visible signs of anxiety have harmful consequences, such as heart attack, insanity or humiliation.
ib.anxiety-sensations-dangerous.cw: When my heart races, something terrible could happen to me.
ib.anxiety-sensations-dangerous.ex: "If I get dizzy, I'll pass out."

ib.symptoms-mean-serious-illness.g: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
ib.symptoms-mean-serious-illness.def: Assumption that unexplained bodily sensations or changes are usually signs of serious illness that must not be missed.
ib.symptoms-mean-serious-illness.cw: If I feel something odd in my body, it's probably something serious.
ib.symptoms-mean-serious-illness.ex: "This headache isn't normal. It must be a tumor."

ib.health-worry-protects.g: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
ib.health-worry-protects.def: Belief that constant health vigilance protects against illness, or that assuming one is healthy will tempt fate.
ib.health-worry-protects.cw: If I stop watching my health or assume I'm fine, something bad will happen.
ib.health-worry-protects.ex: "The moment I relax about my health, that's when they'll find something."

ib.need-eight-hours.def: Unrealistic sleep expectation that one must get a fixed amount, often eight hours, every night to function.
ib.need-eight-hours.cw: I need a full eight hours every night or I can't function.
ib.need-eight-hours.ex: "I only got six hours, so today is a write-off."

ib.poor-sleep-ruins-functioning.def: Belief that poor sleep will seriously impair next-day functioning, mood or health.
ib.poor-sleep-ruins-functioning.cw: If I don't sleep well tonight, tomorrow will be a disaster.
ib.poor-sleep-ruins-functioning.ex: "If I don't fall asleep soon, I'll mess up the presentation."

ib.sleep-out-of-control.def: Worry and helplessness about insomnia: belief that sleep is unpredictable, beyond one's control or permanently damaged.
ib.sleep-out-of-control.cw: I've lost the ability to sleep, and there's nothing I can do.

ib.need-sleep-medication.def: Belief that sleep medication is the only way to sleep or cope, and that sleeping without it is impossible.
ib.need-sleep-medication.cw: Without a sleeping pill, I won't sleep at all.
ib.need-sleep-medication.ex: "I can't risk a night without my tablet."

ib.worth-judged-by-shape-weight.g: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
ib.worth-judged-by-shape-weight.def: Belief that one's worth as a person depends largely or exclusively on shape, weight and controlling them, the core eating disorder belief.
ib.worth-judged-by-shape-weight.cw: How I feel about myself depends on my weight and shape.
ib.worth-judged-by-shape-weight.ex: "I gained a pound, so I'm disgusting and worthless."

ib.strict-dietary-rules.g: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
ib.strict-dietary-rules.def: Rigid rules about when, what and how much to eat, where any break is judged a failure.
ib.strict-dietary-rules.cw: I must stick to my food rules, like never eating after six.
ib.strict-dietary-rules.ex: "I must stay under 1,000 calories every day."

ib.eating-means-losing-control.g: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
ib.eating-means-losing-control.def: Assumption that eating certain foods or amounts will lead to uncontrolled eating or rapid weight gain.
ib.eating-means-losing-control.cw: If I eat one cookie, I won't be able to stop.
ib.eating-means-losing-control.ex: "If I have one slice of pizza, I'll binge on the whole thing."

ib.substance-anticipatory.def: Anticipatory belief that using a substance, or an addictive behavior, will bring pleasure, energy, confidence or social ease.
ib.substance-anticipatory.cw: A few drinks will make the party fun and help me relax.
ib.substance-anticipatory.ex: "I'm much funnier after a couple of drinks."

ib.substance-relief.def: Relief-oriented belief that using is needed to relieve craving, withdrawal, pain or distress, and that one cannot cope without it.
ib.substance-relief.cw: I can't handle this feeling without using.
ib.substance-relief.ex: "I'll never get through tonight without a drink."

ib.substance-permissive.def: Permission-giving belief that justifies using despite risks or goals, such as deserving it or one time not mattering.
ib.substance-permissive.cw: I deserve it, and just one won't hurt.
ib.substance-permissive.ex: "After the week I've had, I've earned a drink."

ib.high-mood-is-best.g: Beliefs about mood states and voices
ib.high-mood-is-best.def: Extreme positive appraisal of activated states: belief that elevated mood or energy makes one more creative, productive or successful.
ib.high-mood-is-best.cw: When my mood is up, I'm at my best and get so much done.
ib.high-mood-is-best.ex: "I don't need sleep when I'm like this. I'm finally achieving things."

ib.voices-powerful.g: Beliefs about mood states and voices
ib.voices-powerful.def: Belief that hallucinated voices are omnipotent and all-knowing, and may be malevolent, so they must be obeyed or resisted.
ib.voices-powerful.cw: The voices are powerful and know everything; I have to do what they say.
ib.voices-powerful.ex: "If I don't do what the voice says, it will punish my family."

ib.pain-means-harm.def: The belief that pain signals bodily damage or reinjury, so any activity that hurts must be stopped or avoided.
ib.pain-means-harm.cw: If it hurts, I'm damaging myself, so I must stop.
ib.pain-means-harm.ex: "If I bend and it hurts, I'll make the disc worse."

ib.grief-reactions-dangerous.def: Catastrophic interpretations of one's own grief reactions as signs of going mad or losing control, which drive avoidance of the loss.
ib.grief-reactions-dangerous.cw: If I really let myself feel this, I'll fall apart or lose my mind.
ib.grief-reactions-dangerous.ex: "If I look at his photos I'll break down and never stop crying."

iv.identifying-automatic-thoughts.def: Helping the client notice and record the thoughts and images present when their emotion shifts, then select the hot thought to work on.
iv.identifying-automatic-thoughts.cw: Noticing what goes through your mind when your mood suddenly changes.
iv.identifying-automatic-thoughts.ex: "What was going through your mind just then, when you went quiet?"

iv.cognitive-restructuring.def: Collaboratively examining an automatic thought's accuracy and usefulness through guided questions, then building a more balanced, believable alternative response.
iv.cognitive-restructuring.cw: Checking whether a thought fits the facts and finding a fairer way to see things.
iv.cognitive-restructuring.ex: "What is the evidence for this thought? Is there another way of looking at it?"

iv.thought-record.def: Structured worksheet linking situation, moods, automatic thoughts, evidence for and against the hot thought, and a balanced alternative, with ratings before and after.
iv.thought-record.cw: A worksheet for catching an upsetting thought, weighing it up and finding a more balanced view.
iv.thought-record.ex: After a friend cancels plans, the client completes a seven-column record and sadness falls from 80 to 40.

iv.decatastrophizing.def: Examining a feared outcome by estimating its realistic likelihood, the worst, best and most likely outcomes, and how the client would cope.
iv.decatastrophizing.cw: Thinking through what would really happen if the worst came true, and how you would cope.
iv.decatastrophizing.ex: "If you did fail the exam, what would you do next, and how would you get through it?"

iv.double-standard-technique.def: Asking how the client would view or advise a friend with the same thought or situation, then applying that kinder standard to themselves.
iv.double-standard-technique.cw: Treating yourself the way you would treat a good friend in the same spot.
iv.double-standard-technique.ex: "If your best friend made this mistake, would you tell her she is useless?"

iv.responsibility-pie-chart.def: Dividing a pie chart among all contributing factors to an event, rating own share last, to correct inflated personal responsibility or blame.
iv.responsibility-pie-chart.cw: Drawing a pie to see how much of what happened was really down to you.
iv.responsibility-pie-chart.ex: The client allots slices to weather, the other driver and roadworks; their own share drops from 100% to 20%.

iv.advantages-disadvantages-analysis.def: Listing and weighing the short- and long-term advantages and disadvantages of holding a belief, keeping a rule, or making a change.
iv.advantages-disadvantages-analysis.cw: Weighing up the pros and cons of a belief, a rule you live by, or a habit.
iv.advantages-disadvantages-analysis.ex: Pros and cons of the rule "I must never say no to anyone".

iv.identifying-cognitive-distortions.def: Teaching the client to recognize recurring biased thinking patterns, such as catastrophizing or mind reading, and label them in their own thoughts.
iv.identifying-cognitive-distortions.cw: Learning to spot common thinking traps so you can step back from them.
iv.identifying-cognitive-distortions.ex: "That sounds like mind reading again: you are guessing what he thinks."

iv.downward-arrow.def: Repeatedly asking what a thought would mean if it were true, to move from an automatic thought to underlying assumptions and core beliefs.
iv.downward-arrow.cw: Asking "and if that were true, what would it mean?" to find the deeper worry.
iv.downward-arrow.ex: "I'll make a mistake" leads to "They'll see I'm incompetent" leads to "I'm a failure."

iv.modifying-rules-and-assumptions.def: Identifying conditional assumptions and rigid rules, examining their costs and origins, testing them with behavioral experiments, and building more flexible versions.
iv.modifying-rules-and-assumptions.cw: Finding the unwritten rules you live by and making them more flexible and helpful.
iv.modifying-rules-and-assumptions.ex: "If I'm not perfect, I'll be rejected" is tested and revised to "Good enough is usually accepted."

iv.core-belief-work.def: Identifying an unhelpful core belief, then constructing and strengthening an alternative belief over time with evidence logs, historical review, continua and experiential methods.
iv.core-belief-work.cw: Gradually building a kinder, more accurate view of yourself, other people or the world.
iv.core-belief-work.ex: Over several months the client strengthens "I am acceptable as I am" alongside the old belief "I am defective."

iv.positive-data-log.def: Daily written record of everyday experiences consistent with a new, more adaptive core belief, countering biased attention to belief-confirming information.
iv.positive-data-log.cw: Writing down, each day, small things that fit a new, more helpful view of yourself.
iv.positive-data-log.ex: New belief "I am likeable": "Neighbor stopped to chat; colleague thanked me for my help."

iv.continuum-technique.def: Rating self or others on a 0 to 100 scale with explicitly defined anchors, to replace all-or-nothing judgments with graded ones.
iv.continuum-technique.cw: Placing yourself on a scale instead of seeing yourself as all good or all bad.
iv.continuum-technique.ex: The client first rates self 0 on "lovable"; after defining the anchors, places self at 65.

iv.imagery-rescripting.def: Recalling a distressing memory or intrusive image in imagination, then changing its course to meet unmet needs and update its meaning.
iv.imagery-rescripting.cw: Revisiting a painful memory in your mind's eye and changing how it plays out.
iv.imagery-rescripting.ex: The client imagines their adult self stepping into a childhood scene to protect and comfort the younger self.

iv.worry-postponement.def: Noticing worry, deferring it to a set daily worry period, then using that period briefly, to weaken worry and test beliefs about uncontrollability.
iv.worry-postponement.cw: Putting worries aside until a set worry time later in the day.
iv.worry-postponement.ex: The client notes worries on a card and saves them for 15 minutes at 6 pm; many no longer seem urgent.

iv.rumination-focused-techniques.def: Functional analysis of rumination, then shifting from abstract, evaluative thinking to concrete, specific processing, absorption in experience, and self-compassion.
iv.rumination-focused-techniques.cw: Noticing when you are going round in circles and switching to more specific, useful thinking.
iv.rumination-focused-techniques.ex: "How did this happen, and what is one step I can take?" replaces "Why does this always happen to me?"

iv.detached-mindfulness.def: Metacognitive therapy stance of noticing thoughts as passing mental events without engaging, analyzing, suppressing or acting on them.
iv.detached-mindfulness.cw: Noticing a thought and letting it be, without arguing with it or following it.
iv.detached-mindfulness.ex: The client notices "What if I get ill?" and watches it like a cloud passing, without starting to worry.

iv.behavioral-activation.def: Structured approach that increases contact with rewarding, valued activity and targets avoidance, using activity monitoring, scheduling and functional analysis of behavior.
iv.behavioral-activation.cw: Gradually doing more of what matters to you, even before you feel like it.
iv.behavioral-activation.ex: A withdrawn client schedules a short walk and a call to a friend on three days and rates mood afterward.

iv.activity-monitoring.def: Hour-by-hour record of what the client does, with ratings of mood, mastery and pleasure, to reveal links between activity and mood.
iv.activity-monitoring.cw: Keeping a simple diary of what you do each hour and how you feel.
iv.activity-monitoring.ex: The diary shows mood is lowest on afternoons spent in bed and higher after seeing people.

iv.activity-scheduling.def: Planning specific valued, pleasurable or mastery activities at set times in advance, then reviewing what happened and how mood changed.
iv.activity-scheduling.cw: Planning specific activities into your week, then checking how they went.
iv.activity-scheduling.ex: "Tuesday 10 am: 20-minute walk to the park; Thursday 7 pm: call my sister."

iv.graded-task-assignment.def: Breaking an overwhelming task or goal into small, sequential steps that are attempted in order, starting with one the client is likely to complete.
iv.graded-task-assignment.cw: Breaking a big task into small steps and taking them one at a time.
iv.graded-task-assignment.ex: "Sort the mail" becomes: open envelopes for 10 minutes, then pay the one urgent bill.

iv.behavioral-experiment.def: Planned activity that tests a specific prediction or belief through direct experience, with a written prediction, belief rating, outcome and conclusion.
iv.behavioral-experiment.cw: A planned real-life test of a worrying prediction, to see what actually happens.
iv.behavioral-experiment.ex: Prediction "If I speak up in the meeting, people will laugh" (belief 80%); outcome: one person agreed.

iv.problem-solving-therapy.def: Structured steps: define the problem, generate options, weigh pros and cons, choose, plan, act and review, alongside work on negative problem orientation.
iv.problem-solving-therapy.cw: A step-by-step way to tackle a real problem: list options, pick one, try it, review.
iv.problem-solving-therapy.ex: The client lists five ways to handle rent arrears, chooses to call the landlord, and plans what to say.

iv.relaxation-training.def: Teaching skills such as progressive muscle relaxation, slow breathing or applied (cue-controlled) relaxation to lower physiological arousal and use as a coping skill.
iv.relaxation-training.cw: Learning ways to relax your muscles and breathing so your body can settle.
iv.relaxation-training.ex: After practicing daily, the client uses cue-controlled relaxation at the first sign of tension at work.

iv.safety-behavior-reduction.def: Identifying safety behaviors and reassurance seeking, then dropping or fading them, often within experiments, so feared outcomes can be disconfirmed.
iv.safety-behavior-reduction.cw: Gradually letting go of the things you do to feel safe, to learn you are OK without them.
iv.safety-behavior-reduction.ex: The client gives a short talk without gripping notes or avoiding eye contact and finds it goes better.

iv.self-monitoring.def: Client records a target behavior, symptom, thought or urge as it happens, with context, to establish a baseline, reveal patterns and track change.
iv.self-monitoring.cw: Keeping track of something as it happens, so we can spot patterns together.
iv.self-monitoring.ex: The client logs each binge urge with time, place, mood and what happened next.

iv.interpersonal-effectiveness-training.def: Teaching and rehearsing clear, respectful requests, refusals and opinions through instruction, modeling, role play and feedback, balancing goals, relationship and self-respect.
iv.interpersonal-effectiveness-training.cw: Practicing asking for what you need or saying no, clearly and respectfully.
iv.interpersonal-effectiveness-training.ex: The client role-plays asking a manager for a deadline extension, then tries it at work.

iv.chain-analysis.def: Detailed step-by-step review of vulnerabilities, prompting event, links and consequences of a specific problem behavior, to identify points where change is possible.
iv.chain-analysis.cw: Going through, step by step, what led up to a problem behavior and what followed.
iv.chain-analysis.ex: Poor sleep, then an argument, then the thought "I can't stand this", then self-harm urge, then relief.

iv.exposure-therapy.def: Repeated, planned contact with feared but objectively safe stimuli, without avoidance or safety behaviors, so new non-threat learning can occur.
iv.exposure-therapy.cw: Facing what you fear, step by step and on purpose, so you learn it is safer than it feels.
iv.exposure-therapy.ex: A client afraid of dogs moves from watching videos to standing near a calm dog on a leash.

iv.exposure-hierarchy.def: Collaboratively listed feared situations with predicted distress ratings, used to plan the order, variety and progression of exposure tasks.
iv.exposure-hierarchy.cw: A ladder of feared situations, from easier to harder, that we use to plan practice.
iv.exposure-hierarchy.ex: Rungs run from riding one bus stop with a friend (SUDS 30) to a rush-hour train alone (SUDS 90).

iv.in-vivo-exposure.def: Exposure to real feared or avoided situations, objects or activities, in session or in daily life.
iv.in-vivo-exposure.cw: Practicing facing feared situations in real life.
iv.in-vivo-exposure.ex: The client with agoraphobia walks alone to the supermarket and stays until the planned task is done.

iv.imaginal-exposure.def: Repeatedly and vividly imagining or narrating a feared scenario or traumatic memory, usually in the present tense, without avoidance, to process it.
iv.imaginal-exposure.cw: Picturing or describing a feared scene or memory in detail until it becomes less overwhelming.
iv.imaginal-exposure.ex: A client with obsessions writes and rereads a script of the feared outcome until its impact falls.

iv.interoceptive-exposure.def: Deliberately inducing feared bodily sensations, such as dizziness, breathlessness or a racing heart, through exercises, so the client learns they are safe.
iv.interoceptive-exposure.cw: Bringing on scary body feelings on purpose, to learn they are uncomfortable but not dangerous.
iv.interoceptive-exposure.ex: The client spins in a chair for 60 seconds to bring on dizziness and rates fear before and after.

iv.inhibitory-learning-strategies.def: Designing exposure to maximize violation of specific feared predictions, vary stimuli and contexts, combine cues, remove safety signals and label affect.
iv.inhibitory-learning-strategies.cw: Setting up practice to test exactly what you fear will happen, in many different situations.
iv.inhibitory-learning-strategies.ex: "What do you predict will happen, and what would tell us the prediction was wrong?"

iv.emotion-awareness-training.def: Teaching the client to identify, label and rate emotions and their components (thoughts, sensations, urges) with present-focused, nonjudgmental awareness.
iv.emotion-awareness-training.cw: Learning to notice, name and rate what you are feeling.
iv.emotion-awareness-training.ex: The client distinguishes "anxious 70" from "ashamed 50" in the same situation.

iv.mindfulness-based-cognitive-therapy.def: Eight-week group program of guided mindfulness practices with cognitive elements, helping people disengage from ruminative patterns to prevent depressive relapse.
iv.mindfulness-based-cognitive-therapy.cw: A course of mindfulness practice that helps you step out of patterns that bring depression back.
iv.mindfulness-based-cognitive-therapy.ex: A client in remission uses the three-minute breathing space when low mood begins to pull into rumination.

iv.compassionate-mind-training.def: Compassion-focused exercises, such as soothing rhythm breathing, compassionate self imagery and compassionate letters, building capacity to meet distress and self-criticism with warmth.
iv.compassionate-mind-training.cw: Practicing a warm, supportive inner voice to use when you are struggling or self-critical.
iv.compassionate-mind-training.ex: The client writes a letter to themselves about a setback from the viewpoint of a wise, kind friend.

iv.distress-tolerance-skills.def: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) crisis survival skills, such as TIPP, distraction, self-soothing and pros and cons, for getting through intense urges without worsening things.
iv.distress-tolerance-skills.cw: Skills to get through a crisis moment without making it worse.
iv.distress-tolerance-skills.ex: With a strong urge to self-harm, the client uses cold water on the face and paced breathing, then calls a friend.

iv.emotion-regulation-skills.def: DBT skills for understanding emotions, checking the facts, opposite action, problem solving, and reducing vulnerability through sleep, eating, exercise and positive events.
iv.emotion-regulation-skills.cw: Learning skills to understand your emotions and change the ones that are not helping you.
iv.emotion-regulation-skills.ex: Shame urges hiding; the client checks the facts, then acts opposite by joining the conversation.

iv.socialization-to-cbt.def: Orienting the client to the cognitive model, the structured collaborative format, homework and their active role, using examples from their own life.
iv.socialization-to-cbt.cw: Explaining how CBT works and what we will do together, using your own examples.
iv.socialization-to-cbt.ex: "When she didn't reply, you thought 'she's angry with me' and felt anxious. Can you see the link?"

iv.sharing-the-formulation.def: Co-constructing and presenting the case formulation with the client, inviting correction, to explain the problem and guide choice of interventions.
iv.sharing-the-formulation.cw: Building a picture together of what keeps the problem going, so we can choose what to change.
iv.sharing-the-formulation.ex: Therapist and client draw the vicious cycle on paper and the client adds a missing safety behavior.

iv.action-plan.def: Collaboratively designed between-session task that applies session learning, with a clear rationale, specific plan, anticipated obstacles and a review next session.
iv.action-plan.cw: A small task to try between sessions, so the changes carry into your week.
iv.action-plan.ex: "Complete one thought record when you feel a strong mood shift; we'll review it next week."

iv.routine-outcome-monitoring.def: Regularly administering standardized measures and reviewing scores and trends with the client to detect non-response and guide treatment decisions.
iv.routine-outcome-monitoring.cw: Filling in short questionnaires regularly and looking at the results together to check progress.
iv.routine-outcome-monitoring.ex: PHQ-9 scores are graphed weekly; a plateau at session 6 prompts a review of the plan.

iv.motivational-interviewing.def: Collaborative, person-centered method for strengthening a person's own motivation and commitment to change by evoking and exploring their reasons.
iv.motivational-interviewing.cw: Talking through your own reasons for and against change, at your own pace.
iv.motivational-interviewing.ex: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is cutting down? Why a 6 and not a 3?"

iv.relapse-prevention-blueprint.def: End-of-treatment written plan summarizing what was learned, helpful skills, early warning signs, likely high-risk situations, and steps to take after setbacks.
iv.relapse-prevention-blueprint.cw: A written plan to keep your progress going and handle setbacks after therapy ends.
iv.relapse-prevention-blueprint.ex: The blueprint lists warning signs (skipping meals, withdrawing) and first steps (schedule activities, call sister).

iv.booster-sessions.def: Scheduled sessions after the main course of therapy to review progress, consolidate skills and address early signs of relapse.
iv.booster-sessions.cw: Check-in sessions after therapy ends, to keep your progress on track.
iv.booster-sessions.ex: Sessions at one, three and six months review the blueprint and a recent setback.

iv.exposure-and-response-prevention.def: Graded exposure to obsessional triggers while refraining from compulsions, neutralizing and reassurance seeking, so fear and urges reduce without rituals.
iv.exposure-and-response-prevention.cw: Facing the things that set off obsessions, step by step, without doing the rituals.
iv.exposure-and-response-prevention.ex: The client touches a door handle and eats a snack without washing, sitting with the urge.

iv.video-feedback.def: Client predicts how they came across, then watches video of their social performance as an observer would, to correct a distorted self-image.
iv.video-feedback.cw: Watching a video of yourself to compare how you felt you looked with how you actually came across.
iv.video-feedback.ex: Predicted "I'll look shaking and red" (80%); on video the client rates visible anxiety at 20%.

iv.cognitive-processing-therapy.def: Twelve-session trauma-focused therapy that identifies and challenges stuck points about the trauma and its implications using Socratic dialogue and structured worksheets.
iv.cognitive-processing-therapy.cw: A structured therapy that helps you rethink unhelpful beliefs about the trauma and what it means.
iv.cognitive-processing-therapy.ex: The client's impact statement reveals "It was my fault for going out," the first stuck point targeted.

iv.stuck-point-challenging.def: In CPT, identifying stuck points (beliefs that keep recovery stuck) and examining them with exploring questions, thinking patterns and alternative thoughts worksheets.
iv.stuck-point-challenging.cw: Spotting beliefs about the trauma that keep you stuck, and examining them step by step.
iv.stuck-point-challenging.ex: "I should have stopped it" is examined against what the client knew and could do at the time.

iv.prolonged-exposure.def: Trauma-focused protocol combining psychoeducation, breathing retraining, in vivo exposure to avoided safe cues, and repeated imaginal revisiting of the memory with processing.
iv.prolonged-exposure.cw: Gradually facing trauma memories and avoided safe situations so they lose their power.
iv.prolonged-exposure.ex: The client recounts the assault in session each week and practices visiting avoided shops between sessions.

iv.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.def: Modifies excessively negative appraisals, updates trauma memory hot spots, discriminates triggers (then versus now), and drops maintaining behaviors and cognitive strategies.
iv.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.cw: A therapy that updates the trauma memory and helps you see that the danger is in the past.
iv.cognitive-therapy-for-ptsd.ex: The hot spot "I'm going to die" is updated with "I survived and the doctors said I recovered fully."

iv.cbt-for-insomnia.def: Multicomponent insomnia treatment combining sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy for sleep-related beliefs, sleep hygiene education and often relaxation.
iv.cbt-for-insomnia.cw: A structured program that resets your sleep habits and the worries that keep you awake.
iv.cbt-for-insomnia.ex: Over six sessions the client keeps a sleep diary, restricts time in bed, and reworks fears about tiredness.

iv.sleep-restriction.def: Limiting time in bed to average actual sleep time from diaries, then adjusting it weekly by sleep efficiency, to strengthen sleep drive.
iv.sleep-restriction.cw: Spending less time in bed for a while, so the sleep you get becomes deeper and steadier.
iv.sleep-restriction.ex: Diary shows 5.5 hours sleep in 9 hours in bed; the sleep window is set at 5.5 hours, then widened.

iv.stimulus-control.def: Re-associating bed with sleep: bed only for sleep and sex, leave bed when unable to sleep, fixed rise time, and no daytime napping.
iv.stimulus-control.cw: Retraining your body to link bed with sleep, not with lying awake.
iv.stimulus-control.ex: After about 20 minutes awake, the client gets up, reads in another room, and returns when sleepy.

iv.sleep-hygiene-education.def: Education about lifestyle and environmental factors affecting sleep, such as caffeine, alcohol, light and exercise; not recommended as a stand-alone insomnia treatment.
iv.sleep-hygiene-education.cw: Tips on habits and surroundings that help or harm sleep.
iv.sleep-hygiene-education.ex: The client moves the last coffee to before noon and removes the phone from the bedroom.

iv.cbt-e.def: Fairburn's transdiagnostic, personalized eating disorder treatment in four stages targeting maintaining processes; usually 20 sessions, about 40 if underweight.
iv.cbt-e.cw: A structured therapy that targets the habits and concerns keeping the eating problem going.
iv.cbt-e.ex: Stage one establishes self-monitoring, weekly weighing and regular eating before shape concern is addressed.

iv.collaborative-weighing.def: Therapist and client weigh the client once weekly in session, plotting and interpreting the trend, replacing frequent self-weighing or weight avoidance.
iv.collaborative-weighing.cw: Checking your weight together once a week and looking at the overall trend, not single numbers.
iv.collaborative-weighing.ex: The client stops weighing daily; the weekly chart shows weight stable despite regular eating.

iv.regular-eating.def: Establishing three planned meals and two or three planned snacks daily, without long gaps, to displace binge eating and dietary restriction.
iv.regular-eating.cw: Eating at planned, regular times through the day, to break the diet and binge cycle.
iv.regular-eating.ex: Meals at 8, 1 and 6, snacks at 11, 4 and 9; binges fall from five to one a week.

iv.addressing-shape-concern.def: Mapping overevaluation of shape and weight, developing other life domains, and reducing body checking, comparison and avoidance that maintain shape concern.
iv.addressing-shape-concern.cw: Reducing how much your body shape and weight decide how you feel about yourself.
iv.addressing-shape-concern.ex: The client's self-evaluation pie is 70% shape and weight; they cut mirror checking and restart choir.

iv.behavioral-parent-training.def: Teaching caregivers to use specific praise, positive attention, clear instructions, consistent consequences and reward systems to improve child behavior.
iv.behavioral-parent-training.cw: Learning practical parenting skills that make good behavior more likely and conflict less likely.
iv.behavioral-parent-training.ex: Parents use a sticker chart for getting ready on time and praise each step within seconds.

iv.organization-and-planning-skills.def: Adult ADHD modules: one calendar and task list, prioritizing, breaking tasks into steps, matching work chunks to attention span, and distractibility delay.
iv.organization-and-planning-skills.cw: Practical systems for planning, organizing and staying on task that suit how your attention works.
iv.organization-and-planning-skills.ex: The client writes ideas on a distractibility pad and returns to them only after a 20-minute work block.

iv.safety-planning.def: Collaboratively writing a prioritized plan: warning signs, internal coping, social distraction, people to ask for help, professional and crisis contacts, and making the environment safer.
iv.safety-planning.cw: A written step-by-step plan for keeping yourself safe if suicidal thoughts get strong.
iv.safety-planning.ex: The plan ends with calling or texting 988 and agreeing who will store medications safely for now.

iv.habit-reversal-training.def: Awareness training, a competing response physically incompatible with the habit, and social support, used for tics and body-focused repetitive behaviors.
iv.habit-reversal-training.cw: Learning to notice a habit early and do something else with your hands instead.
iv.habit-reversal-training.ex: When the urge to pull hair arises, the client clenches fists for one minute and records it.

iv.contingency-management.def: Providing tangible incentives, such as vouchers or prize draws, contingent on objectively verified target behaviors such as negative drug tests or attendance.
iv.contingency-management.cw: Earning rewards for reaching specific goals, such as clean test results.
iv.contingency-management.ex: Each drug-negative urine test earns a voucher whose value rises with consecutive negative tests.

iv.high-risk-situation-coping.def: Identifying personal high-risk situations for substance use and rehearsing coping responses, including handling lapses to limit the abstinence violation effect.
iv.high-risk-situation-coping.cw: Planning how to handle the situations most likely to lead you back to using.
iv.high-risk-situation-coping.ex: The client rehearses refusing a drink at a work party and plans what to do if a lapse happens.

iv.normalizing-rationale.def: Presenting unusual experiences as understandable and on a continuum with common experience, for example under stress or sleep loss, to reduce distress and stigma.
iv.normalizing-rationale.cw: Understanding that unusual experiences can happen to many people, especially under stress or without sleep.
iv.normalizing-rationale.ex: "Many people hear voices after long sleep deprivation. Could stress and poor sleep be part of this?"

iv.early-warning-signs-plan.def: Identifying the client's personal early signs of mania or depression and agreeing specific early action steps, often with family and prescriber.
iv.early-warning-signs-plan.cw: Spotting your own early signs that a mood episode may be starting, and agreeing what to do.
iv.early-warning-signs-plan.ex: Signs: sleeping under five hours, starting many projects; actions: protect sleep and call the prescriber.

iv.trap-analysis.def: Mapping one recent episode as trigger, emotional response and avoidance pattern, including avoidant thoughts, to show how short-term relief maintains avoidance.
iv.trap-analysis.cw: Breaking down a time I avoided something: what set it off, how I felt, what I did.
iv.trap-analysis.ex: Trigger: big project. Response: overwhelmed. Avoidance pattern: "I work best at the last minute," then sorts email instead.

iv.trac-plan.def: Planning an active coping step for the same trigger and response that usually lead to avoidance, then trying it and reviewing the result.
iv.trac-plan.cw: Planning what I'll do instead next time the same trigger and feeling show up.
iv.trac-plan.ex: Same trigger and overwhelm; alternative coping: break the project into a 15-minute first step and start it.

iv.implementation-intentions.def: Linking a specific cue to a planned action in an if-then statement, so the action starts when the cue occurs instead of relying on willpower.
iv.implementation-intentions.cw: Deciding ahead: if this happens, then I will do that.
iv.implementation-intentions.ex: "When I notice the thought 'I'll just do it later,' I will work on the task for ten minutes."

iv.solution-analysis.def: After a chain analysis, choosing a skill or change for each link, vulnerability and prompting event, plus ways to repair consequences.
iv.solution-analysis.cw: Working out what I could do differently at each step, and how to put things right.
iv.solution-analysis.ex: Vulnerability: no sleep, so plan bedtime; link "I can't stand this": use a distress tolerance skill.

iv.crisis-response-plan.def: A brief, collaboratively written card listing personal warning signs, self-management steps, reasons for living, social supports and crisis contacts for suicidal crises.
iv.crisis-response-plan.cw: A pocket card we write together listing what I'll do and who I'll contact in a crisis.
iv.crisis-response-plan.ex: Card: warning signs, take a walk, look at photos of my kids, text my brother, call or text 988.

iv.activity-pacing.def: Breaking activities into planned, time- or quota-limited portions with breaks, regardless of pain level, to avoid overactivity and underactivity cycles.
iv.activity-pacing.cw: Doing activities in planned chunks with breaks, on good days and bad, instead of overdoing or stopping.
iv.activity-pacing.ex: Gardens for 20 minutes, rests for 10, then 20 more, even though pain is low today.

iv.graded-exposure-to-movement.def: Exposure to a hierarchy of activities the client fears will cause pain or harm, to test those predictions and reduce pain-related fear.
iv.graded-exposure-to-movement.cw: Gradually doing movements I've feared would hurt or damage me, to find out what really happens.
iv.graded-exposure-to-movement.ex: Bending to lift a light box after predicting "my back will give way."

iv.grief-exposure.def: Guided, repeated confrontation with memories of the death and avoided loss reminders, to integrate the loss and reduce avoidance in prolonged grief.
iv.grief-exposure.cw: Gently facing memories and reminders of the death I've been avoiding, so the loss can settle.
iv.grief-exposure.ex: Retelling the day of the death in session, then visiting the grave for the first time.

mp.avoidance-cycle.def: Avoiding or escaping feared situations brings short-term relief that negatively reinforces avoidance and prevents learning that the feared outcome is unlikely or manageable.
mp.avoidance-cycle.cw: Staying away from what scares you feels better now, but keeps the fear going.
mp.avoidance-cycle.ex: Skips the team meeting, feels relief, and finds the next meeting even harder to face.

mp.procrastination-cycle.def: Putting off difficult or boring tasks brings brief relief, but tasks pile up, setbacks confirm negative beliefs, and avoidance grows.
mp.procrastination-cycle.cw: Putting things off feels easier today, but the pile grows and I feel worse about myself.
mp.procrastination-cycle.ex: Leaves a tax form unopened for weeks, then thinks "I'm hopeless with paperwork" and avoids it more.

mp.safety-behavior-cycle.def: Actions taken in a feared situation to prevent a feared outcome; the non-occurrence is credited to the behavior, so threat beliefs are never disconfirmed.
mp.safety-behavior-cycle.cw: The things I do to stay safe stop me finding out I'd have been okay anyway.
mp.safety-behavior-cycle.ex: Grips a shopping cart so as not to faint, then thinks "I'd have collapsed if I hadn't held on."

mp.reassurance-cycle.def: Repeatedly seeking reassurance from others, online searches, or doctors lowers anxiety briefly, then doubt returns stronger, maintaining preoccupation and straining relationships.
mp.reassurance-cycle.cw: Asking "are you sure?" calms me for a moment, then the doubt comes back worse.
mp.reassurance-cycle.ex: Asks their partner several times a day whether a mole looks cancerous and searches symptoms online at night.

mp.experiential-avoidance.def: Unwillingness to stay in contact with unwanted thoughts, feelings, sensations, or memories, with efforts to change or escape them even when this causes harm.
mp.experiential-avoidance.cw: Doing almost anything to not feel or think something painful, even when it costs me.
mp.experiential-avoidance.ex: Drinks every evening to numb sadness after a breakup and avoids photos, songs, and conversations that bring it up.

mp.rumination.def: Repetitive, passive dwelling on one's distress, its causes, meanings, and consequences, without moving to problem solving; deepens and prolongs low mood.
mp.rumination.cw: Going over and over why I feel bad and what's wrong with me, without getting anywhere.
mp.rumination.ex: Lies awake for two hours replaying "Why do I always mess things up? What's wrong with me?"

mp.worry.def: A chain of negative, relatively uncontrollable thoughts about possible future threats, an attempt at mental problem solving that rarely reaches a resolution.
mp.worry.cw: My mind jumps from one "what if" to the next and I can't switch it off.
mp.worry.ex: "What if I lose my job? Then we can't pay rent, then the kids..." running through the whole commute.

mp.worry-about-worry.def: Negative appraisal of one's own worrying as uncontrollable or dangerous, which raises anxiety and drives unhelpful attempts to control or avoid worry.
mp.worry-about-worry.cw: Worrying that my worrying is out of control or will make me ill or crazy.
mp.worry-about-worry.ex: "If I can't stop worrying I'll have a breakdown," so tries to push worries away, and they keep coming back.

mp.anticipatory-processing.def: Detailed rehearsal before a feared social event of likely failures and negative self-images, which raises anxiety, primes self-focus, and often prompts avoidance.
mp.anticipatory-processing.cw: Going over everything that could go wrong for days before something I'm dreading.
mp.anticipatory-processing.ex: Spends the week before a wedding toast imagining going red and forgetting the words.

mp.post-event-processing.def: Detailed, self-focused review after a social event that dwells on perceived failures and negative self-impressions, strengthening beliefs of social inadequacy.
mp.post-event-processing.cw: Replaying a conversation afterward and picking apart everything I think I did wrong.
mp.post-event-processing.ex: After a dinner party, replays for hours how awkward they sounded and concludes everyone found them boring.

mp.self-focused-attention.def: Attention shifts inward to anxious sensations, behavior, and a distorted self-image, used as evidence of how one appears while external cues are missed.
mp.self-focused-attention.cw: Being so focused on how I'm coming across that I miss what's actually happening.
mp.self-focused-attention.ex: During a meeting, pictures their own red face and shaky voice and doesn't notice colleagues nodding.

mp.threat-monitoring.def: Preferential, often automatic, attention to threat-related cues in the environment and repeated scanning for danger, which inflates perceived threat and sustains anxiety.
mp.threat-monitoring.cw: Always on the lookout for danger, so I notice every possible threat around me.
mp.threat-monitoring.ex: After an assault, constantly checks faces and exits in every room and notices every raised voice.

mp.body-focused-monitoring.def: Repeated attention to and checking of bodily sensations, which makes normal sensations more noticeable and supplies apparent evidence of illness or danger.
mp.body-focused-monitoring.cw: Keeping a close eye on my body, so I notice every twinge and worry about it.
mp.body-focused-monitoring.ex: Takes their pulse several times an hour and prods a sore lymph node each morning.

mp.interpretation-bias.def: A habitual tendency to resolve ambiguous situations, sensations, or social cues in a negative or threatening direction.
mp.interpretation-bias.cw: When something could mean several things, I tend to read it the worst way.
mp.interpretation-bias.ex: A friend doesn't reply for an hour and the immediate reading is "She's annoyed with me."

mp.memory-bias.def: Selective recall of negative or threat-related information, and overgeneral rather than specific memories, which keep negative views of self and world feeling true.
mp.memory-bias.cw: The bad memories come easily and the good ones are hard to reach.
mp.memory-bias.ex: Asked about a happy time, can only say "I've never really been happy," but recalls failures in detail.

mp.belief-confirming-processing.def: Information fitting a core belief is noticed and remembered, while contradicting information is ignored, discounted, or distorted, so the belief survives contrary evidence.
mp.belief-confirming-processing.cw: I notice everything that fits how I see myself and brush off anything that doesn't.
mp.belief-confirming-processing.ex: Believes "I'm unlikable," dismisses three invitations as pity, but treats one unanswered text as proof.

mp.hasty-data-gathering.def: Reaching firm conclusions on little evidence and gathering less information before deciding; linked to the formation and persistence of delusional beliefs.
mp.hasty-data-gathering.cw: Making up my mind very quickly, before I've checked all the facts.
mp.hasty-data-gathering.ex: Hears neighbors laugh once and becomes certain they are plotting against them, without seeking other explanations.

mp.thought-suppression.g: Thought control and appraisal of intrusions
mp.thought-suppression.def: Deliberately trying to push unwanted thoughts out of mind, which often produces rebound, more frequent intrusions, and a sense that thoughts are out of control.
mp.thought-suppression.cw: Trying hard not to think about something, which makes it pop up even more.
mp.thought-suppression.ex: Tells themself "Don't think about harming anyone" and the image returns dozens of times that day.

mp.misinterpretation-of-intrusions.g: Thought control and appraisal of intrusions
mp.misinterpretation-of-intrusions.def: Normal unwanted thoughts, images, or urges are read as significant, revealing, or dangerous, which turns ordinary intrusions into persistent, distressing obsessions.
mp.misinterpretation-of-intrusions.cw: Taking a random nasty thought as a sign of who I really am or what might happen.
mp.misinterpretation-of-intrusions.ex: "Having this thought about harming my baby means I'm secretly dangerous."

mp.intolerance-of-uncertainty.def: A tendency to find uncertainty unacceptable and threatening regardless of likely outcome, driving worry, checking, reassurance seeking, and avoidance of ambiguous situations.
mp.intolerance-of-uncertainty.cw: Not knowing for sure feels unbearable, even when the bad outcome is unlikely.
mp.intolerance-of-uncertainty.ex: Can't settle until routine test results arrive and plans for every possible outcome in the meantime.

mp.clinical-perfectionism.def: Self-worth depends heavily on pursuing demanding self-imposed standards despite adverse consequences; performance is judged all-or-nothing and standards rise when met.
mp.clinical-perfectionism.cw: Feeling only as good as my last performance, and it's never quite good enough.
mp.clinical-perfectionism.ex: Rewrites a report until 3 a.m., calls the A-minus a failure, and sets a higher target next time.

mp.catastrophic-misinterpretation-of-bod.def: Normal or anxiety-related bodily sensations are read as signs of imminent disaster (panic) or serious illness (health anxiety), increasing anxiety and the sensations themselves.
mp.catastrophic-misinterpretation-of-bod.cw: Taking normal body feelings, like a racing heart, as a sign something terrible is happening.
mp.catastrophic-misinterpretation-of-bod.ex: Notices palpitations after climbing stairs and thinks "I'm having a heart attack," so the heart races faster.

mp.negative-appraisal-of-trauma.def: Excessively negative meanings given to the trauma or its consequences (symptoms, others' reactions, life changes), producing a sense of serious current threat.
mp.negative-appraisal-of-trauma.cw: What happened, and how I've reacted since, seems to mean I'm damaged or still in danger.
mp.negative-appraisal-of-trauma.ex: "It happened because I'm weak," and "These flashbacks mean I'm going mad."

mp.disjointed-trauma-memory.def: Trauma memory is poorly elaborated and contextualized, with strong perceptual priming, so reminders trigger intrusive reexperiencing with a here-and-now quality.
mp.disjointed-trauma-memory.cw: Memories of what happened come back in pieces and feel like it's happening all over again.
mp.disjointed-trauma-memory.ex: The smell of gasoline brings back the crash so vividly they duck, without knowing why they feel scared.

mp.dietary-restraint-cycle.def: Rigid dietary rules and restriction lead to rule breaks and binge eating; compensatory purging or further restriction follows, which in turn invites more binges.
mp.dietary-restraint-cycle.cw: Strict dieting makes me more likely to binge, then I cut back harder, and it repeats.
mp.dietary-restraint-cycle.ex: Eats nothing until evening, breaks a "no bread" rule, thinks "I've blown it," binges, then skips breakfast.

mp.mood-intolerance.def: Difficulty tolerating intense mood states, managed with behaviors such as bingeing, vomiting, exercising, or self-harm that relieve emotion briefly and maintain the eating disorder.
mp.mood-intolerance.cw: Strong feelings feel unbearable, so I use food, purging, or exercise to shut them off.
mp.mood-intolerance.ex: After an argument, binges and vomits to get rid of the tension, then feels calm for an hour.

mp.sleep-effort.def: Worry about sleep and its daytime effects, monitoring for signs of poor sleep, and deliberate effort to sleep raise arousal and inhibit automatic sleep onset.
mp.sleep-effort.cw: The harder I try to fall asleep, and the more I worry about it, the more awake I get.
mp.sleep-effort.ex: Checks the clock at 1 a.m.: "If I don't sleep now I'll fail tomorrow's presentation," and feels wide awake.

mp.conditioned-arousal.def: Repeated wakefulness, frustration, and activity in bed turn the bed and bedtime into cues for arousal rather than sleep.
mp.conditioned-arousal.cw: My bed has become a place where I lie awake, so I feel alert as soon as I get in.
mp.conditioned-arousal.ex: Nods off on the sofa, but feels wired the moment their head touches the pillow.

mp.sleep-compensation.def: Coping with poor sleep by spending more time in bed, napping, sleeping in, or keeping irregular schedules, which weakens sleep drive and fragments sleep.
mp.sleep-compensation.cw: Trying to catch up on sleep by going to bed early or napping, which backfires.
mp.sleep-compensation.ex: Goes to bed at 9 p.m. "to get more chances to sleep" and naps after lunch, then lies awake for hours.

mp.withdrawal-inactivity-loop.def: Low mood leads to withdrawal from activities and people; reduced reward and mounting problems deepen low mood, prompting further inactivity.
mp.withdrawal-inactivity-loop.cw: Feeling low makes me do less, and doing less makes me feel even lower.
mp.withdrawal-inactivity-loop.ex: Stops going to the gym and seeing friends, spends weekends in bed, and feels more worthless each week.

mp.self-criticism.def: A habitual hostile, condemning stance toward oneself after setbacks, which activates threat and shame and blocks self-soothing and recovery.
mp.self-criticism.cw: Talking to myself in a harsh, attacking way when things go wrong.
mp.self-criticism.ex: Drops a glass and thinks "You useless idiot, you ruin everything."

mp.emotion-dysregulation.def: Difficulty noticing, accepting, and modulating emotions, with high sensitivity, intense reactions, slow return to baseline, and impulsive or avoidant regulation attempts.
mp.emotion-dysregulation.cw: Feelings hit hard and fast, take a long time to settle, and push me to act rashly.
mp.emotion-dysregulation.ex: A brief criticism at work sparks rage within seconds, a slammed door, and hours of distress.

mp.interpersonal-cycle.def: Expectations about others prompt behavior that elicits responses confirming those expectations, so beliefs and relationship problems maintain each other.
mp.interpersonal-cycle.cw: Expecting people to reject me, I act in ways that end up pushing them away.
mp.interpersonal-cycle.ex: Expecting rejection, stays quiet and cool at a party; others drift away, "proving" nobody likes them.

mp.family-accommodation.def: Family members change their behavior to reduce a relative's distress, by joining rituals, giving reassurance, or enabling avoidance, which maintains anxiety or obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
mp.family-accommodation.cw: When family steps in to ease my anxiety, it helps today but keeps the problem going.
mp.family-accommodation.ex: A parent rewashes the child's clothes three times and answers "Are you sure it's clean?" twenty times.

mp.substance-relief-cycle.def: Using a substance relieves distress, craving, or withdrawal quickly, negatively reinforcing use, while consequences and withdrawal raise distress that cues further use.
mp.substance-relief-cycle.cw: Using takes the edge off fast, but the fallout makes me feel worse and want more.
mp.substance-relief-cycle.ex: Drinks to calm social nerves, wakes anxious and hungover, and drinks again by afternoon to settle.

mp.abstinence-violation-effect.def: After a lapse, self-blame, guilt, and a sense of lost control lead the person to abandon the goal, turning a single lapse into full relapse.
mp.abstinence-violation-effect.cw: One slip makes me feel I've blown it completely, so I give up and keep going.
mp.abstinence-violation-effect.ex: Has one drink after 60 days sober, thinks "I'm a failure, I've ruined it," and drinks all weekend.

mp.extreme-appraisals-of-internal-states.def: Changes in energy, mood, or arousal are given extreme personal meanings (success, catastrophe), prompting ascent or descent behaviors that escalate mood swings.
mp.extreme-appraisals-of-internal-states.cw: When my energy shifts, I read it as huge news, and how I respond makes swings bigger.
mp.extreme-appraisals-of-internal-states.ex: Feeling energized at 2 a.m., thinks "This is my genius coming through," skips sleep, and starts three projects.

mp.pain-catastrophizing.def: An exaggerated negative mental set toward actual or expected pain: ruminating on it, magnifying its threat and feeling helpless to manage it.
mp.pain-catastrophizing.cw: Getting stuck on the pain, expecting the worst from it and feeling unable to cope.
mp.pain-catastrophizing.ex: "This pain is terrible and it's never going to get any better."

mp.fear-avoidance-cycle.def: Pain read as threatening breeds pain-related fear, avoidance and hypervigilance, leading to disuse, low mood and disability that maintain pain.
mp.fear-avoidance-cycle.cw: Fear of pain makes me avoid moving, which leaves me weaker, lower and in more pain.
mp.fear-avoidance-cycle.ex: After a back twinge, stops walking and lifting, loses fitness, and every movement hurts more.

mp.activity-cycling.def: Overdoing activity when pain is lower, then resting for long periods after the resulting flare, so activity and pain swing widely.
mp.activity-cycling.cw: On good days I overdo it, then pay for it with days stuck resting.
mp.activity-cycling.ex: Cleans the whole house on a good day, then spends two days in bed.

mp.poor-loss-integration.def: The loss is not integrated into autobiographical memory and self-knowledge, so it feels unreal and reminders trigger intense, intrusive grief.
mp.poor-loss-integration.cw: Part of me still can't take in that they're gone, so reminders hit hard.
mp.poor-loss-integration.ex: Two years on, still expects her husband to walk through the door each evening.

mp.anxious-avoidance-of-loss.def: Avoiding reminders, thoughts and feelings about the loss, often from fear of being overwhelmed, which blocks integration and keeps grief intense.
mp.anxious-avoidance-of-loss.cw: Steering clear of anything about the death, because facing it feels too dangerous.
mp.anxious-avoidance-of-loss.ex: Keeps the bedroom door shut and never says his name.

mp.depressive-avoidance-after-loss.def: Withdrawing from activities, relationships and plans that could foster adjustment, often from beliefs that life is meaningless without the deceased.
mp.depressive-avoidance-after-loss.cw: Giving up on people and things I used to do, because nothing seems worth it now.
mp.depressive-avoidance-after-loss.ex: Stops seeing friends and quits the choir because "there's no point without her."

ms.phq-9.def: Nine-item self-report of DSM depressive symptoms over the past two weeks, scored 0 to 27, with severity cutpoints at 5, 10, 15 and 20.
ms.phq-9.cw: A short questionnaire about how often depression symptoms have bothered you over the last two weeks.
ms.phq-9.ex: Score 14 (moderate); item 9 is endorsed, so suicide risk is assessed in the same session.

ms.phq-2.def: First two PHQ-9 items (depressed mood, loss of interest), scored 0 to 6; a score of 3 or more prompts fuller assessment.
ms.phq-2.cw: Two quick questions about low mood and loss of interest over the last two weeks.
ms.phq-2.ex: PHQ-2 score 4 at a primary care visit, so the full PHQ-9 is given.

ms.bdi-ii.def: Twenty-one-item self-report of depressive symptom severity over the past two weeks, each item 0 to 3, total 0 to 63.
ms.bdi-ii.cw: A questionnaire about depression symptoms over the last two weeks.
ms.bdi-ii.ex: Intake score in the moderate range falls to the minimal range by session 14.

ms.qids-sr16.def: Sixteen-item self-report covering the nine DSM depression domains over the past seven days; highest item per domain is summed, total 0 to 27.
ms.qids-sr16.cw: A questionnaire about depression symptoms over the past week.
ms.qids-sr16.ex: Total 16 (severe) at baseline; 5 (none) after treatment indicates remission.

ms.epds.def: Ten-item self-report screening for perinatal depression over the past seven days, total 0 to 30; includes one self-harm item.
ms.epds.cw: A short questionnaire about how you have felt over the past week, during or after pregnancy.
ms.epds.ex: Score 14 at six weeks postpartum, and the self-harm item is reviewed immediately.

ms.gad-7.def: Seven-item self-report of generalized anxiety symptoms over the past two weeks, scored 0 to 21, with cutpoints at 5, 10 and 15.
ms.gad-7.cw: A short questionnaire about how often anxiety and worry bothered you over the last two weeks.
ms.gad-7.ex: Score 12 (moderate) at intake; 10 or more prompts assessment for an anxiety disorder.

ms.gad-2.def: First two GAD-7 items (nervousness, uncontrollable worry), scored 0 to 6; a score of 3 or more prompts fuller assessment.
ms.gad-2.cw: Two quick questions about feeling nervous and being unable to stop worrying.
ms.gad-2.ex: GAD-2 score 3, so the full GAD-7 is completed.

ms.bai.def: Twenty-one-item self-report of anxiety symptom severity, weighted toward physical symptoms, each item 0 to 3, total 0 to 63.
ms.bai.cw: A questionnaire about anxiety symptoms, especially body symptoms, over the recent past.
ms.bai.ex: High somatic item scores support a panic-focused formulation.

ms.oasis.def: Five-item self-report of anxiety frequency, intensity, avoidance and work and social impairment across anxiety disorders over the past week, total 0 to 20.
ms.oasis.cw: Five questions about how often anxiety affects you and how much it gets in the way.
ms.oasis.ex: Used weekly across a mixed anxiety caseload to track overall change.

ms.pdss.def: Seven-item measure of panic disorder severity: attack frequency, distress, anticipatory anxiety, avoidance and impairment, each 0 to 4, total 0 to 28.
ms.pdss.cw: Seven questions about panic attacks, worry about them, avoidance and how they affect your life.
ms.pdss.ex: Weekly self-report scores fall from 16 to 5 over interoceptive exposure work.

ms.asi-3.def: Eighteen-item self-report of fear of anxiety-related sensations, with physical, cognitive and social concern subscales, each item 0 to 4.
ms.asi-3.cw: Questions about how frightening you find the feelings and signs of anxiety.
ms.asi-3.ex: High physical concerns subscale supports a panic formulation and interoceptive exposure.

ms.spin.def: Seventeen-item self-report of social anxiety over the past week covering fear, avoidance and physiological symptoms, each item 0 to 4, total 0 to 68.
ms.spin.cw: Questions about fear and avoidance of social situations and body symptoms over the past week.
ms.spin.ex: Score 42 at intake supports a social anxiety disorder assessment.

ms.lsas.def: Rates 24 social and performance situations separately for fear or anxiety and avoidance, each 0 to 3, giving subscale and total scores.
ms.lsas.cw: A list of social and performance situations rated for how anxious you feel and how much you avoid them.
ms.lsas.ex: Avoidance subscale highlights eating in public and speaking to authority figures as exposure targets.

ms.shai.def: Eighteen-item self-report of health anxiety: 14 items on illness worry and likelihood plus 4 on feared negative consequences, total 0 to 54.
ms.shai.cw: Questions about worry about your health and what being ill would mean for you.
ms.shai.ex: Score well above the clinical range with frequent body checking supports a health anxiety formulation.

ms.pswq.def: Sixteen-item self-report of trait worry, its excessiveness, pervasiveness and uncontrollability, each item 1 to 5, total 16 to 80.
ms.pswq.cw: Questions about how much you tend to worry and how hard it is to stop.
ms.pswq.ex: Score 68 supports pathological worry as a primary treatment target.

ms.ius-12.def: Twelve-item short form measuring reactions to uncertainty, with prospective and inhibitory anxiety factors, each item 1 to 5, total 12 to 60.
ms.ius-12.cw: Questions about how you react when things are uncertain or unpredictable.
ms.ius-12.ex: High inhibitory subscale suggests uncertainty leads to freezing and avoidance.

ms.hads.def: Fourteen-item self-report with seven anxiety and seven depression items, designed to limit overlap with physical illness symptoms.
ms.hads.cw: Short questions about anxiety and low mood, designed for people with physical health problems.
ms.hads.ex: Used in a cardiac rehabilitation service to screen for anxiety and depression.

ms.dass-21.def: Twenty-one-item short form of the DASS with seven-item depression, anxiety and stress scales over the past week; scores doubled to match DASS-42 norms.
ms.dass-21.cw: Questions about low mood, anxiety and stress over the past week.
ms.dass-21.ex: Stress subscale is elevated while depression is normal, guiding focus on tension and irritability.

ms.scared.def: Forty-one-item child and parent report of anxiety symptoms with five factors paralleling DSM anxiety disorders, each item 0 to 2.
ms.scared.cw: Questions for you or your parent about worries and fears.
ms.scared.ex: Separation anxiety subscale is elevated on both child and parent forms.

ms.rcads.def: Forty-seven-item youth or parent report with subscales for separation, social, generalized, panic and obsessive-compulsive anxiety and major depression.
ms.rcads.cw: Questions for you or your parent about worries, fears and low mood.
ms.rcads.ex: Major depression and social anxiety subscales are both elevated in a 14-year-old.

ms.scas.def: Forty-four-item child report (38 scored, 6 filler, each 0 to 3) with six anxiety subscales; parent and preschool versions exist.
ms.scas.cw: Questions for you or your parent about worries and fears.
ms.scas.ex: Separation anxiety subscale T-score above 60 on both child and parent forms.

ms.pcl-5.def: Twenty-item self-report of DSM-5 PTSD symptoms over the past month, each 0 to 4, total 0 to 80; a provisional cutpoint of 31 to 33.
ms.pcl-5.cw: Questions about how much trauma-related problems bothered you over the past month.
ms.pcl-5.ex: Score falls from 52 to 24, a drop of more than 10 points, indicating response.

ms.caps-5.def: Thirty-item structured clinical interview assessing the 20 DSM-5 PTSD symptoms, onset, duration, distress, impairment and dissociative subtype; 45 to 60 minutes.
ms.caps-5.cw: A structured interview about trauma-related symptoms and how they affect you.
ms.caps-5.ex: Used to confirm a PTSD diagnosis before starting trauma-focused therapy.

ms.itq.def: Eighteen-item self-report of ICD-11 PTSD and complex PTSD: six PTSD items, six disturbances in self-organization items, and six functional impairment items.
ms.itq.cw: Questions about trauma-related symptoms and difficulties with emotions, self-worth and relationships.
ms.itq.ex: Criteria met for complex PTSD, so the plan adds emotion regulation and relationship work.

ms.y-bocs.def: Clinician-rated interview with a symptom checklist and 10 severity items (five obsessions, five compulsions), each 0 to 4, total 0 to 40.
ms.y-bocs.cw: An interview about obsessions and compulsions and how much they affect your life.
ms.y-bocs.ex: Score falls from 26 to 12 over a course of ERP.
